It's is also a little chilly inside the tube (abt 8 degrees C) The place is also dim so some agility is needed to prevent slipping but it is generally safe. Just walk slowly. Overall it's an enjoyable experience as we marveled at the forces of nature that made the tube possible.

We went with my 63 year old mom, husband, and 15 and 6 year olds. It was great! It's waaaay longer, wider, taller and more interesting of a lava tube than at Volcanos national park in Hawaii! The largest accessible in the world. Bring a waterproof camera, hiking shoes or at least tennis goes, a raincoat or jacket. Won't wear white. I still can't get the ash stain out of my sons sleeve after he fell in a puddle. It's only a few dollars to get in. Do the quick museum first, if you want to know more about it. Cold, wet, dark, tired but Loved it!

Visited this place which is really a lava tube rather than a cave.  It is about 1 kilometer from end-to-end.  Inside the tube you can see different rock formations created by the lava flow, among them the turtle-shaped rock at 600-meter mark.  It is cool inside the tube and water is dripping everywhere.  It is recommended that you wear appropriate footwear while taking this tour as it could really be slippery and some areas are not so well-lit.  Maybe this is intentional to give the place a more realistic feel.

Too fascinating when seeing all the traits of massive lava flow in the cave, which is actually part of the lava tube. Must bring along a powerful torch if you want to enjoy from the ceiling to the ground. Relying just on the phone torch or the lights inside will hinder your enjoyment and appreciation of this natural masterpiece as you will be only focusing on your steps. Do walk the entire 1 km so you can see the big massive lava lumps which stretches from the ground to the ceiling. Water drippings and water patches are common, wear a cap and windbreaker will help. In fact the temperature inside is a few degrees lower than the outside

This place is for geography lovers. You get to learn about how lava tubes are formed centuries ago, the history of the volcanic eruptions, how the lava flowed, how the lava stalactites are formed, how the different rocks are formed etc. The cave is very wet, cold and dark as water is dripping from the stalactites. You will have the chance to walk for about 1-1.5km into the middle section of the tube, where you will be able to take picture in front of the famous Lava Column. After that, you will U turn and return to the entrance. The whole journey takes around 1-1.5 hrs. The paths consist of harden lavas and steps, a really authentic experience. You might want to bring along your torchlight if you want to see the rocks clearly.

This is quite an interesting place to visit. Do remember it's a long lava tube cave.Take note:1) Stairs to the cave can be steep.2) The floor of the cave is in its natural form. It's wet, slippery, jagged and uneven. There are large puddles everywhere so watch where you step.3) When we went, there isn't really any special colorful lighting in it. It was quite dim. We used our cellphone as our flashlight in some of the darker and very uneven floor areas.4) It's cold so wear some warm clothing. There may be water dripping from the ceiling as well. Overall we enjoyed the lava cave.

This is all about geology.... How lava tubes are formed during volcanic eruptions and the rock formations produced. It's something different from what most resort islands offer. A journey to the center of the earth.... cut short to about 1 km. Yes 1 km. So, if you aren't into walking for 1 km in and 1 km out, this is not the place for you. Especially so since the temperature drops significantly as you descend down the steps. It was the month of May, with outside temperatures ranging from 25-28 degrees Celsius, but as you walk into the cave, the chill can get to you. The ground is uneven and wet, with water dripping from the cave ceiling. Be prepared for all this.

One of the real highlights for my visit to Jeju Island. It's absolutely fascinating and I've been to a few different caves before. It's different because it's a lava tube cave and there are a few different information boards in there to explain the different features which helped to understand how it was formed. It's very well and cold in there so bring a wet jacket and comfortable walking shoes (waterproof/ resistant if possible) with good traction. There is a small descent but other than that it's rather flat in there so most people should be able to do it, just watch out for the wet surface. If you go to Jeju, you must visit this cave.

Jeolmul Natural Recreation Forest, walking through these wood is believed to enhance cardiovascular function and to prevent asthma and tuberculosis. This is the most famous forest on Jeju island and here you can taste mineral water that is thought to relieve muscle and gastrointestinal problem

Believed to be formed about 2,00,000 ? 3,00,000 years ago, this UNESCO protected heritage centre, the Manjjanggul Lava tube tunnels said to be one of the longest ( around 7.5 km) and well maintained Lava tube tunnels in the world. Though there would not be much to see around, the sheer excitement one experiences just walking into the dark ,rocky ,slippery tunnel is worth the money paid for.Important things to remember.-Those who are having difficulty in walking should avoid getting down the tunnel as the floor is rocky,slippery and uneven.-A good pair of shoes is a must. No high heeled footwear please.-Carry or wear warm clothes as the inside temperature would be much lower than outside.-Wearing a cap/hat would be also good as water would be dripping on your head as you walk.-The Tunnel is open for 1 KM for the Public and with minimal lighting. Carrying a low intensity torch would be best.

At the entrance of this huge garden layout is lush, green plants  there is a bonsai garden, herb gardens, an array of flowers, a subtropical garden, water garden and a stone display as you travel along a palm garden road. There is a fair amount of walking.This display of trees, plants and gardens is a wonderful experience although its the caves, limestone tube-shaped structures growing downward from the ceiling of the cave and stalagmites that grow from the floor up. Structures are formed  containing calcium-bicarbonate. Fossilized seashells, frozen lava, and numerous other structures which enhanced our walk through the caves.  Visit the stone exhibition hall, see the parrots and the various species of birds. A must see attraction.

Anyone who can appreciate nature, especially geology, will love this. There are only about 5 countries in the world where you can go walk in a lava tube and South Korea is one of them.It's inexpensive to enter (2000won for those over 24, discounts for younger ages) and it is worth it.There are lights installed, but bring lights if you can. The ground is not paved and it's easy to trip. The cave also drips water, so there are puddles around. It was suuuuuper cold inside the cave in March-so cold that when we came outside to the 40 degree weather it felt like summer!!

I have visited a number of limestone caves before and this is the first lava tube cave I ever visited. I found it fascinating. Be warned that the floor is undulating and wet and one needs a pair of hiking shoes and a rain jacket to really enjoy this place.

We travelled on a rare rainy day in Jeju, but June, our tour guide, made our trip happy and smooth with her professional arrangement, detailed introduction of the scenic spots, fluent English, sharing on Korean culture and her personal experience on how she feels about Jeju. I am particularly impressed by the guided tour she gave us in the Manjanggul Lava Tube, her intriguing story of haenyeo and their livelihood and our hiking experience at Seongsanilchul Pong. In as short as a day we have seen most of what lies in the northern and eastern coasts of Jeju Island, felt for ourselves the beauty of the natural landscapes and understood how inhabitants of this island have lived since the last century. It was an amazing travel experience and we give credits to June for the nice private tour.

The lava tube is different from other lime stone or erupted caves I seen before, this one is very big and the its formation and feature is fantastic.  Try to avoid the high crowd and prepare jacket, poncho and hiking shoes.  We took good camera and tripok to take picture.

My family (2 adults & a 10 year old) recently spent 3 days doing a combination of private and small group tours of UNESCO sites in Jeju Island with June of Core Travel. It was a great balance of energetic activities (hiking craters, exploring lava tubes), museums and cultural attractions, and relaxing activities such as a sampling session at a tea farm or DIY foot massage at a herb garden.
I enjoyed it more than the group.  It's geared for those who are used to hiking.  Long lava tube - you don't have to walk the whole thing, but why not?  It is just 1 KM in and 1 KM out.

Definitely a special cave. As it is a lava tube, the floor is also made of solid lava, aka uneven flooring. Bring good hiking boots as it takes at least 40 minutes to reach the end. Advice to use a tripod for good photos.

We decided to pop over to the maze park as we were visiting mangajul lava tubes. We were greeted by a ten to fifteen cats basking in the shade. It seems like the owner loves cats. That was a great treat for my cat loving family. The maze itself was great fun and especially if you are in a group. Not very difficult but not as easy. We could easily go around with a stroller though there are a few steps. Has a small cafeteria for icecream and coffee. Overall great fun.

Walking through a lava tube is an incredible experience. You can see the flow of lava on the ground, the different historical depths of lava flow is visible on the wall due to the layers of layers, and other features such as the world?s largest lava column and lava rafts. Truly remarkable and easy to see why UNESCO regards this sight so highly.

this is the largert lava tube in the world (well, that we have found) and it's fascinating.  Really huge tube, interesting rock formations all through.  The walk is quite easy (a little uneven and damp, headlight recommended) and the informative signs are useful.  Not that expensive and well worth the trip.

If you like caves, then you have to visit Manjunggul Cave. It is simply fascinating! It is an extremely cheap entry fee and an easy kilometer walk inside the lava tube. Though the weather outside was rainy and wet, we thought the cave would be drippy and wet as well. It was quite dry. The interior is spacious and equipped with fairly good lighting along the guided route. For kids learning about volcanoes and the structures of the earth, this is a great field trip.

We were taken to Manjanggul lava Cave as part of a day tour. I've never been in one before and this was pretty neat. Comfy shoes are a must. The feeling under your feet is a slippery one and one of many uneven ridges. The cave is dimly lit which does give it atmosphere but does pose problems if you are unsteady on your feet. The 1km tube takes about 25 mins to walk to the middle of where the volcano erupted. You can't go any further in. We thoroughly enjoy this fab experience and would highly recommend it. It is not suitable for people in wheelchairs or strollers. There are lots of information boards through out the lava tube giving you lots of nformation. The coloured lighting adds to highlight the different textures and forms of the rocks.

We learned a lots about how lava tube was formed and get to experience these natural phenomenon hands on. The kids thoroughly enjoyed the walk as well. Walking inside can be a bit tricky as it?s not flat and some part can be a wet and slippery. Overall a very educational trip for us.
Walking through the lava tubes is just an amazing experience.  It is surreal and beautiful to see what millennia of lava flow has created.  One of the best places to see on Jeju Island.
This was my first visit to a lava tube or cave.  It was a great little walk through a dark and amazing cave.
The lava tube is very interesting to walk around. It can get pretty chilly underground so prepare accordingly.
Really the Tubes are fascinating but a little redundant. Was a long walk in the dark for a six (6) year old BUT the park is well equipped w/ Toilets and a Local Resto & Taxi Cabs!!! Enjoy.

It was an amazing experience to visit this place. It's good that they only put on a few lights just so that we could really see how the various unique designs on the wall and the rocks look like. The tourist could somehow imagine walking through the lava tube in the dark. True nature artistry !

it was a hot summer day when our tour guide took us to this park. It has a very large variety of plants and bonsai. Some of the bonsai plants are more than 100 years old!! The most interesting bit in my opinion was going into the lava tubes which are like under ground caves with unusual rock formations. Wear comfortable shoes. Its not strenuous but best to be comfortable when walking.

An interesting outing to learn about volcanic activity and how the lava tube was formed. Not suitable for elderly visitors with the dim and uneven terrain. Many information board to explain unusual structures. Educational. Some wooden boardwalk in certain areas. The stairs at the entrance leading into the tube can be steep and slippery.
An experience not to be missed. Walking for 1km underground through a subterranean tunnel created thousands of years ago by molten lava. Where else can you see such amazing lava tubes?

Amazing one they have a lot of inhabitants and also nice aquashow. They implemented some nice solutions for example you can walk under the penguins aquarium and also seals can swim through all three levels in a giant tube) And of course the huge aquarium wit sharks. Cool place. Also there are places to eat for a reasonable price

입력주소: 제주 서귀포시 성산읍 섭지코지로 95 아쿠아플라넷 제주

review: Well worth the visit, especially if geology is your interest.Plenty of stairs in and out of the cave so not too advisable for elderly, or families with babies/ toddlers. (though i did bring both!) Being a lava tube, the flooring can be uneven and slippery within the cave so wear proper footwear.It will be cold and dimly lit down in the lava tube, so bring your sweaters if chill is a concern.The walk long to and fro the end, so be prepared.After the first half to the end, it can get boring for some especially the kids. That said it is still a unique experience for many.

We were very excited to visit Manjanggul Cave, and it did not disappoint.It is quite a large cave, and if you walk slowly and look around at the cave carefully, you can see the changes of the lava formation colours and shapes.Make sure you walk the entire length to check out the lava tube, I mean - when will you get another chance? Also make sure you wear comfortable shoes, as my recommendation of walking slowly is not just to check out the different sections, it also means you won't trip, as the ground is pretty uneven and the cave is quite dimly lit!

Visiting this caves/tubes you can walk trough the geology! A huge tunnel made by lava rivers 300 thousands years ago, now accessible and well explained. A lot of lava stalactites and stalagmites and huge lava stones felt down from the ceiling. It is unbelievable how   untouched   their rest through the millenni. Nice job by the administrators of the park. It costs only 2000 won.You can also enjoy a free car parking and a small restaurant.

Very cool trip and 2km walk underground in the lava tube. Largest in the world. It is dark, cool and damp. The walking surface is cooled lava, so I'd recommend appropriate footwear. The lighting is respectful for the nature of the cave and energy efficient. Plenty of photo opportunities, for the low entrance price I was very pleased!!I wouldn't recommend any strollers or children who are learning to walk unless you plan to carry them the entire cave visit.

Unlike other caves, this cave was a natural lava tube...worth experiencing, if you've never been to one.  However, there are a lot of steps to get down to the cave level, and the walk itself is not smooth...basically dried lava beds from thousands of years ago, uneven, yet well preserved.  There was sufficient lighting, but not bright enough for great pictures, so make sure your camera is capable of this.  Cave was cool and dark in most areas, and you may experience drips from stalactites above!

This was our first visit to a lava tube, and we enjoyed it very much. The lava tube cave is maintained in natural state. Hence the floor is uneven and you need to watch your step. It is also very wet and little cold in side. Apart from that the walk is very enlightening. We learned many new things about lava tubes.The lava column at the end of the cave is a must see and is the highlight of the whole walk.Must visit.

This is the longest lava tube in the world.  It's 7kms long and only 1km is open to the public.  It's rather spectacular to be in it, to appreciate the wonders of Nature.  For the cynics, you would probably ask yourself why you want to part with money to walk in almost darkness, through a wet and uneven surface, just to affirm yourself that you are visiting one of the UNESCO's accredited natural wonders of the world.  For me, it's a been there, done that experience.  Enough said!

This is one of the longest lava tubes in the world and a World Heritage Site. You are able to walk for about 1km and return. We enjoyed the walk, especially as it was so hot outside and nice and cool inside.

This is a seriously big lava tube. In fact, as lava tubes go I think it's one of the biggest. Definitely a whopper! The whole thing is almost 8km long, but the section open to the public is just 1km. You descend steps and walk along the dimly lit tube. There are some things to look at like lava 'rafts' (lumps of lava that have floated along) and lava stalactites (lumps of lava that have dripped from the ceiling) and at the end a lava column (where lava has poured in through a hole in the ceiling and formed a column). In short, it's lava-ly!

This is a most unusual feature on the North-East coast of the island of Jeju, South Korea. Although there are a few around the world, these tubes are some of the best preserved ones and it is a Unesco World Heritage site. It is also accredited as a Global Geopark.You can walk 1km of the tube at Manjanggul (there are over 7 km but not open to the public)- it is damp and dark so go prepared with shoes that won't slip and also have an extra layer. The temperature drops quickly: it was 28C outside when we visited in late September but only 15C inside. However, they are very 'manageable'.The caves are well-preserved and present themselves as a long tunnel which displays various features. Though it is dark and so difficult to take photos, you can clearly see the lava flowlines and the lava shelves whilst the floor is ropy lava. At various points along the walk, you are directed to other features such as lava columns and lava stalacmites. Only one entrance of the 3 existing ones is used by the public.Well worth a visit, and especially so if interested in geography/ geology.

One of the best UNESCO place. Worth it to come here and visit this place. We spent approximately 50minutes here included walking and taking photos. The addmission fees is ??2,000 per person still affordable for me and the rate still the same as we went here last year. The parking space were spacious with numerous parking units available for visitors. Gentle reminder, please be cautious on your steps as some of the areas are quite dark and jacket is a must to wear to enter this lava tube place.
nicely labelled signs to explain the lava tubereally awesome to see the marks left by nature it's about a slow walk of about an hr, wear good shoes and a jacket as it gets cold

Manjanggul Cave came to me as a surprise. To walk in a lava tube is an enchanting experience. There are steep stairs and long walk so be prepared. Don't bring heavy bags. Wear jacket because its cold inside the cave. Bring good camera. As you enter the cave, you will see the limestone that looks like lava flow (see picture attached). The path is dim that completes the enchanting atmosphere. By the end of the road, you can see the lava column.

Love Hallim Park! My expectation was a quick walk around an outdoor park, but it was so much more! Easily taking an entire day if you want it to, you can meander through under ground lava tubes, fruit orchards, small animal zoos, bonsai tree forests, etc.! Highly recommended.

I've never been in a lava tube before, but it was a lot like a cave. The formations inside are pretty interesting and the park does a good job lighting them colorfully. It was a nice walk. However, it is very touristy and if you've been to bigger caves in other parts of the world it's just cool, not extremely impressive.

Its definitely a worthwhile trip to make and just walking through the Lava Tube is quite an experience.  It is not everyday one has the opportunity to walk through and see the various formations, the caves formed, columns, the different textures formed, etc.One needs to be relatively fit to do the walk with comfortable shoes as the location tends to be wet. Elderly should have a walking stick which will help and carry a torchlight.  Its a few degrees lower underground.

It's a natural wonder.  Amazing how lava can create a tunnel as large as this. Must visit when in Jeju.  Wear a pair of walking shoes and an autumn jacket as temperature falls to around 15 inside the tube. It'll take you at least 30 minutes to walk 1km in and then another 30 minutes out.  So,  it's pretty chilly if you are without a jacket. Floor is wet therefore walk carefully & enjoy the unusual sights especially the walls & ceiling of the tube. Walk until the end as there's a lava column in there, the only one.
It will be a good place to visit for educational purposes. Nice to be walking in a lava tube. Not a must go attraction but if you have children, it will be good to bring them there.

It is interesting but not quite a must-see in Jeju. If you miss it, it is still no grave regret unless you love geology. An extremely long volcanic lava tube but due to the number of tourists, I believe the condition of the cave is not as well preserved as the caverns in Europe. Careful walking in the first 100 metres... can easily twist one's ankles.
If you have not experience going into a lava tube, you have to try Manjanggul Cave. A nice 30 mins walk inside the tube, and you will find a beautiful Manjang-gul at the end of the tube.

If you have an opportunity to visit these lava tubes, then make sure you do!   We have lava caves in New Zealand and I have seen the lava tubes on Hawaii, but these are giants in comparrison.  The grounds of Manjang Caves are well kept.From the carpark it is only a 3 or 4 minute walk along a concrete path to the entrance of the caves.   We were expecting big, but these caves are huge!There are a number of steps leading down into the mouth of the cave and then you are inside this amazing formation.   It was quite an eerie feeling as we ventured deeper and deeper inside the tube which measures approx 5meters wide and up to 10 meters high.   The temperature is quite pleasant inside the caves and it is a little damp.   Even though we all had good walking shoes on, we still had to be quite careful of where we walked on the uneven, slippery  floor.   It is true that there is not a lot of light inside the cave, but we felt that the dim lighting added to the atmosphere.   In hindsight, a torch might have been helpful.All in all, definitely well worth the visit and would highly recommend to all. I would recommend that this is probably not a safe place for the elderly and very young children.  My elderly parents waited for us at the main building where there was a restaurant, shop and toilets.

If you are interested in caves at all, this one is unique.  Easily accessible, this horizontal lava tube demonstrates the vocanic processes happening over 100,000 years ago.  Cool, wet and accessible with helpful descriptions in multiple languages and little anthropromorphizing of geological shapes.  A quick visit taught us a lot....and our 7 and 10 year old kids enjoyed the walk.  Modest fee.

I was excited to see the Manjanggul Lava Tubes up close and personal, but I was rather disappointed after my visit..The Caves were poorly lit and without using a flashlight, one can barely see the markings on the rocks. The ground is very uneven and understandably so. However, for older people, children and people prone to ankle injuries, the lighting does not allow one to see where one is walking and injury can can easily occur.

For those who are interested in geology as my family is, this is a fascinating, and not too difficult, walk through a lava tube created by the molten lava. Worth a visit and the entrance fee is extremely cheap. UNESCO heritage.

About 1 kilometer of the lava tube  is open to walk through. You descend a long staircase into the cave. You will be walking on the old lave flow, so the floor is uneven & pitted, and full of puddles. There is dim lighting, so you really need to bring your own flashlight to see where you are stepping. The wall are fairly smooth & rounded, you will only be seeing a few small formations. If you are a nature geek (like me) you will enjoy this. If you want  lots of stalactites & large formations, this is not for you.

A lava tube showing the flow of lava and various natural formation such as the lava shelves or columns. Inside the cave is chilly (around 11c when outside is around 25c), dark, wet and slippery. Bring your jacket and sturdy shoe for this visit. Heels is a definite no no. Forget about your camera (too dark for photo taking) and just enjoy the brisk walk. To and fro takes you around 45mins-1hr.

My family and I visited this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument cave on a late afternoon for 2 hours. There were not many visitors and we didn?t find any tour buses when we reached here.   Getting there & fees: Manjanggul Cave is located in the north western part of Jeju-do. To get (drive) to Manjanggul Cave, key in GPS coordinate 7834818. There is no parking fee at the huge car park. Entrance fee is 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.Manjanggul Cave Museum: Upon climbing up the stairs from the car park, you will reach the Museum and a cafeteria/restaurant on its right. You could go in and have a look at the interesting exhibits, including how the Manjanggul Cave was formed from the volcanic activities.Manjanggul Cave: To get to the underground Cave, we followed the sign-posts ? it?s within 5 minutes? walk from the Manjanggul Cave Museum. Trek the entire 1 km stretch that?s opened to public and you will end with a colourful lit lava column - created from the dripping of lava from a hole in the ceiling ? which at about 8 meters high, is the tallest lava column on Earth. Nevertheless, there are a few things you have to take note while you are in the Cave:(1) The entrance to the Manjanggul Cave is also the exit ? there?s no exit at the end of the 1 km trail, which means you are walking 2 km return (2) Make sure you bring and wear a jacket or sweater with you because it?s freezing cold and chilly inside the cave. (3) Wear a cap or the jacket or sweater can be waterproof because you get water ocassioanlly dripping from the cave top onto you (4) The surface (floor) of the Cave is full of solidified lava flow terrain (i.e. extremely uneven surface) and water puddles, so you have to wear a pair of good walking shoes and walk carefully. Hold on to the railings of the stairs.(5) You probably don?t need a torchlight because the Cave is illuminated just enough by ground lightings. Some parts of the cave even have colourful lights shining at the dome shaped ceiling (cupola) (6) If you would like to take photographs inside the cave, you would need a tripod and switch to manual mode for long exposure (I used 4 seconds to 10 seconds exposure on my digital SLR).   There are displays at certain parts of the cave in English explaining the geology of the cave and the formation of the interesting structures (e.g. stalactites). In particular, there?s one structure ? ?Stone Turtle? ? in which the shape looks like Jeju-do Island, and which you could reach in about 30 minutes of one-way walking as it?s about 400m from the entrance. Along the Manjanggul Cave wall, we saw varied patterns of lava flow lines, some are straight while some are wavy. Really interesting! I have been to over 10 limestone caves around the world, but this is my first visit in a lava tunnel cave or lava tube cave (and Asia?s longest lava tube cave for that matter). You have to experience being transported to another world in this ?out of this world? cave for yourself ? don?t miss it!

It's a mixed review.  The ticket price is 10,000KRW per adult and since other natural attractions are around 2,000KRW, this park should be well worth it.  Highs: The caves are really cool as well as the Bansai and Stone Garden. The park is easy to walk and has shops and toilets easily available.  Transportation is also easy as it's just the 702 bus from the Jeju Intercity Bus Terminal for 1 hour. Lows: The park is dated, like late 90s with its signage and information cards.  The bird exhibit, stone exhibit and flower garden are average at best.  While the park trail is easy to walk, you do walk through gift shops for the next exhibits (so a bit too tourist-y). Overall, it makes for a decent easy afternoon, especially with kids or elderly.  The park needs some updating to be worth the ticket price, but it is close to the beach (just 5 mins walking).

Back in the days of yore --  how far back, no one can be certain --  three demigods came forth from three holes in the ground located near the northern coast of an island to the south of Korea.  These three demigods lived as hunter-gatherers until a ship arrived bearing three princesses, domesticated farm animals and seeds for growing grain. The princesses married with the demigods, and the Tamna Kingdom was born. Today, we know Tamna, which ended in 1404 with the coming of the Joseon Kings -- Korea's last imperial dynasty -- as Jejudo or Jeju Island.  We know that beloved and mystical site as Samseonghyeol (  sam   means three in Korean). It is a special place and, particularly for history buffs, a   must-see   in Jeju.  The holes, which likely were once active thermal vents on this volcanic isle, are surrounded by a protective Stonehenge-like ring and a mini-forest/park of lush and majestic, mature trees and flowers.  It is quite pleasant, and on a warm summer's day, a cool respite from the city that has grown around it.  There's a small museum showing a film about the founding of Tamna.  The film is in Korean, but if you look at the exhibits there before watching the film, you will understand it much better.  It is not readily possible to actually photograph the holes unless you have a ladder, a drone, a long selfie stick or happen to be about 8 feet tall...this would be my one disappointment about the site.  But there is an official photo mounted nearby.  If you have the time, plan to spend 1-1.5 hours there, to take in the walking trails, museum, movie and various historic buildings.  You will also be greeted by some of the original 18th century dolhareubangs (protective   stone grandfathers  ) remaining on the island.  It's a good outing for singles, couples, friends and families.  Even young children can enjoy the birds, flowers, stones and many benches located throughout the park.  Admission is quite nominal...2,500 KRW adults, 1,700 teens; 1,000 children 7-12.

A great museum well set out, very informative. Theres a short film, in English or Korean. Then a self directed tour of museum. Exhibits are well laid out with English translations. I would love to have had a translation of the interviews with the Haenyeo   women of the sea  . There is also a Haenyeo trail from the museum, taking in some of the traditional places the women divers used including the Bulteoks. You would need quite a lot of time to do both museum, park, and trail.

While visiting a friend who works in Jeju my family drove around to visit places casually with a flexible schedule. We planned to visit the temple for half an hour but stayed more than an hour. The name of the temple means medical spring and the flowing water from a 3-dragon-head fountain next to the temple store tasted good and sweet. Although the temple was built for only around 20 years the buildings and layout followed the traditional design. The main building faces exact south that can view the sea. The bell tower is located in the east for sunrise and the drum tower is located in the west for sunset. The main building's first floor wooden windows are beautifully carved with inspiring stories covered by traditional white paper but not glass. There is a traditional Korean painting exhibition of Buddha of Compassion in the basement and it's gorgeous. The best part of our visit was that not many people around. We got the chance to enjoy the quietness and even used the mats inside the temple at the back of the first floor to meditate a short while. There are grapefruit trees in the yards along the way to bathroom.
We spent over 3 hours in the park and exhibition building.Gives you a perfect view on the history and evolution of mother earth. We really enjoyed and learned a lot.

We didn?셳 spend much time here which was a pity but in any case there were too many tourists. Would be a better experience when less crowded. The buildings are stylish and there is a nice view of the tea gardens. You can try the tea and they explain the tea making process. This was my second trip to this museum.  The beautifully made exhibits address much about the history and lifestyle of the diving ladies. One exhibit also compares the Korean divers to the Japanese divers.  The viewpoints from the museum are lovely

This site explains everything one needs to know about the island's historical past.  It has a long walkway leading one through outdoor exhibit areas each section with attendants who can give information.  There also was a traditional musical performance available to view.  It was chilly when we were there so we left earlier than desired but if we had known there was a cafe in which to warm up and perhaps have lunch we could have made a day of it.  One perk of going in February was that the crowds were very very small here and at other locations.

This is a fun place for the family !  To enjoy this place to the max you must not be shy about lying on the floor or doing funny expressions to pose to achieve the photo effect .  We had great fun as a family n have a good laugh as we review the photos taken.  There's also a outdoor sculpture park which we enjoyed doing funny pose with the sculpture ! There are several Alive Museums in Korea and Singapore.  Each features a series of themed scenes for trick-art photos.  You can pose as directed for each scene and create a funny memorable photoThis one is located in the Jungman Tourist Resort area on the southern side of Jeju Island.  We ended up going there on a rainy day when it was just too blustery to be on the beach.  Unfortunately everyone else had the same idea and it was too crowded.  We had to wait so long to take photos that we ended up not getting very many views for our memory book. I think we only took about a half-dozen.  It was so crowded in fact that it was even difficult to walk.  And it is a big place!  There are also interesting photo ops outside the building such as with various types of vehicles and statues.  I think the Alive Museums would offer a better service to visitors by following the system used by museums for special exhibits:  issue a limited number of tickets for a specific time period allowing one group to move through to a certain point before starting the next.  Really the best part about our visit is that we purchased a combo entrance ticket purchased there for 12000 Korean won  (about $10 USD) that allowed us to visit the nearby African Museum which was FANTASTIC and well worth the time spent there.  So if you go to the Alive Museum try to go early or pick a sunny day.  Or if you don't mind crowds and lots of jostling about it can be part of your rainy-day beach retreat.  Either way get the combo ticket!

The place is nice with exhibits of the tea culture and evolution. however the cafe is often crowded with visitors and finding a seat can be challenging. the exterior view is fantastic! visitors should also explore the area outside the museum!

review: In five visits to South Korea in four years I have not come across a museum palace or historical building I did not like.They are all well-maintained offer good information in Englishoften have multilingual guides and free tours and are free or cheap to get in.The Jeju National Museum is no exception. Our hotel was about 4km away and we walked to and from there seeing many interesting sights on the way and eating lot of local food.I am an unabashed fan of the curating skills of the Koreans; they do a very good job.Here they provided a great overview from prehistoric to modern times offering interesting exhibits and information.There was also a special exhibition on Canopus a star of great significance to the people who lived here.Entry is free. There are buses from the city and taxi fares are reasonable. We like eating so we need to walk.

If you`re a Zippo lover  this is a must visit spot. Museum locates in the ground floor of a modern seaside building with breathtaking pacific ocean view. There is 2 exhibition halls  one of those displays many special designed zippos in large size  and the other in fact is a zippo shop  you can see and buy different limited edition zippo there and many are designed by local designer.

I was not expecting a lot when I drove into the car park but I was very pleasantly surprised with it visit. It only cost 2000 won entry and I spent about 1.25 hours.Firstly the guide will set up the video for you and it is pretty gruesome with the brutality of war shown. Then you walk through the exhibition area which has good information about the tunnel system and how Jeju was included in Imperial Japan's last stand at the end of the Pacific War plus weapons and memorabilia. All with English explanations. Then you walk up the hill and go into the tunnel system. When you come out you can follow the less used path and go to the top of the hill for good views.  Lastly there is a tank you can climb into just before you leave. Absolutelyrecommended for all ages.

I took my girlfriend here as she absolutely loves all things aquatic  especially shells  and she loves to go diving. A highlight of this museum is that the owner/operator collected all the exhibits herself  from oceans all around the world  and the museum represents literally a lifetime of work and passion for the sea.Taking that into consideration  if you love to dive  and love the sea  this place is simply amazing  my girlfriend was absolutely in awe  snapping picture after picture and commenting on the rarity and difficulty of finding she'll after shell in such amazing condition. The museum was an interesting oddity for myself  and I understand the reviews saying you could go through the whole thin g in 20-30 minutes  but for someone who is truly amazed by seashells  and the sea in general  you could easily spend more than an hour here (we were there somewhere around 2 hours) If you love seashells  an absolute must see  my girlfriend visibly lit up from the minute we walked in   all the way till we were back to our hotel in ?쒖＜??if you're not passionate about the shells  it's still worth a look at only 6$ (6 000?? per person. Some truly amazing art  especially if you consider it all came from the mind  hands  and worldwide dives of one very cool lady.

I participated in an event focusing on renewable energy and green growth at this superb convention centre. It is modern with meeting rooms upstairs having amazing almost panoramic view of the Jeju coastline. It has large exhibition floor  with large conference rooms on the three floors  but also bilateral meetings rooms that are convenient and centrally located. The catering and banquets were simply exquisite with great Korean cuisine and the banquet room and service were just incredible. I found it very convenient place for participating and networking.

Fabulous collection of contemporary art. Interesting installations and sculptures. Worth visiting. Some important artists shown. I love that Sth Korea has really good contemporary art to view. There are also other exhibition spaces included in the ticket. Amazing really.

As the Chocolate Land is within 10 minutes??walk from the Teddy Bear Museum in the Jungmun Resort area ??just follow the direction on the sign-posts ??my family and I had no hesitation to visit it on a rainy Sunday.Getting there and fees: First and foremost  you have to note that Chocolate Land is different from Chocolate Museum. Chocolate Land is in the south central part of Jeju while Chocolate Museum is in the south west Jeju. We didn't need the GPS coordinate/code for Chocolate Land but it's 7381197 for anyone who's driving there directly. The entrance fee for adults is 3000 won and 2000 won for children. A voucher was given back for every purchased ticket which can be redeemed at the gift shop or the caf챕 or the Chocolate School.The Museum/Attraction: After going past the ticketing counter  you then turn right. The section on the left is a caf챕 and photograph/selfie stops of different types of Korean houses and benches with toy bears. There's even a figurine of Santa Claus in front of one house  which was interesting considering Christmas is still some 6 months away. The section on the right is the exhibits on the history of chocolates  with the words written only in Korean. We went down the stairways to the level below in which there's a Chocolate School which teaches chocolate making at 120 000 won with lessons starting every hour from 10am to 6pm (I think the children would be more interested than adults). We didn't go into the School; instead  we walked past M&M figurines and a Christmas tree (again interesting) and reached the chocolate shop where there are interesting exhibits of chocolates (behind glass) from America  Europe and Asia. The gift shop has an extensive selection of chocolates (I think slightly more than outside). The prices of the Jeju chocolates of the same brand at the gift shop were slightly more expensive compared to those selling outside Chocolate Land. However  the Chocolate Land chocolates became slightly cheaper than those outside when we utilised the discount vouchers. Unique local Jeju chocolates are those with pink cactus flowers  mandarin oranges and hallabong fillings. We couldn't wait till Christmas?쫤e ate some of the chocolates before we left Jeju  and these were yummy!There is a small observation area (Chocolate Garden) outside the building where the view looks towards the sea. There's also a statue of Willy Wonka from the 1971 movie ?쁗illy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory??where you could take a photograph and selfie with. But we couldn't go outside because it's raining.I recommend visiting the Chocolate Land if you have the time and if you have an appreciation of chocolates. Otherwise  I think you wouldn't miss much if you decide to skip it.

A great place to start off is the Women Divers exhibition center to see the old photos and explanation from the staff on the history of Women Divers. Than a slow walk up the peak for a great view ....  the wind was hallowing when we climb up and the local told us its a normal day ...   plenty of great eateries just a short walk from the entrance after the climb . A MUST visit .

The server here spoke English and was really nice even helping people take photos at the cave   photo spot.   We enjoyed the small tea museum too but would have appreciated translations for the exhibits. Overall a fun couple of hours.

review: We love the story around the Innisfree Jeju House. It's organic and farm to table supply chain and mission is admirable. We had the the diver's special bento and it was delicious. My wife had the blue colored tea ade and I had fresh carrot juice and all of it was great. The have beautiful cakes in the shape of Halla mountain and tiramisu with delicate flower designs. The prices are in the higher end but well worth the refined quality and experience for those who like this sort of thing. My wife loved the purity of the food and calm views of the tea plantation.They also have products for sale as well as a tea extract exhibit. They have fun hands on tea soap making as well you can purchase and do there. Or they have other ones you can purchase and take home to do. Great place to calm down, re-energize, and enjoy.

We had only a metre of visibility when we went, it was cold, rainy and foggy. My review probably doesn’t do it justice, we were just super unlucky that day. Don’t visit on a rainy day. Very worthwhile museum to visit on Jeju.  Gives an in depth view into Haenyeo culture, female free divers who gather shell fish.  Since the culture of the Haenyeo is beginning to die out, the museum is an important way to keep the knowledge alive.  Movie and exhibits, with beautiful walks through the village and surrounding farm fields.

Unlike Hello Kitty, I think most of us have cuddled or have in possession a toy teddy bear at a certain stage of our lives. So it is no wonder that the Teddy Bear Museum has such a wide appeal and which surely be included as a ?compulsory? destination on the itinerary of the independent travellers (especially those with children) and tour companies alike.Getting there and fees: We visited Teddy Bear Museum (GPS coordinate/code 7387600) on a rainy day, which was appropriate since the exhibits are predominantly indoor, except for the Teddy Bear Garden and Park where there?re a few teddy bear figurines outside and a park with great views of the sea.  The admission charges are 10,000 won for adults won, 9,000 won for teens and 8,000 won for children.The Museum/Attraction:  This Teddy Bear Museum is the first and largest teddy bear museum in South Korea. Once you enter, you are greeted by this huge teddy bear, who gives you a ?grand? welcome to further explore the five sections spread over 3 levels: The History Hall, The Art Hall and The Project Exhibition Hall, Gift Shop (all indoors) and an outdoor Teddy Bear Garden and Park. There?s also a caf챕/restaurant. Be prepared to spend at least 1 hour looking and taking photographs/selfies at all the interesting exhibits. The History Hall comprised of the history of bear manufacturing and some of the earliest toy bears, many of which are antique and rare. It also showcases milestones in human history, with the bears enacting several famous (human) historical scenes from different eras. This is indeed a refreshing concept for a museum! I particularly liked the teddy bears enacting the Titanic, landings on the moon and the iconic celebrities like the Beatles and Gandhi.In the Art Hall, you could see the world-famous artworks and designs in an art gallery form as well as animation characters beloved by children. I liked the Mona Lisa and two of the most expensive bears in the world - the Louis Vuitton teddy bear and the Diamond Bear. In the Project Exhibition Hall, you would meet teddy bears grouped to suit the theme of each exhibition. Not forgetting the large Gift Shop on the first level. While it offers plenty of gifts, these are nonetheless pricey. Nevertheless, you could take photos with Michael Jackson bear, Steve Jobs bear and a wedding couple bear amongst others. There?s also a mother panda with her baby pandas on display too.  We certainly enjoyed the wonderful experience of the Museum bringing out the child in each of us, and making us feel young again. Despite the pricey entrance fees, I still think the Teddy Bear Museum is worth visiting, and to me, once would be sufficient. But if you don?t like teddy bears at all, then it would be prudent to skip this attraction.

This is an excellent museum featuring contemporary art as well as traditional art. The buildings themselves, which were designed by Tadao Ando, were amazing. It was great just walking around inside while perusing the exhibits & or going for a stroll outside. My favorite part was the sculpture garden, which featured 3 pieces. You can go on the rooftop as well to see another sculpture as well as a great view of Jeju. I was also fortunate to have an opportunity to see Yayoi Kusama's Pumpkin & Infinity Mirrored Room. I don't know if it was because I went during off-season, but the museum wasn't crowded at all, so I was able to take my time. I would definitely come back here again if I had a chance

There were bears of every color and design imaginable: there was an Elvis bear, Marilyn bear, Mona Lisa bear, Chinese bears, countryside bears and even Goong (the Korean drama) bears! It really was a bear wonderland. The only problem was that the commentary was all in Korean, it would have been better if there was English translation as well. But if you love bears, than it should be worth a visit.For more on my experience and photos, please check out my blog: http://www.travelbytez.com/2015/03/an-impromptu-visit-to-teddy-bear-museum.html
thank you for the visit and lovely review as well. as you mentioned, we exhibit the historical moment of human history more than 100 years decade by decade at the gallery 1.

Located next to   Loveland   this museum is small modern place with beautiful outdoor features such as a reflecting pool sculptures and a small surrounding forest. There was a little bit of everything from an exhibit about a famous national artist who lived for decades on Jeju to an interesting video and poetry collaboration of Korean rappers talking about social issues. The upstairs is currently showcasing drawings and sculptures made by Korean schoolchildren in a surprisingly cheeky cheerful exhibit. Much of the museum was in English but others were only in Korean. The price of admission was only 1000 won well worth it for the experience. There were several pieces that didn't wow me and some outdoor floorboards that need repairs but all in all this is a nice little museum. Korean women divers are called haenyeo. They dive in the ocean without any special tools to gather abalone, clams or seaweed. Wearing a lead weighted  vested and goggles, they plunge into 20 meter depths and stay underwater holding their breaths for two to three minutes.  Once they come up to the surface, they make a whistling sound, which is their unique way of breathing out carbon dioxide and breathing in fresh oxygen. The museum is in a four story building and housed many exhibits.  Gallery 1 on the first floor depicts the haenyeo's way of life. On the second floor at Gallery 2, you can see haenyeo's working life.  On the third floor at the observation area you can get a view overlooking the sea.  Gallery 3 displays exhibits of the sea around Jeju.  Outside the museum there is a lawn with statues, including one honoring the haenyeo. You can also admire the architecture of the museum. Further down, we chanced upon the haenyeo who were starting their show by singing a song. We were indeed lucky on that Tuesday afternoon as we managed to watch the show which started at 1.30.
Kids will love this museum but lesser for adults. There's around 3 levels of exhibition, but you can view them all pretty quick.

It wouldn't usually be my first choice to visit on an island filled with so many views but it was a rainy day so it seemed reasonable. Wasn't disappointed. The indoor exhibition is well arranged and themed: there was jungle, desert, and other sections. You can climb to the last floor of the tower in the middle for a nice view of the area. Can't go wrong in any way if you stop by. Didn't see the outdoor gardens since it was pouring rain but wasnt disappointed even with the indoor one alone

Innisfree Jeju House can be got to by taking a bus to the O'Sulloc tea museum stop. The tea museum is a very short walk away from Innisfree Jeju House.The place is quiet and peaceful, save for the calming music they play and the chatter of tourists and other visitors, but that wasn't too bad when I was there. There's an area devoted to DIY lessons/sessions where one can try making their own soap. There's a few pretty exhibits where one can smell various scents or read a little about the Innisfree brand and its products. There's a store area, with a few products that are exclusive to Innisfree Jeju House. And there's a cafe with various light food, drink and dessert options.Outside, there are tables and benches that overlook a nice view of the tea plantation, which you can go and take pictures in. Rows upon rows of tea leaves and a few windmills. It's all very pretty and is probably the biggest selling point of the whole compound containing both Innisfree Jeju House and the nearby tea museum. It's really very pretty.I enjoyed my time there, but if Innisfree products are not for you, or if you're the thrill-seeking type, perhaps you should skip this place.

I LOVE... this museum!!! I am a teddy bear fan so this museum feels like heaven to me aside from being a K-drama fan. Before visiting Jeju, I researched on the top sites recommended to be visited, i got fascinated with the reviews about Teddy Bear museum plus knowing that some of its Teddy Bears where featured in one my favorite Korean Drama of all time PRINCESS HOURS. The teddy bears are just so cute, you can see them perform different functions and dressed of different profession and famous personalities such as Marilyn Monroe, Steve Jobs, Madonna etc. Afetr visiting the exhibit halls, we then went to the lower ground floor area where tall Teddy Bears are on display alongside Teddy Bears items that are for sale.A must visit for Teddy Bear Lovers.

I couldn?t resist visiting this place on our way from Jeju city to Seogwipo. It made me giddy as a child. Entry fee is now 14,000 won per adult, and either 11,000 or 13,000 for children. This place has optional guided tours and accepts credit cards. Small room of Hello Kitty history and how her image has evolved since 1976. Original design merch on display. Lots of interactive rooms for kids and 3 floors to play. As an adult I still had fun and enjoyed a Hello Kitty hot chocolate (her face is in the cream), and Hello Kitty-shaped strawberry mousse cake in the cafe. You?re paying for the experience, here, so if you or your child is not a Hello Kitty fan, don?t waste your time. The maze on the roof is shaped like Hello Kitty from an aerial view and is strictly for children?the maze walls are only about 2 feet tall. My favorite part was the art exhibit (2nd floor) and all the small, unexpectedly perfect details (heart shaped straws, Hello Kitty toilet paper!). Souvenir shop: a mechanical pencil costs 7,700 won (more than $6)?I guess this is slightly more than American Sanrio store prices. But, if you?re willing to visit this museum, you?re probably also willing to pay for a momento of your experience.

We've enjoyed looking at the exhibits tasting free samples of tea and bought delicious green tea ice cream (KRW4500). Then we walked over to Innisfree to make our own soap which was so much fun - KRW15000 for one kit that makes three soaps but two people can share the kit so it's a really fun experience! You get to gift-wrap them at the end so they'd make a lovely present. You can naturally buy soap much cheaper but the experience was great and you customise and prettify the soaps as much as you like.Both O'Sulloc and Innisfree can get quite busy - as we were leaving a massive coach party arrived. It's not super-easy to find a table in the O'Sulloc cafe so beware. I saw several couples cruising around desperate to find a table while their ice cream was melting rapidly.The only negative for us was the journey: from the intercity bus terminal in Jeju-Si it took over an hour: the traffic was awful both ways! According to our travel guide it should have been 40 minutes. If you're catching the bus from the bus terminal it's number 755 from platform 10 but beware as the bus leaves before the time stated on the board/your ticket and it's a 50 minute wait for the next one (we've learnt the hard way!)

Went there in May 2015 by jeju golden city bus tour (which sucked!) and totally enjoyed our 1 hour visit! The exhibitions were amazing and the atmosphere itself is beautiful there! Adm fee is good: just 1000 won as much as I remember. Though the prices at a coffee shop were pretty expensive.

This was a stop of a bus tour through the weestern part of the Island. The so called tea Museum is a building where they sell  tea in all kinds of packaging such as bags and boxes. The word Museum is barely justified by the few pots and cups that are exhibited. You certainly should not come here from Europe because of the tea Museum. For those that never have seen the harvest of tea leaves is worth a stop.

The museum is located opposite of Jeju Korea Tourism Organisation and can be reached from Seogwipo or Airport on bus number 600. The entrance fees is 2000 won and there are 3 levels of teddy bears exhibition and the ground floor is where all sorts of teddy bears are being sold. There is a cafe within the museum and a theater showing Elvis Presley lookalike teddy bear singing Elvis's songs. It is about a 15 minutes session.

Run by a tea company that touts itself to be a premium tea brand the tea museum is nothing more than a small exhibition of some historical earthern ware and the owner's/ company statement about bringing back Korean tea culture to modern society.It has a tea shop (their tangerine and Camellia teas are good) cafe (very crowded but has really good green tea sets  for two consisting of ice cream a drink and green tea Swiss roll) and a tea workshop area called the Tea Stone situated in a garden. There's also a tea plantation where you can score some good photos or just simply take a quiet peaceful stroll through the greenery.Nearby is the innisfree Jeju House which also has a cafe selling some of their beauty products. The selection isn't great and they don't  give you free samples though you could score some Jeju only products. I find going to Myeongdong for your K beauty haul much more satisfying and easier on the wallet. Or if you just wanna stop by for their DIY soap making activity (they also sell the kit at the store so you can do it on your own) it seems like a peaceful way to escape the hustle and bustle of the city.

On a 3 day trip to jeju we needed more indoor activities due to the daily snowy conditions and found Jeju National Museum. With low expectations and dampened spirits as we were expecting to visit more outdoor activities we were pleasantly happy with our choice.This museum was easily accessible from our hotel as it was only a 28 minutes bus ride (costs us 1150krw). The bus stop just outside the museum.The museum itself is quite out of the way from the city centre but so was all the other places we wanted to visit and therefore was not an issue for us.Highly recommend you taking your time to read and inspect each exhibit. It is quite amazing how history laid out the changes made due to advancement through discovery. Although for a quick browser it may only take you half an hour (it took us more than 1 hour).Entry was free and I'm not sure if this is the norm but surely worth a visit even if just as a time filler.

All the promotions are for Koreans only even though I showed them my membership abroad. Really not enthusiastic to do business with tourists. Why do I have to spend my money here? Let?셲 be honest I didn?셳 have to buy this brand compared to all others available. The tea museum next door is also just a one room exhibition and place for shopping.

Admission to both main and special exhibits are free. The exhibition items and artifacts are well maintained and very informative. Easily accessible by numerous busses. A good place for children as well.

You can reach this place with Jeju tour bus - if you're going to the Roe Deer Observatory as well, I suggest you go there first and then walk downhill to the Peace Park (less than 10 mins). If you do it the other way round, you'll have to trek uphill. The admission for the Peace Park is free and everything is in English. The museum offers a comprehensive account of a controversial point in Korean history: some exhibits are quite chilling and upsetting but I think it's important to understand the history of this island: Jeju is not all about tangerines, erotic statues and kitschy teddy bears.

You can get here from Seogwipo on the 701 bus - costs 3,300 KRW each way and takes about 80 minutes.  After the bus drops you off, turn off one of the streets to the right and keep walking until you find the parking lot and entrance way.  There's a small exhibition before the ticket office, but there's not much in there, lots of photos and a little signage.  There's also a water drinking fountain just outside if you need to fill up.Note there are no garbage bins, so you will need to take all rubbish away with you.  Entrance fee is 2000 KRW.  All well signposted and lots of steps.  It will take about about 20 minutes to walk to the top.  There are lots of places to stop and sit and take photos and there are lookouts at the top for photos in all directions.  When you get to the top, all you can do it look around and come back down again.  You're not able to walk around inside the cone or around the edges.  (so yes we took our picnic back down again).When you walk back down, be sure to go to the small cove on the right hand side where you will see a (FREE) exhibition of women divers.    This happens at 130pm and 3pm.  Five older women divers took to the water, with their full old wetsuits on and 10 minutes later started coming back in with the octupus that they had caught. Only two caught some while we were there and came back out of the water clutching it, straight to the area where they sell the seafood that you can buy and take into the restaurant area to get it cooked for you.It's a pleasant way to spend an hour or so, but its a pain to make a specific trip here from Seogwipo (and longer from Jeju City), so plan something else around it.

We went with high expectation, thinking that we could go into the larva tube. To our utmost disappointment, besides a 4-D movie, It was just a museum with some picture exhibits, and glassed up exhibits of a very small part of the larva tube. Admission was W3,000. It took us a long time to get there, as the bus was a 50 minute wait and it was extremely cold that day.

This place was really unexpected. Through the Yeha Bus tour this was one of the stops and I am glad we visited this place. A lot of mini exhibits with bears dressed up according to the theme and the gift shop is great as well. For teddy bear lovers and lovers of all things cute, we recommend this place.

The weather was raining on the day I decided to do sightseeing on Jeju, so I was left with only a visit to the botanical gardens. You can reach it from the airport limousine bus route and behind the fast food shops near SK Energy shop.Luckily the garden exhibition was under glass roof, so it provided a good informative shelter from the rain.The botanical gardens are organised into themes, eg. Aquatic garden, cactus garden, etc. I guess this eliminates confusion for tourists and displays the plants in an educational fashion too. On a sunny day, there is more to do on the outside.There is a curio shop inside the gardens for some gifts but I did not see a coffee shop at the attraction.It will be educational for the kids!

The history facts in this memorial hall recalled me of the one in Oswiecim, Poland... This memorial hall will help you to understand Jeju people's local history. Whenever I visit war related museum or places, we should stop fighting for nothing but losing the precious lives. I was even cried when I read 2 young men who could not enter the military school due to the wrong record of this tragic incident. I read all of explanation in Korean and English. I skipped some clips but I tried to watch 2 or 3 min's clips. Very well prepared in English and Korean. One of best museum. It is FREE. Only I concerned, there is no chairs to take a rest from time to time. And there was a decent with 15ish people, her voice was too much loud to make big echo in the hall area! I think they have to pay attention with other visitors who look into all scripts! I was a bit mad because she was too passionate to proceed her job. I think you do not need a docent because all of exhibits are perfectly translated in English. There are many heart breaking stories, but when I entered into the cave Darangshi(?), I could keep saying   oh my god..   I feel very sorry for all deceased, and their family members who survived at the same time witnesses. I strongly recommend this museum if you are interested local history, and history buff. It is a must. In fact, there is no restaurant, there is a coffee shop only. If you rent a car, within 10 min's drive, there are some. The bus #343, or #344 go to 4.3 Peace Park. From this park, Jeju Jeolmul Natural Recreation Forest is 5 min's drive away, and 20 min's walk on foot. This Forest is wonderful. I recommend to combine these 2 places to visit at once. History and Nature are very good combination! The last stop of 343 &344 is this forest.

The exhibits were pretty interesting actually but as mentioned in the title, it's a mainly outdoor venue! The glass sculptures look better in the day time or at night when the lights are on.. SO..! If the weather is not helpful, save it for another day! It's pretty far out, so if u are gonna go, do the O'sulluc tea museum and this together... Don't leave too late coz it's terribly difficult to get a cab, unless you have a pre-arranged driver. That said, the staff there really are very, very nice.. We were actually the last few patrons out and we were stranded without a cab, in the bloody freezing rain.. We had 3 ahjussis trying to help us call cabs and eventually one of em offered to drive us to the nearest bus stop instead coz no one was responding, and FYI the nearest bus stop is abt 10mins out too..
Small museum, but provides nice insight into Haenyeo business. You can miss it, though - the exhibition was not that interesting

O'Sulloc Tea Museum is a small building set in a tea farm. It's a well designed lovely space with a display area about the history of tea and an exhibit wall of teacups and pots a shop where you can try some tea (only one kind though) and a restaurant featuring green tea beverages and sweets. You can also walk around outside there is a garden area in and around the building and also small rows of tea bushes just outside. There's no admission fee and it's not so much of a museum as a commercial venue for selling O'Sulloc products although items can be pricey for the budget traveller. I visited O'Sulloc with a few other backpackers (5 foreigners 1 Korean) and we all had a terrible experience of their customer service. The staff were sour faced and gave us the impression that we were not welcomed glaring at us and tidying their display in a huff when we looked at the product samples (these are samples ok - they're meant to be touched and looked at!). The staff at the counter literally sneered in disdain at my Korean travel companion when he tried to make friendly small talk while we were purchasing our items. This was the worst experience I've had in my 3 weeks in Korea. All the other customer service staff I've encountered in Korea were either very polite and lovely or just neutral. I'm writing in formally to the management about this so hopefully by the time other TripAdvisor members visit they would have improved.In spite of that I did enjoy my visit (no point letting the staff spoil it) but I would recommend coming here only if you've done all your   must-do's   in Jeju or on a rainy day.
