review: Ultra modern building houses green tea related information and displays.But you really want to snack on green tea themed ice creams or others and walk in the garden of lush green tea shrubs.As garden is outdoors you want to avoid visiting during rain showers.
This is where you get to see the volcanic rock formations by the ocean! It is beautiful and stunning. The walk was nice and breezy. Would highly recommend for anyone who can walk.
The Jusangjeolli Cliff is a beautiful geographical site with lava rock formations against the beautiful ocean. Great scenery for pictures and a relaxing stroll along the boardwalk.

Rock formations on the coast with goemetric patterns as though machine cut by man!Nice at sun setting into the sea. Walkable from ICC and we just stumbled into this place when we went for a stroll! Pleasant surprise indeed.

Just a quick visit to tick off the must do in Jeju. We came early in the morning hence not many people yet. I presume there there will be huge crowd later in the day as this is popular place to see rock formation without much walking to reach the site

It was an interesting experience walking through the immense cave network. It's mind-boggling that this is only a very small part of a much larger system formed through volcanic activity. Do go to the visitors center to find out more information before venturing in.

it was a hot summer day when our tour guide took us to this park. It has a very large variety of plants and bonsai. Some of the bonsai plants are more than 100 years old!! The most interesting bit in my opinion was going into the lava tubes which are like under ground caves with unusual rock formations. Wear comfortable shoes. Its not strenuous but best to be comfortable when walking.
It is very unique with all the breathtaking stone formations. Althought it might request some walking but it is worth to visit!

It is interesting to see and then read how did these lava columns came to formation. It?s worth a quick walkaround. Place is not big so it gets pretty crowded but people are understanding to disperse so that you can have a chance to take some pictures too.
Good walk around the park and the cliffs were quite spectacular! Very interesting rocok formations that were built by lava flows.

For 2000w you can walk into the park. The lookouts for the rock formations allow great photos. Similar natural rocks to those seen in Ireland. The park has some Jeju stone statues otherwise not much else to see. The parking was free.

An interesting outing to learn about volcanic activity and how the lava tube was formed. Not suitable for elderly visitors with the dim and uneven terrain. Many information board to explain unusual structures. Educational. Some wooden boardwalk in certain areas. The stairs at the entrance leading into the tube can be steep and slippery.

An interesting 2km round-trip walk through the Manjanggul lava cave in cool conditions. Was told by our guide that the temperature stays like this all year round. Really intriguing to see the various histotical lava formations and literally walk through a part of Jeju's history.

We were very excited to visit Manjanggul Cave, and it did not disappoint.It is quite a large cave, and if you walk slowly and look around at the cave carefully, you can see the changes of the lava formation colours and shapes.Make sure you walk the entire length to check out the lava tube, I mean - when will you get another chance? Also make sure you wear comfortable shoes, as my recommendation of walking slowly is not just to check out the different sections, it also means you won't trip, as the ground is pretty uneven and the cave is quite dimly lit!

Very interesting cave, which has been created by the vulcano. 1km long tunnel available for tourists inside of old not active  vulcano. Not difficult to reach and walk. Little dark, but lamps inside are giving sufficient light. Very good level of safety. Info how long to walk, communication system with support team,  stairs, bridges, walking paths. Information boards describing what you can see in cave. Even young children like 3-6y can easily enjoy this trip.
Unique rock formations, but you will see them quite from a distance. Too many people around. Good in Summer for a short walk, nice breeze from the sea.
This was kinda close to our place. This area is beautiful. The rock formations  & the ocean  are stunning. We stayed there to chill , took some pictures and walked to the next scenic area.

This ?Unesco? lava grot is quite nice. You can walk a kilometer underground in a dark cave with lots of information panels in English and Korean/Hangul. The Floor is uneven and the temperature is ten degrees Celsius. We did not expect something special, but overal it was a nice experience with a rewarding pilar at the end of the walk.
The texture of the cave and the formation were very interesting and unique. The walk into the cave was a bit tedious due to the uneven ground. Otherwise, had a great outing.

The floor is uneven and the lighting is dim, not for those with walking issues. Nice place to see the strange wall formation due to lava. Only 1 km and mostly even.  The tourists can be a bit noisy, hope the bats in the other parts are not too disturbed

The cave has a number of formations throughout and there are information boards explaining what they re, and the English is good. The cave was a cool 13 degrees when I went down but outside was 34 so it was a welcome temperature.The steps down are a little deep so if you have vertigo or need help walking, it could be a little tough. It is wet under foot, I walked in flipflops and it was ok, but if you are a bit unsure of your footing, wear trainers. The cave is lit well  but some lights shine up into your eyes, which I found incredibly annoying, as it ruined my night vision. There are some areas with wooden bridges over the areas very difficult to walk on, so you aren't constantly in need of watching your footing.Worth a visit, as it it is not something you will see in many other places. I have been twice now, and it seems much more tourist friendly now.

Place for everyone who like caves, volcanos or geology. The cave is long, but the one kilometre available for tourists is enough. There are many interesting lava formations, described in English. Beside that the cave is just beautiful. The temperature inside is around 10째C, humidity close to 100%. If you are not very fond of caves, stones or walking, probably you should skip it. :-)
Nice walk along the shore and take a few photos near the airport, tourist information, gift shops and casino.

just walking distance to Jeju convention center is a vast scenic place complete with flowers, stone statues and the sea!There are also nice rock formations.There is an entrance fee of usd2 but it is so worth to see.

Jeju stone park was rated A by Korea Ministry of Culture and Tourism, in recognition that this park is excellent in term of its specialization in the theme of stone, differentiation from other facilities, and characteristics relating to mythology and the life of the people in the region.Get the map at the entrance and follow guided park course. Don't miss out the Jeju stone museum to know how the formation of Jeju Island. After a short nice walk from the entrance,the museum is just located in the basement of a building opposite the Sky Pond. Follow the map to look for Jeju traditional village with thatched roof houses. Before at the end of course, drop by the unique Gallery in the park which you may find artworks of domestic and foreign artists.It is indeed best travel Korea during Autum because even though it was sunny day, but the breeze was so cooling and the air was very refreshing. It is a museum as well as an ecological park. It is a very remarkable cultural park which sublimating nature in art ,really very fantastic.

I've never been in a lava tube before, but it was a lot like a cave. The formations inside are pretty interesting and the park does a good job lighting them colorfully. It was a nice walk. However, it is very touristy and if you've been to bigger caves in other parts of the world it's just cool, not extremely impressive.

Its definitely a worthwhile trip to make and just walking through the Lava Tube is quite an experience.  It is not everyday one has the opportunity to walk through and see the various formations, the caves formed, columns, the different textures formed, etc.One needs to be relatively fit to do the walk with comfortable shoes as the location tends to be wet. Elderly should have a walking stick which will help and carry a torchlight.  Its a few degrees lower underground.

It was an interesting experience to walk through the 1km long tunnel if you enjoy understanding and seeing the various structures and rock formations formed from the lava flow. Wear comfortable shoes with good grip, tunnel is rather slippery and rocky.  On a side note, I think I enjoyed walking through the Manjanggul Caves better than the DMZ Third Tunnel. :)

It was a dream come true to see these beautiful hexagonal columnar formations made of lava. Also, seeing some haenyeo (women free-divers) at work near one of the lower cliffs was a nice addition. After walking along the paid promenade, we ventured down a steep paved hill to the left of the entrance (where you'll see a big conch shell sculpture and some big maps). After going down the hill, we walked along the large stones to the right, then up the large lava formation, and saw the hexagonal shapes up close and personal. What a cool little gem to find! We were the only ones there!

It is a lava tunnel. It's interesting to see but not a must-see. There were some stairs to descent into the tunnel at the entry and it gets pretty dark inside. Your eyes will need to adjust, and there isn't any place to grip along the wall. Please wear comfortable shoes and some layers since it gets wet and chilly inside. Walking paths are uneven on some areas, and most are not well-lit. The tunnel is purposely not well-lit to preserve the natural habitat of its resident animals. A round trip from the entrance will take about 30-40 mins if you're strolling through the tunnel. We visited this cave as part of Yeha East course tour. If you have interest in geological formation, stalagmite, and nature, you may find it interesting.

In my opinion, there are two world heritage sites that visitors to Jeju must visit. One is Manjanggul Cave and the other one is Seongsan Illchubong. Manjanggul Cave is unique as it was formed by lava movement thousands of years ago. It provides an insight into Jeju's geographical structure. The temperature in the cave could be chilly, so bring a jacket along. Visitors to the cave usually walked for about 2 km to reach the end, where photos with a large stalactite pillar could be taken. Other features in the cave include lava formations that look like elephant feet, turtles and book shelves.

If you love nature and have never seen any volcanic formation before, it would be worth the visit. Personally,  i enjoyed walking inside the cave and having a look at the volcanic formation.  It's like you can almost imagine how the lava flowed inside the tunnel a few thousand years ago :) i was in awe of how powerful mother nature can be. It was quite cold inside. Wear layers and proper shoes.  Can be quite slippery as well.

If you have an opportunity to visit these lava tubes, then make sure you do!   We have lava caves in New Zealand and I have seen the lava tubes on Hawaii, but these are giants in comparrison.  The grounds of Manjang Caves are well kept.From the carpark it is only a 3 or 4 minute walk along a concrete path to the entrance of the caves.   We were expecting big, but these caves are huge!There are a number of steps leading down into the mouth of the cave and then you are inside this amazing formation.   It was quite an eerie feeling as we ventured deeper and deeper inside the tube which measures approx 5meters wide and up to 10 meters high.   The temperature is quite pleasant inside the caves and it is a little damp.   Even though we all had good walking shoes on, we still had to be quite careful of where we walked on the uneven, slippery  floor.   It is true that there is not a lot of light inside the cave, but we felt that the dim lighting added to the atmosphere.   In hindsight, a torch might have been helpful.All in all, definitely well worth the visit and would highly recommend to all. I would recommend that this is probably not a safe place for the elderly and very young children.  My elderly parents waited for us at the main building where there was a restaurant, shop and toilets.

I would highly recommend this place for an extremely hot or wet day.  Being covered and large enough, it was an enjoyable walk.  There was adequate lighting and enough fellow tourists not to make the cave walk too scary.  Despite the unevenness of the terrain - they are dried lava and so quite uneven, most people would be able to walk comfortably.It's certainly a nice change from limestone caves although some people may miss seeing amazing rock formations like the stalactites and stalagmites in limestone caves.  In fact, I was not overly impressed with the gigantic lava mass on display at the end of the walk.  For me, the enjoyable walk was good enough.

I was staying at the Lotte Hotel in Jungmun and decided to go for an out door walk to enjoy the beautiful weather. I was walking along the coastline and it eventually lead me to this attraction. Although it is wonderful to see these unique rock formation, this attraction is rather small.

I haven't been anywhere else in the world where there has been the option to walk a couple of kms through a volcanic cave. The experience is quite surreal. From 30+ degrees on the outside you soon plummet down to perhaps 10-15 degrees, damp and dark. The rock formations are stunning and they've done a good job to keep it natural without too much human interference.Bring sensible shoes.

I find this cave beautiful as it is made by nature. It is just 1km long, it is good for a short trip. The place is cold, that's why Koreans go here in the summer. If you get bored easily, this place is not for you as the cave doesn't have a variety of rock formations.Furthermore, if you do not like to walk in rocky paths, you may not appreciate this. This place is dimly lit to preserve the cave, so you have to be careful. Overall, a good place to visit if you appreciate nature.

Hmm... Where to start?Well, Jeju Island, being volcanic in nature, must really have places like this!Honestly saying, it wasn't something so jaw-dropping and spectacular!Just more like a place with rock formations due to the cooling of lava!The trek inside isn't hard and what I really liked was that it was chilly while we did it!It was a nice sidetrip nonetheless if you like walking and if you like all these geo stuff!If you're in Jeju, maybe you can give it a try

Certainly my first experience entering a natural geological occurrence like this one. A nice walk on a seasoned path, although some parts were slippery, it was safe for most people. Senior citizens must take extra care as the uneven path were dimly lit. Here were many features to be amazed by and the information centre gave visitors a better understanding of the geological occurrence. Worthy visit.

About 1 kilometer of the lava tube  is open to walk through. You descend a long staircase into the cave. You will be walking on the old lave flow, so the floor is uneven & pitted, and full of puddles. There is dim lighting, so you really need to bring your own flashlight to see where you are stepping. The wall are fairly smooth & rounded, you will only be seeing a few small formations. If you are a nature geek (like me) you will enjoy this. If you want  lots of stalactites & large formations, this is not for you.

A lava tube showing the flow of lava and various natural formation such as the lava shelves or columns. Inside the cave is chilly (around 11c when outside is around 25c), dark, wet and slippery. Bring your jacket and sturdy shoe for this visit. Heels is a definite no no. Forget about your camera (too dark for photo taking) and just enjoy the brisk walk. To and fro takes you around 45mins-1hr.

Yes! I love this place for its natural scene and beautiful environment. It is really quiet and peaceful except at the base where there are plenty of tourists. Note there are several hiking trails of different distance and demands. Be sure to read to it and do note the closing time in different seasons. Some closes as early as 1330hr in winter due to early sun set. Most charged entries for vehicles into the car park. Small car (Kia Morning) which I rented from rentalcar.com was charged 1000 won (peanut) Put on right shoes and gear. There are air blower (See pic) available to dust off the mud or dirt from your shoes before u step into your car. Love that. Enjoy the beauty.

We were hoping to climb up to the summit. However we ere told to be there before 9 am. We hiked the Yeangsil Trail instead. It was a great experience. The trail was as per the Trod advisor reviews. Make sure you have the right shoes with the right traction. It was not that hard except for some parts of the trail. We enjoyed it very much. We bought some snacks on the trail but had to carry the trash back to our hotel!! The trail is well kept and marked. Will go back again but before 9 am so we can go to the summit. The views were fantastic . We saw a couple of deer. It was worth the visit. Make sure you arrive before 9 am if you want to go to the summit.

We went in winter with 2 young kids (6 & 8) and it was easy going but cold. Lots of locals ply this route and it?s 5km to the witsoreoum rest area where you can transfer to other trails or have a nice pit stop. Trekking poles and good shoes would be a good idea. The scenery is marvelous with very nice panaromic vistas all round

We end up at the wrong trail and did not have the time to complete it. Choose the right trail for your budgeted time. Weather is pleasant enough in late Sep but the trail requires proper hiking shoes if you don't want to hurt your knees and avoid sprain.

Took the longest trail to Mount Hallasan peak (Seongpanak Trail) - 9.6 km - but started a bit late and did not make the cut-off time at the Jindalrae shelter (7km). However it was a great walk and I visited the Saraoream peak on a side tril on the way back.  This was well worth it as there is great view and also a beautiful crater lake.  It is key that you start early and take enough water with you.  Also need good shoes. Although it was August - most of the trail is in the forest - so not so hot.

There are 7 trails that you can climbs the mountainBut there are 2trails  only to reach to the top.Since i took 4courses i will explain where i visited that is also most people goTo SummitTrails : If you want to go to the top there are 2trails Seongpanak and Gwaneumsa  trail. Normally people go up by Seongpanak and go down by Gwaneumsa since Gwaneumsa is more difficult to go upTaking time : round trip takes 9 to 10hours so you better start your day early otherwise they will stop you to go up in some area Especially Jindalrea shelter will close at 1230pm or 1pm which can be vary depends on seasonAlso on your way to Jindalrea shelter there is another short trail Sara oreum which is really beautiful and takes only 40min. so it is YOU MUST VISIT place unless you are not hurry by time.How to get to : from Jeju bus terminal there is a bus that ofpen goes every 15min and takes 30min For beautiful viewTrail : Yeonsil trail and Eorimok Trail People normally go up by Eorimok and go down by Yeongsil but for me the opposit is betterTaking time : round trip takes 5hours and easy to walk if you like climbingHow to get to : there is only one time every hour so you better check in the termimalEorimok takes 35min from terminal and Yeonsil is 2stops more from EorimokPersonally i prefer Eorimok and Yeongsil trails.Also i highly recommend you to have climbing shoes otherwise your feet will be beaton up by rocks and enough waterall trail has shelters that sell food and drink but you better bring your own water Even it rains it is another feeling climbing mountain very attractive to go with lots of fogI never thought it is good to climbs when raining but i liked it a lotHowever prepare a nylon raincoat  from jeju bus terminal since it is very windy Poly raincoat would be ripped It is double price from the entranceThis is the best montain among i have visited in Korea

The park is very big so wear comfy hiking shoes!  We only saw 1 wild deer after walking the whole trail. There are however deer in captive just after the entrance. Not a bad place if you have the time and effort.

It is stunning.  You can wear walking shoes or sandals to trek along the coastline. Most of the trail is paved with wooden boards.  This place offers many scenic sites for photos. The photos don't give this place its justice.  Have to see it in person to take it in.   There are small cafes along the trail offering refreshments and a place to sit.

Good place to visit for experiencing the lava tube. But.... Pease please please prepare a good walking shoes if you were to visit this place. You'll need to walk on rough and uneven surface and the trail is pretty long. Not recommend to bring kids and elderly to visit this attraction.

You know that line movie critics love to use when it comes to B-grade chick flicks?   Have low expectations, then you'll enjoy it.   The same can be said of Manjang Cave.The lava tube was not as spectacular as I expected it to be, but it did offer a few interesting sights here and there. Walking all the way to the end of the trail and back took about an hour, but if you walk quickly, you can complete the journey within thirty minutes.Take note that the ground is wet and rocky, so be sure to wear your walking shoes. Also, it can get quite cold, so a jacket would most certainly come in handy. For photography lovers, you may not fancy the fact that it's a bit dark in the cave, but there's nothing a few adjustments here and there can't do!Facilities include, but are not limited to, souvenir shops, toilets and lockers. Bear in mind though that there are no toilets in the cave itself. Tickets are cheaper for children, but you'll need passports for proof!If you're spending more than a day in Jeju, you may want to consider checking this place out. If not, you're better off exploring other places such as the Hallasan National Park.

Wow! I'm glad I saw this before leaving! Jeju is full of surprises and this is one of them. We were extremely lucky this was a foggy day because seeing this place in fog was really special.  The amazing display of wood carvings etc at the wood exhibition place was amazing as we're all the large insects carved out of cedar wood. It's a 20 min drive from Jeju City. Apparently in summer you have to protect your lunch from the crows! A nice easy walk and an oreum (hill) trail if you want something a bit harder. There are lots of carved statues all along the way and one of those stone paths which you can walk on with your shoes off.  I manage about 2 feet, too hard for me! Haha!

With a few different trails to choose from, climbing Hallasan is an experience I'd recommend to anyone visiting Jeju and wanting a close experience with its nature. Careful preparation of equipment is still necessary, as the easy trail was quite slippery even while wearing winter shoes. The change in scenery when ascending the mountain was magnificent, even though the snowstorm at the top prevented us from seeing the scenery at apparently one of the best sightseeing spots in all of Jeju.

Went on a day hike up and down the Seongpanak trail! It was a gorgeous day, about 18C and I couldn't have asked for better weather. It took about 10 hours round trip. Started around 8:30am and made it down by 6:30pm. Luckily the sun didn't go down until 7:15ish so I had plenty of light to guide me.Now, I am not a hiker by any means and this was one of the toughest hikes I've been on. To be honest, it wasn't because the trails were all that difficult - it was actually quite pleasant through the woods and there were 2 rest stops along the way. The first stop is basically a bathroom break and the 2nd had some food available before heading up the last (somewhat steeper) trail to the lake up top. Oh, by   food   I mean some cup ramen and snacks. They also sold water and sports drinks. It would be helpful for you to bring food of your own. They also have no garbage cans so you need to carry and dispose of your own trash once you get back down.The reason why this trail was difficult for me was because I simply wasn't ready for a 20km hike! By the last 5km of the descent, I felt my feet and legs were going to fall off or give in to becoming jelly due to all the stairs and rocks. Make sure you have proper shoes! All in all, I'm glad I did this hike - it was worth it when I got to the top and was able to experience amazing views and clean air. And the flowers!! It was simply beautiful. Just expect to have sore calves for a few days following :)

Wear the right clothes and shoes - else be prepared for plenty of thrills and spills. We also discovered a   gentle   trail may be not so gentle even though it was during our descent. Moral of the story - preparation beforehand is essential to build stamina and leg power.

We were lucky to start the hike with a beautiful warm Autumn day and clear skies. We started around 7 in the morning at the Gwamneumba campsite, getting a taxi ride from Jeju city was easy and cheap - about 10500 won gets you right in front of the gate. We chose to go Gwamneumsa - Seongpanak, as research suggests that most people who did it preferred to avoid masses of people.. Gwamneumsa also boasts the best views, and it sure lived up to it.The Gwamneumsa trail was lovely at first, most tranquil. But then shortly afterwards, it started getting quite difficult having to balance hopping between and stepping up uneven surfaces of lava rocks..Great views came 2/3's in and at the very last part of the trail.. There's also drinking water available at a small fountain in front of a bridge 2/3 way in. The bathrooms on this trail were pretty gross, one of those toilets that pile waste at the bottom - only that the bottom wasn't very far down.. I would say the bottom was less than a metre, many outdoor bathrooms have their toilets down 20m!.. But consider oneself to be lucky to have bathrooms!We reached the summit around 1pm, having taken countless 2 minute breaks along the way. We were quite slow and took it easy. The lake at the top looked much like a drying pond, I think views would probably have looked better in the Spring. There's nothing much else there, a resting area, a helipad and a wifi tower.Next - Climbing down Seongpanak trail.. The first check point on the Seongpanak trail sells FOOD! We didn't know that, as many sources state there are no food stalls on the mountain.. There's 2 minute noodles, chocolate, bottled water, pocari sweat, tissues, etc. Then on the checkpoint after that you have a small fountain of drinking water.The rest of the trail was a nightmare. We didn't have the correct hiking gear and very underprepared trekking in sneakers and boots. Many say that Seongpanak is easier because its a slope, but having to balance each step as we walked on lava rocks was most tiresome. 99% of the time you're just looking down at your feet making sure it lands on a rock, and you're doing it in a hurry because you're trying to reach the end before the sun sets! And you'd probably be doing that for about 6km.It would have been much easier to go up Seongpanak and down Gwamneumsa, as it is much easier to go down by steps rather than on a slope with uneven rocky terrain.Make sure you have the correct hiking gear - sticks and shoes. Our legs ached! Mostly caused by keeping our balance on the uneven, rocky terrain. My partner ended up with a crook knee, micro ligament tear. We reached the exit gate at 5:30pm! Taxi ride back to Jeju city was about 15000 won.I give this 3 stars because a lot of effort is involved for minimal reward. Yes it is a mountain, and I have hiked other incredible mountains with magnificent views like huangshan and wulingyuan. My expectations were very high as well, the most you get are views of the city, mountain fauna ( though very beautiful), and the drying lake. Do it for the enjoyment of experience and go the other direction, climbing down Gwamneumsa would be so much easier as there are better stairs, not just kilometres of rocks on a slope! And with the right gear! ;)Enjoy!

We were dropped by a taxi at the beginning of the Seongpanak trail (a little way up the volcano), but you can catch the bus there if you prefer and there is a bus stop right near the entrance. The track is 9.6km (19.2km return), and took us about 6 hours return walking at a medium pace, including breaks at Sokbat shelter (4.1kms up - toilet facilities only) and at Jindallaebat shelter (7.3kms up - toilet and small kiosk). We had initially wanted to walk up the Gwaneumsa trail and then down the Seongpanak one, but were too tired to get up before 6am to achieve it in one day. Walking the Seongpanak trail up and down was a great experience in itself, even though it is apparently not as scenic as others. But, because it's one of the easier ones, it is packed with tourists, most of whom are not seasoned walkers, so be prepared for being held up a fair bit (and witnessing some pretty avoidable but hilarious injuries!).The trail is quite an easy one in comparison to other hikes we have done - no really steep bits or actual climbing - more of a gentle incline, with boardwalks in parts, dirt paths and as you get higher, rough rocky paths. The only strenuous thing about the trail is that it is long? It will take you all day, and you have to start early so you reach the Jindallaebat shelter before a certain hour (changes depending on the season, but in September it was 12:30pm) or the ranger won't let you continue - for obvious reasons, there's no lighting at night to climb back down, so he doesn't want to come and find stupidly lost tourists! You can check the times on the official Hallasan website. You don't really need proper hiking boots/other equipment for this hike (we did it in light walking shoes), but if you have weak ankles I would probably recommend wearing hiking boots with ankle support, especially for the walk back down the rocky paths. Take plenty of water and snacks - don't rely on the shelters like the Koreans do, they may sell out/be extremely busy, and you have to get to Jindallaebat by 12:30! We just bought some muesli bars, fruit, WATER and energy drinks like gatorade/powerade at a 7/11 before we left Jeju city in the morning, and were almost the only ones who had thought ahead! On the way back down, the Jindallaebat shelter will be quieter, so it's the perfect opportunity to then buy some of their hot ramen noodles or a chocolate bar. I would also recommend bringing a light rain jacket, and a waterproof backpack/cover for your backpack - it showers sporadically within the fog. I also took a plastic bag to put my camera in to keep it dry.When we began our walk, it was quite chilly at the entrance and the local walkers laughed at us wearing shorts - but by the time you get a few kilometres in, you'll be stripping off layers of clothing, so totally wear shorts if you want to - it's quite warm in the sun on the summit, so everyone will be peeling off their layers anyway! There was a thick fog hanging low over the volcano for about 2/3 of the walk, so it's a bit muggy, but the side of the mountain is lush and green, an eerily quiet forest. As you get higher, suddenly you notice you're climbing above the fog - feels like you've popped out above the clouds, on top of the world! The last part of the track is quite windy, and you can see how the wind has beaten its wooden steps, which are strewn everywhere. Be careful in the last part and beware pushy tourists! But, once you get to the summit, at Dongneung Peak (no facilities on the summit, by the way), the view is breathtakingly beautiful - like nothing I've ever seen before! The crater when we were there was overgrown with vegetation, with a small crater lake. Such a wonderful experience, and most definitely a highlight of our trip to South Korea! You must hike Hallasan during your stay at Jeju-do!

We wanted to hike to the summit of the Hallasan mountain, and decided to use the Seongpanak trail.It's roughly 9 kms from the parking lot to the summit, and it took us around 2h50m at a constant pace with few stops. This is a very scenic hike starting in the middle of the forest, and close to the top through prairies. The hike is properly maintained with stairs and paths, but some parts have many rocks, and thus proper hiking shoes are highly recommended.The views from the summit are spectacular!

We walked up the Gwanmeusan Trail, only 20 minutes from downtown Jeju-si. It took us, going slowly with lots of rests about 9.5 hours. Good hiking shoes required. We witnessed multiple shoe failures. You have to hike back down shoeless if your shoes rip apart and they will due to the volcanic rocks used on the rrail. The rocks are cute until they aren't. They are murder on the feet, ankles, knees, and legs on the way down.We went in April 20 and it was warm... only one water stop about 3/4 way up.18+ miles round trip. Please ask questions if you have concerns. It is quite breathtaking but a strenuous hike. Many turn back early. Must make it to the Samgakbong shelter by 12:30. No support on the trail.... 2 bathrooms though about 1/4 and 3/4 way up. Must start return hike by 2PM... still took us 4 hours to down due to strenuous terrain and infinite number of stairs.

We visited the National Park as well as Mt. Hallasan during our trip to Jeju-do. It is a beautiful park with average to good hiking trails. We took the long trail (Seongpanak, 9,6km) up to the summit, which took us 2,5 hours (i will take you much longer if you hike slowly and take breaks!). The view from the Summit was just stunning! Definately worth it! I'd advise anybody hiking this trail to wear boots or other firm shoes since the trail is very steep and rock at some parts. You also have to start early in the morning (~8am) since you have to reachthe second station until 1pm to be allowed to go to the summit. Geaneumsa trail is currently closed!

We visited Mount Halla National Park yesterday, Aug 25th, and it was an excellent experience and great views!It is very easy to get there by the 740 bus from Jeju Bus terminal, now here is the tricky part.. there are several entrances and trails. All of them are intense hiking. Use comfortable shoes, take lots of water and snacks.. there is nothing to buy up until the very top, which is noodle soup, water and chocolates......We took the Eorimok trail to go up to Witsae Shelter and took the Yeongsil trail to return down and my recommendation is:Take Yeongsil train, the view is by far much better than the one from Eorimok trail.In order to get there:Take 740 bus and get down on Yeongsil ticket office (@45m) and from there take a taxi to the main entrance (there is a taxi that goes up and down all the time and charges 5000). Please take the taxi, otherwise you will end up walking uphill for @2km. Once at the entrance... just follow the signs to Witse Shelter. Take lots of pictures along the way!Again ... it is uphill .. from @900m to @1750m, with lots of stairs and rock trails on both trails. Up and down in @5 hours is an ok time.Enjoy !!

We visited Jeju only for Hallasan mountain! There are two ways on top, one easier and one harder! We took the easier to get on top and the harder to get back down! Once on top you will have a beautiful view over the national park and the island! Take some good shoes with you if you want to take the harder trail! The park is easy to reach by bus

We visited Hallasan National Park in mid December. We ascended via Gwaneumsa trail (8.7km) up to the peak and descended via the Seongpanak trail (9.6km). Gwaneumsa is shorter but more challenging on the way up, it is easier on the knees. We started at 07:30hr, which is the sunrise time. The initial hike was relatively flat, walking on uneven big rocks. There were signs throughout the trail, indicating where you are, distance and estimated time to the peak. Snow started to appear midway and we had to put on crampons on our boots. We took about 3 hours to reach the shelter and another 1 hour 45 minutes to reach the peak. Unfortunately, the weather was cloudy at the peak with low visibility. It was very windy and cold. We joined the queue to have photos taken at the iconic landmark.We started our descent at 12:45hr, arrived at the shelter at 15:15hr, had a short break before descending the remaining 4.1km. We took about 4 hours for the entire descent, exhausted by then.This is the first time my friend and I hiked in snow during winter. We took longer than expected as we were extra careful and also took many photos. Overall, it was a great first time experience hiking on snow.Tips for winter hiking:1. Start as early as possible so that you are not pressured to reach the shelter before 1200hr.2. Wear comfortable shoes, preferably water resistant or waterproof.3. Be extra careful when stepping on the big rocks during the initial trail. They are uneven and may twist your ankles. 4. Crampons are necessary, while trekking poles are optional.5. Wear layers of clothing so that you can add/remove when necessary.6. Wear beanie hat and neck covering to protect your ears/neck from the cold, especially at the peak.7. Bring your own food, snacks and water/energy drink. There are no food stalls nor toilet at the peak.8.Toilet facilities are only available at the shelters, hence relief yourself before proceeding.Hope you enjoyed the hike.

We took up this challenge in early April, just stepping into Spring. We took the bus from Jeju Express Bus Terminal, took about 40 minutes to reach the Eorimok bus stop. Before taking the bus though, we highly recommend to check with the Tourist Information Center just outside the bus terminal on the last returning bus. Thankfully we checked, the last bus in March period was 4.55pm at Eorimok. Summer periods probably have a later last bus back. This bus serves the Yeongsil trail entrance as well.There is still a ~20 mins walk along the road before reaching the entrance to the Eorimok trail. Impressive mountain views once you reach the park entrance.The Eorimok trail starts off deceptively tame for about 500m. Once you get the past the wooden bridge, the tough hike starts. For the next 2km, we experienced the toughest climb of the entire trail. Steep and large steps at times, with large, uneven rocks littering the way up. The view is mostly green at this point.Near the end of the first 2km, we started to see melting ice along the trail. Certain parts were still iced up; we had to climb on top of the ice to traverse. Due to the melt, it was quite slippery. A hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended, though we had not brought any for our trip.After 2km, the trail leveled off into a plateau, a welcome rest after a seemingly endless slog. Strong winds and rain pummeled us that day, but all the more made the challenging climb more exciting and enjoyable. The rest of the way to the Witse Oreum was of average difficulty, and the landscape was foggy and snowy/icy. We encountered many instances that we had to walk on the ice so be sure to be equipped with good shoes to reduce the chance of slipping on the ice.We finally reached the Witse Oreum after about 3 hours, and bought and slurped down the ramen and its soup, as well as a chocolate energy bar. They also carried stuff like crampons and plastic sheet raincoat (we bought it for the heat trapping characteristic rather than for shielding against rain, we foolishly did not expect snow and ice in April tbh :P).We originally wanted to go down via the Yeongsil trail which meets the Eorimok trail at the Witse Oreum, but a pair of local, seasoned hikers who turned back for Eorimok warned us that the Yeongsil trail is still mostly frozen over and is very difficult to traverse at this time. Due to the lack of proper equipment, we heeded their advice and went back down Eorimok instead.The trip down was much faster, but hurt our knees more due to the impact. Tread with care as the uneven terrain may cause slip and falls.The journey down took approximately an 1.5 hours.Overall it was really challenging but fun.Things to note:1. Take note of the last bus timing or you may have to hitch a ride back to town.2. And of course, cater buffer time to reach the bus stop, there is still a 20 min walk to it.3. Hiking gear, especially proper shoes and a hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended.4. Early April features unmelted snow in the terrain, wear proper clothing.5. The same bus goes to the Yeongsil trail, may want to try hiking that as well (on different days of course)6. The Eorimok is pretty challenging for a novice like myself, heard from locals that the Seongpanak trail on the Eastern side is more relaxing but longer.7. The Eorimok trail does not reach the summit, if you want to reach the summit, try the Seongpanak or Gwaneumsa trails instead.

We took the Seongpanak trail for both ascend and descend, took us a whooping 9 hours! Please wear a good pair of shoes as the trail is rocky, that explains why we couldn't run up and down afraid of slipping and fall. Parking is very limited there, we reached at 8am and parked at the roadside because there weren't any parking left inside. Beware of the time as you would need to reach the last rest house at 12.30PM in order to continue your hike to the summit. Great view at the summit but it was very crowded. Overall, it wasn't a very difficult climb but it'll take you a whole day.

We took the Eorimok trail up and the Yeongsil trail down. It was snowy and we didn't have cramps on our shoes, better take some cramps. The last bus (740) back to Jeju-city goes about 16:30,  later you need to use a taxi.

We took the eomorik trail up - the first 1/2 or so was a tough climb, but through the woods so it was shaded. The second 1/2 was in open space - mostly on a Boardwalk type pathway. The path is clearly marked throughout the trail and there are signs to indicate how far you've come and how much you have left. The view was just average. It took us two hours to reach the top and we are not experienced hikers nor were we wearing hiking shoes, but we only took one short break for 10 minutes so we were always moving. We took the yongsil trail down and this was much more scenic with beautiful views of the mountains and rocks. Most of it was not shaded and most of the trail had steps so it was easy going down, but the look on people's faces as they were coming up showed how tiring it was to climb all those stairs! It took us about 1 hour and 15 minutes to get down. There were no taxis when we reached the bottom so we had to walk 30 minutes to the ticket booth to catch the bus. Since we just missed the bus and they don't run very frequently, we got a cab to take us back to our car at the eomorik entrance which cost about 10,000won.

We took bus to 1100 road then continue up in a taxi. Cost 2 of us 23000won but i feel it is worth paying because the taxi took us all the way to yeongsil entrance.excellent climb along yeongsil trail. It took us 2.25hrs to climb up including photo taking stops and 2 hrs down eorimok trail. Do wear climbing shoes due to many uneven rock surfaces. To take bus home, walk down main road for 15mins, on the left u will see bus stn no 780

We started with Yongsil Hiking trail passing through: Byeongpung Rock, Witse Oreum till the South Wall Folk and then to go down we followed the Donnaeko Hiking Trail. The way up is ok, the way down is quite difficult, ai recommend proper shoes.

We started at 8.30 at Yeongsil and exited at 1 pm from Eorimok . Lovely walking and climbing experience. Fresh air, lot of greenery, lot of birds. Just us and nature and fellow hikers. It was fun. Very exhausting but refreshing.One must have good pair of shoes. It has lot of rocky patches.Carry water and some snacks. Sunhat is must. The trail is well guided with sign boards and emergency numbers. It becomes windy on top so a jacket is useful.Must visit place.

We selected yeongsil trail since we rarely hike in own country and it is recommended for beginner. We started our hike at 9:30am and it took us 3 hours to reach the shelter while 2 hours to come down. We used back same route to come down since we drove there. The cup noodle shop was closed when we reached the shelter, grateful we brought some biscuit and roti else we will starving after long hike hours. We didn?t expect still having ice on mountain since it is turning spring. This get bit challenging especially to me as my shoes a bit tough to walk on the ice. But luckily a korean lady offered her stick to me and hold my hand to cross the ice path. It really make a different with the stick support. It is really recommended to get prepare self well with good hiking shoes, enough water and food.

We drove over to Sunrise Peak on a rainy, windy day in October and knew that we would be back the following day when the rain was supposed to be gone. Thank goodness, we came back, it would have been a miserable and somewhat dangerous hike in the rain. The ticket for the hike was less than $4 USD for two adults. The hike is full of stone stairs, and if you follow the signs (please follow the signs, don't be that person) there are plenty of places to stop, rest, and enjoy the view. At the halfway point, there is even a small shop with drinks and a souvenir stand that will char a wood sign for you with your name. When we got to the top, and enjoyed the clear, clean skies (so different from Seoul) we could watch the fishing boats and could even see some of the Women Divers of Jeju at the bottom. My suggestion is to get there early, the trails opened at 0730 and enjoy your hike. The bus tours and most other Korean tourists won't be out that early. Wear good shoes and comfortable clothing and bring your camera. It was a lovely sight in October. By the time we came back down after enjoying the views and watching the divers, the parking lot was starting to fill up with many bus tours. This place would still be gorgeous, but not as fun, if we would have had to share the stone stairs with 3,000 of our closest tourists.

We did the seongpanak trail. Check the weather the day before embarking, and make sure you have proper hiking shoes as the climb is rocky and some parts are pretty steep. Stretch your muscles before the climb or you'll end up sore the next day (or you can tote along some muscle rub)! Bug spray is also recommended, for those prone to mosquito bites. Try to get an early start if you can; as you have to pass the second rest stop before 1.00pm if you want to make it to the summit, otherwise the staff will not allow you to proceed. On average you would take 7-8 hours to hike to the summit and back, depending on the number of rest stops you make. There are 2 rest shelters along the way (one selling food like cup noodles and choco pie, pocari sweat and bottled water). There are toilets at both rest stops, but no water; no washing hands or flushing systems. Generally, the climb path is divided into thirds - beginning (relatively easy, mostly uneven but flat ground) - first rest stop - second leg (rocky ground, with some portions made up of many steps) - second rest stop - final leg (fair warning it gets really tough for beginners, as the terrain gets pretty rocky and steep) - summit!

We did the Gwaneumsa trail up Mount Hallasan to the peak and back is over 18 miles round trip, over 3500 feet of climbing and then descending it. But it's worth it. I offer only a few points of advice. It is tougher, 800m longer, but more scenic than the Seongpanak trail. To find the Gwanmeusa trail entrance parking lot, plug in the number for the Unesco Hallasa Gwaneumsa Office: +82-64-756-9950 (you only need the last 7 digits on Jeju GPS systems if driving).1) Be prepared with good hiking and walking shoes. We saw two shoes blow out, one about 2.5 hours in. The poor guy had to walk back. There is no rescue if this happens. Also, a girl's shoe blew out on the way down about 3/4 way down, it still nearly 1.5 hours to the end depending on how slow you go. I will discuss in #3 why good shoes are so important.2) Go early, and go slow if you are not in shape or do not do activities often. Hallasan is definitely attainable by nearly anyone but it is tough, very tough because of the steep steps. Unless you are in shape and do many physical activities all the time, I recommend starting at 6AM. You MUST be at Samgakbong shelter by 12:30PM otherwise they will turn you around. It is 3/4 way up the climb. From here it is another 2 hours to the peak of the Halla.3. The volcanic stone paths and the stairs will make your legs very very tired and your feet sore. I believe they made Gwanmeusa trail challenging with rocks on purpose. These are not small rocks, they are big ones that challenge each step. Walking sticks are highly recommended. The stones seem pretty and authentic until halfway up then they are tough. Then on the way down, each step seems like a sadistic joke played by the planners. Eventually you will be relieved to make it to the bottom to your car or bus.4. Be prepared for wind. We got lucky and it was warm the day we went... in fact low warm temperatures will seem even warmer due to humidity about 1/2 the time up the mountain and back. It is a little cooler and windier at the top. Wear light, polyester clothing in layers. long sleeve tech shirt, with light jacket and light rain cover. You should be OK. Gloves and hat or scarves during cooler time. Very light during summer due to heat and humidity.After you get down on Gwanmeusa trail, there is a small restaurant with Korean snacks like pajeon and gimbap, as well as a 7/11 next door. Drink some local mokkoli or soju with with the hot snacks/food! We had a great time. Only 20 minutes out Jeju City when there is no traffic. However with rush hour traffic, or busy time it takes about 45 minutes to get back into Jeju City.

We are a relatively fit family, but were not properly prepared for hiking Halla Mountain.  We made it as far as the Observatory (approx. 6 hours round trip). Since it rained days before, the summit was closed due to poor trail conditions.  Although some portions of the hiking trail are level & nicely paved (w/ wooden planks), the majority of the trail is very steep & rough (comprised of large, uneven volcanic rocks). Unfortunately, we wore Nike running shoes & Converse tennis shoes which did not provide adequate support & protection needed on the feet.  Since the incline & steps are uneven, you need to be careful where you step in order to prevent ankle or knee strains/sprains.  We saw some people fall on the jagged volcanic rocks & get scrapped pretty badly.  We found wood branches along the way to use as hiking sticks for balance.  This hike is alot tougher than the hike to the upper falls of Yosemite.  So we recommend that you come prepared:- sturdy hiking shoes and hiking poles- at least 2 bottles of water per person (there are 2 drinking wells w/ a communal drinking cup; we drank it & had no stomach probs)- bug repellent (we were there in the humid summer)- cooling scarf (to wet & wrap around neck)- energy food (power bars, fruit/nuts)- backpack (carry out your trash)- small first aid kitTip: There is a parking fee to park in front of the entrance.  All of the parking spots are usually taken very early.  Otherwise, if you park on the street or arrive by taxi/bus, there is no fee to enter the park.

Took the Seonpanak trail, one of the 2 only trails that will lead to the summit. It is a longer route compared to the other but was supposely less challenging. Well, still a very tough hike to me. Much of the path and climbs are big rocks so good hiking shoes and walking stick will be very helpful. No water along the way though one sign mentioned there is one, which was WRONG and not updated. My son believed in that signboard and finsihed his water way before half into the hike. Big mistake!Not much to see along the way, except if you take a detour to view sara oreum. Took about 3.5hrs to reach Jindalrae office/ shelter (which is 1500m high) and after much thought, decided to turn back due to lack of drinking water.Descending is much tougher for me and took longer time. Deers and boars were spotted.Do go early so that you do not have to park too far from the park entrance as the carpark gets filled up fast and you will need to park along the roadside. Go during weekdays if possible to avoid the crowds.Take note there is time limit to reach Jindalrae so that you can continue to the summit.

TLDR:Long hike, not that easy if you're not fit. 8-9 hours, 19.6km in total.Bring at least 3L of water each. They do sell water at the checkpoint, though only in 600ml bottles.Wear shoes with good sole and ankle protectionConsider taking a small towel (or two) to wipe away sweatBring a warm jumper and possibly a clean, dry shirt. Even in summer it's cold at the topStart the hike before 8.30am if you want to reach the peak because if you don't make it past the checkpoint at around 7km in, before 12.30pm, you won't be allowed to go to the peak.Bring a plastic bag for your rubbish because there are no bins at all on the hikeFor those who want moreRemember that this hike is longer than an average work day and you will need to replace water lost through sweat. Pack around 3L of water per person. Also pack some protein and carbohydrate heavy snacks such as nuts and dried fruits to keep up your energy levels. If you sweat a lot, consider bringing an electrolyte drink sachet to use halfway (or buy a can of Pocari sweat at the checkpoint). At the checkpoint, you can buy instant noodles, 600mL water bottles and Pocari sweat. If you don't want noodles for lunch, bring lunch. But keep in mind it's cold at the top so some warm noodles can be perfect. The noodles are a bit spicy though, so if you don't like spicy food, maybe bring your own lunch. There are absolutely 0 facilities for heating or preparing food. They won't even give you hot water for any noodles you don't purchase from them. Also there are no rubbish bins on the entire hike so you'll need to bring a plastic bag to carry out your own rubbish. The toilets are pretty gross and may or may not have toilet paper so consider bringing tissues. Also the toilets generally have no sinks, so bring some hand sanitiser gel.A small towel or two to wipe away your sweat wouldn't go astray, and a warm coat/jacket and clean, dry shirt will make your time at the peak much more comfortable (addressed in a later section).We took the 781 bus from Jeju city hall at around 6.55am. We arrived at the Seongpanak stop around 7.25am.Make sure you give yourself enough time to get to the Jindallae Shelter (checkpoint around 7km into the hike) before 12.30pm. If you don't make it to the shelter before 12.30pm you will not be allowed to continue up to the peak. It's very disappointing, I'm sure, to hike for 7km, hoping to see the peak and then be told you can't go because you missed the 12.30 deadline. I can't stress this enough. At the shelter, we heard some Americans complaining that they had missed the deadline by 24 minutes (they had started the hike at 10.30am) and that there was no information available on the trail or online about this rule. They were wrong on two counts- there are at least 5 signs along the trail up to the shelter stating that you need to pass by 12.30pm (in English). Also there are a number of blogs about this hike online which also talk about the rule. Now we started at around 7.30am and made it to the shelter by 10am, but we didn't stop to rest at all before the shelter. The walk up to the shelter is 90% easy level with gentle slopes and a few short harsher sections. If you are fit enough to contemplate doing a 19.4km hike then this section should be fine for you. If you start the hike around 8.30am, you will have no issues making it to the checkpoint in time and you should make it back to the bottom by 6/6.30pm. Earlier if you don't rest too long and are relatively fit.Note: there are several places that you can stop to rest just after the shelter. If you are running close to the 12.30pm deadline, just get past the shelter and then stop to rest once you've gone past. Just make sure you don't rest too long because you've probably got another 5-6 hours before you get back to the end of the trail including the rest of the walk to the peak, and you don't want it to get dark or have to rush on the way down.The next section after the shelter is graded as 'normal' by the signs along the route. This section does have a few challenging sections but also some easier stretches as well. If you have regular short rests then it's manageable for people of minimal to moderate fitness with some huffing and puffing.The last 1-1.5km of the walk to the peak is where it starts to get difficult. By this stage you've already hiked uphill around 8km and for probably 3-3.5 hours. The way to the peak is hundreds and hundreds of stairs often with many oddly shaped rocks to navigate around whilst traversing increasingly steep steps. If you're not super fit then you will struggle on this section. At one point we were setting ourselves goals to make it up 3 sets of staircases before we would rest for 1 minute then start again. But the important point is you are so close to the top now, so just keep pushing.The top can be quite crowded. We made it by around 11.30am and hung around for about 30mins to take photos and admire the view. My next piece of advice is- bring a warm jumper because the wind is cold up there and if you're anything like me, you will be sweaty which makes the wind even colder. Another point: if you're a sweaty person, consider bringing an extra dry/warm shirt (or two) with you to change into at the top (and possibly on the way back down). If you're prone to sweat a lot, this can make a huge difference to your enjoyment at the peak because you will by dry and warm. Your photos won't look so sweaty either. Make sure you take a picture of all members of your party with the peak stone marker or the crater to prove that you reached the top.Keep in mind that the way back down can take longer than the way up because you are now passing many people on their way up and going down is very hard on your already exhausted legs and feet. It can take 4-5 hours to get back down from the peak. We started going down at 12pm and made it to the bottom by 4pm, but we stopped several times.The path is quite narrow so on your way down, you will have to stop to let people pass in the other direction many times (unless it's significantly past the 12.30pm deadline, in which case everyone will be going down). The section between the peak and the checkpoint is very hard on your feet and legs. It will feel like forever but just remember that the track gets gradually easier and gentler the closer you are to the end. Stop at the checkpoint for lunch if you haven't already had it, or you feel like some hot noodles to warm you up.Keep on all the way down, being very careful not to slip. There are many rocks and if they are slightly wet, they are very slippery. Eventually you'll make it to the bottom. Then you can take your photographic evidence of reaching the peak to the little tourist office and for 1000 won each, you'll get a certificate saying that you reached the 1950m summit of Mt Hallasan. Congratulations!Sore feet and legs and weary bodies, you can catch the 782 bus back to Jeju city for a well earned rest.

Tips & things to take note:- Bring LOTS of water. On average 2litres per pax.- Bring sufficient food - basically breakfast,lunch,dinner.- Got to reach the checkpoint by 1pm to be allowed to attempt summit- Got to start descent from summit by 2.30pm- Gets cold and windy at the peak so bring a windbreaker.- You have to carry your own trash down. No bins on the mountain at all.We took 11hours and took the Seongpanak trail up and Gwaneumsa trail down. Seongpanak is easiest as its gentler but its the longest trail. Gwaneumsa is much more scenic. We were beginner hikers and hence probably took longer. The tourist  centre told us it would take ~9hrs. Spotted a deer on our way down on the Gwaneumsa trail. It was pretty scary though, we walked for 1hr+ without spotting a single human. (probably cause we were slow)My legs ached for 4 days straight but I have no regrets. My knees and ankles were insanely sore by the end of the hike. If you've even the slightest knee/leg issues, please think THRICE before you attempt Hallasan.Also, toilets are only available at the bottom (before the hike) and at the checkpoint. The toilets are GROSS. I couldn't do it no matter how hard I tried. Toilet was damp and stinky and lots of flies. No water system & its a squat system for ladies. Basically peeing into a hole filled with other people's waste. Saw another lady peeing in the woods instead...Also, all the announcements are in Korean, though signboards are in English.Aim to start hiking by 7am-8am. Any later, you may not reach checkpoint/summit in time unless you have a good enough stamina.Hiking sticks and shoes would help tremedously. Though we did it with regular sneakers. LOTS OF BUGS. Bring insect repellent though again, we didn't have one.Overall, its worth it and wouldn't do it again but have no regrets.

This review will be written from the point of view of a middle aged woman of average fitness, not someone for whom a 20 km trek is a walk in the park.Mount Hallasan is the highest peak in South Korea and if you are on Jeju island it's definitely worth visiting. We took the Seongpanak trail, a scenic , easy route which reaches the summit. Plan on one day for the trek up and down. Here are some tips:1. It goes like this - You take a bus or taxi to the Seongpanak trail, and start climbing. It's a mix of  some steps and an easy trail. After a while you reach the first stop - I forget the name - where you can use  the restroom. There's a small shelter where we had our packed sandwiches. After this, the trail becomes a little steeper, and you reach the next stage - the jindeballat rest stop.( Times by which you must reach the Jindeballat stop and when you must start your descent are posted on the trail). There are restrooms here - but inspie of information to the contrary , there was no food for sale. After this the climb becomes a little tricky , and you need around 2 hours to reach the summit . The views are amazing from the summit. The Koreans hiking the mountain were not only super fit, they were the sweetest people I've met. When I became tired near the summit, so many encouraged me with words like   Fighting!     Turn around and see how far you have come.  Tips :1. Wear good hiking shoes - at points , the trail is slippery, and good shoes with ankle support are helpful.2. Carry a stick. You can get your own hiking stick or buy one from the store at the bottom.3. Carry plenty of water and snacks.4. Take a selfie at the summit and you can get a certificate at the bottom stating you have completed the climb ( costs 1000 won)5. You do need a certain degree of cardiovascular fitness to make the climb comfortably. But apart from that, the uneven  rocks and boulders are a little tough to climb, so make sure you do some core and lower body exercises too. 6. If you climb down slowly, it gets a little dark by the time you reach the base. Carry a head lamp.

This post is about logistics and what to expect from the hike. My partner and I hit Hallasan around 6:45 in the morning on a Saturday to avoid the crowds. We drove to Seongpanak parking lot (free and was filling up quickly. A tour bus with dozens of hikers was already there) which was about a 30-minute drive from Seogwipo. From there we took a $15.00 taxi ride to the Gwaneumsa parking lot. As this was not a loop trail, we wanted to take the steeper/harder route in and have gentler descent (easier on our knees) back to our car. Turns out, doing it this way we avoided what felt like hundreds of people ascending when we were heading back later in the day. The Gwaneumsa parking lot has a fee. (Sorry TA fans, I didn't get the amount since we took a cab --- I am sure it is nominal, like all fees in RoK:) People are allowed to camp at the Gwaneumsa section of the park and I saw a few people starting their day as we marched to the trailhead. We were under tree cover and walked along a dry river bed for the first couple of miles. At this time of day, we only ran into seven other hikers on this trail. After you cross the river via bridge, the hike starts to get a little steeper. About two hours in, you hit a large, modern shelter and toilets. Good time to take a break and snack. Or keep carrying-on as you will get a chance to sit, eat and gaze at another resting place. After the shelter, you will cross a much larger, newer suspension bridge. Fresh water available here. The climb will get a bit harder for next half quarter mile. Continue past the foundation of the destroyed shelter. After you ascend the 18-22 inch tall stone steps, you will reach a ridge which is the other good stop.  No shelters (in fall you should opt for the shelter), but a nice wooden platform from which to gaze at how far you've come. Crows will land in search of scraps. At this point you are very near the top, only a couple more hundred feet to go.The crater was dry when we visited (first weekend in October), but still a wondrous site. The seasoned, local hikers brought burners and ramen and were happily chowing down near the crater. Darn! That would have been nice. The  t-shirt, fleece jacket and windbreaker I was wearing barely sustained me, so the hot ramen sounded freakin' great.The hike down Seongpanak was not nearly as enjoyable since we were bombarded by the late starters heading up. At one point, the hikers coming up were in a jam ? seriously, no one could move, there were so many people. There?s a large shelter a third of the way down. As another reviewer noted, be sure to wear supportive shoes with rigid shanks as you're constantly stepping on uneven rock.  I had on trail runners, which was fine going in, but heading down, my feet were pretty battered. The boardwalk was a nice breather when we could get it.*Seongpanak gentler ascent, (and descent) but be prepared to share the trail with dozens and dozens of other people.*Free parking at Seongpanak -- fills up quickly as early as 7am on weekends.*Toilets available on trail.*Take bimbimbap for a nutritious, affordable, and portable snack. Mandoo is another good one -- good balance of carbs and fat.*Listen and look Nuthatches, Wrens, Great T*ts, and other winter birds on the Gwaneumsa trail.*The park states you must hit the summit by noon. I think this is why so many people were rushing to hit the peak at the same time.

This is purely an activity you should do if you actually enjoy adventures! The guides say to get to the peak it will take 4.5 hours, 8-9.5km depending on which trail you take. We took the popular one, seongpanak because there is a direct bus route from the Jeju intercity terminal (number 781). Here's my itinerary for the day:08.45: arrived at seongpanak trail start09.45: arrived at Sokbat shelter11.10: arrived at Jindallaebat shelter12.30: arrived at peakSo in total 3.45 hours including breaks. I had around 1 hour at the top to sit, eat, take photos, luckily we chose such a clear day so everything was so visible!At 13.30, you have to head down, staff will tell you to move. We decided to take the Eorimok route (8.7km) down and made it to the bottom at 18.00. Things to note:- you have to reach Jindallaebat by 12pm or you are not allowed to the peak. - there are no trash cans, so you have to carry all rubbish. - on the seongpanak route, there is also the Saraoreum Observatory (extra 40 minute walk) which is supposed to have great views!- hiking boots or sturdy shoes are needed!I exercise everyday and managed it fine. My friend who does no exercise made it eventually and was super proud of herself!

This is my first ever hike and it was a real learning experience. Make sure to bring proper hiking shoes as the trail is VERY rocky and it can be easy to lose your footing and hurt your ankles. Walking stick is useful for the decent because it is MURDER on the knees. Coming down was much harder for me than going up. The view of Jeju at the top is amazing. But it was really crowded and I felt that the lake itself was a bit of a letdown looking like it was half drained... But overall, great hike and it's a good hike for first-timers! Bonus: I got to see a baby deer!

This is a very well maintained mountain park as expected of any Unesco World Heritage site. My wife and I visited on a Monday and it was packed with people. We climbed up from Yeongsil and climbed down to Eorimok. It's impossible to lose your way. The hike is moderate and you don't have to be very fit to do it. Trainers or tennis shoes are adequate in May. You can do it at a leisurely pace or try to break a speed record. Hot noodles is available at the top (this is not the summit trail) or you can pack your own lunch and there are also a couple of water stations along the way on the Eorimok trail. The view from around the top is expansive but hardly breathtaking. Overall it's a pleasant and enjoyable hike.If you park at Yeongsil and return at Eorimok or vice versa, you can take a taxi back to your car for 20,000 wons.

This beautiful hike did not disappoint. It's easy to get to by city bus, and foreigner friendly upon arrival. The trek itself takes about 10 hours total. My friends and I are active hikers, and I initially thought we could do it in less time... but with 2 shelter stations along the way, there seemed to be no rush. The earlier you go the better. You cannot go to the top if you arrive at the last shelter past 1 o'clock. It'll take you about 4 1/2 hours to get to that final shelter. BRING YOUR OWN SNACKS AND WATER SUPPLY. The final shelter has noodles and bottled water for sale, but that's it. So be sure to bring your own. Once you reach the top you'll be blown away by the crater and then view. Pictures do not do it justice. Be sure to bring:- food- water- plastic bag (for your garbage... there are no garbage bins)- good hiking shoes - the trail is very rocky at points.. the more grip the better- a hat- a sweater - depending on the wind, it'll be cooler at the top- a cameraHappy hiking!

There are only 2 trails that lead to the peak of Hallasan. Gwaneumsa and seongpanak trail. We took the seongpanak trail up and gwaneumsa trail down. It was no easy hike for sure. It took us 10 hours to hike up and back down ( late 20's, amateur!). We thought we give it a go and hike all the way to the peak since we were there. The scenery was breathtaking and definitely worth the hike. autumn foliage was amazing (but our leg muscles were aching real bad the next day). tons of people though. best to start the hike early about 6.30am if you wish to reach the top and if you are an amateur hiker with not-so-active lifestyle. be well prepared with adequate clothing, proper shoes and snacks

The whole trail takes about 45 mins to an hour to complete. It was truly interesting to be inside a lava tube and during the walk, there were informational signs to explain parts of the tubes! I would recommend bringing a hoodie and water proof shoes as it is very wet and slippery inside :) The dampness will make you feel cool even in the summer.

The trail was well setup for safety except the last mile to the peak but acceptable.The trail challenge level is medium and fit for all ages, stamina is required and right shoe is essential.The scenery at the peak is a good reward for achiever.  There were signboards along the way to provide the distance to the peak but no time estimation specially decent as the time required almost same time when you go up to the peak.

The Seongpanak Trail is the easiest, though the longest trail to hike up Mount Hallasan (bit over 9km). It's a beautiful path with a gradual ascent and some steep sections. The difficulty in this trail is the surface, as the majority of the time you are walking on volcanic rocks that make your footing uneven and it does wear you out. I hiked in Chaco sandals and was ok, but I'm used to it. I highly recommend wearing comfortable shoes. I also suggest getting an early start, before 8am. Because it's the most gradual ascent, this is also a busy trail with hikers constantly going both directions. Bring snacks and plenty of water. There is a re-filling spring water station a bit more than half way to the peak. Highly recommend if you are an outdoorsy person and can handle long walks/hikes.

The Jeju Olle Trail is an island-wide wooden path that takes you to the hills, rivers, beaches, and into the woods of Jeju. This is the perfect break from the busy urban jungle or if you want a break from the treadmill. Once on top of a hill, you will be offered a great view of the island.I took route 8 and connected to another route. I jogged some parts of the path and walked some (as some parts of the path are composed of stairs). It may be safer to walk since some parts of the path have no railing.Bonuses:There are huts and platforms that serve as resting areas. I encountered a local doing yoga in one of the huts.The river-side path has toilets and emergency rescue equipment ( life buoy, life vest, rope). Tips: Bring a camera, some sights are worth capturing; wear running shoes; and bring a phone, your GPS can be helpful in estimating your location.The path goes through or into private properties so be mindful not to trespass.

So I read a review that the hike up Hallasan was not very difficult so I thought I could do it in my Asics running shoes...well, I don't recommend that you do the hike up Hallasan without proper hiking gear.  Pack lots of water and food so that you can replenish yourself on the long hike up.  We went in early October and it was warm so dressing in layers was a godsend.  The route we took was to take Seongpanak up to the summit and then take Gwaneumsa trail down.  Taking Seongpanak to the summit took approximately 4.5 hours with 1 lunch break at the 3rd resting place before the summit. The resting place had washrooms and also a snack bar.  I saw people with cup ramen etc. Be prepared for the washrooms to be stinky.  It's the nature friendly kind.  The last stretch up to the summit on the Seongpanak trail is quite steep and some parts very rocky.  But the view makes up for it all!  Instead of hiking down the same trail, we came down the Gwaneumsa trail and wow, the views were breathtaking.  There were times when I had to stop and just take in the view just a bit longer because it was so beautiful.  T he Gwaneumsa trail doesn't have as many resting places so use the washroom when you can.  It took us a total of 9.5 hours to hike up and down Hallasan and I would do it again the next time I am in Jejudo Island!!

Seonpanak is known to be the more difficult route, however both to the summit have their difficulties. Seonpanak definitely has nicer views than Gwaneumsa, thats why we chose to walk down this trail, as your back is facing the beauty on the way up. This route has TONS of rocks which make it hard to balance and hike without the proper shoes. There are 4 or 5 base camps, only one offering water, and one with (disgusting) squat toilets. It took about 3 1/2 hours to hike from the summit, to the bottom. My legs are KILLING ME. But, it was worth it!

One of the most popular trails in Hallasan National Park.To get here, take bus 781 from Jeju City. The fare was 1 800 KRW (the driver can give change). The journey is about 40 minutes. The stops are announced in English. The stop is Seongpanak.Set out early as you have reach Jindallaebat shelter by 1 pm in summer (12 pm in winter). Otherwise you wouldn't be allowed to reach the summit.The trail is 9,6 km long (one way), about 4,5 hours without breaks. The trail is in some parts very ROCKY so good hiking shoes and walking holes are strongly recommended. Don't worry you wouldn't climb alone. A lot of Korean will be faster than you.The view on the summit is well worth and rewarding.Bring water and sun block.You can buy a certificate for 1 000 KRW.

One of my objective in my Jeju trip is to climb Mt. Halla and I did it! Of course it was not an easy trek up and down. I took Seongpanak trail going up the peak which was abt  9.6 km. And took the Gwaneumsa trail on my way down, which was about 8.7 km. I was staying in Seogwipo and I took bus #780 and it dropped me exactly in front of Seongpanak. However, there was no bus at Gwaneumsa, but there were several taxi. You can asked them to dropped you the nearest bus stop going to Jeju. But I think you can walk going there. But as it was raining so hard that afternoon and my legs were about to give up, I took the taxi. But it was quite near and the driver asked me 5000 won (not sure if that was cheap ir not). Dont forget to bring a raincoat and chocolates and sweet for energy while trekking. And if you want some souvenir, you can get a certificate of yout climb (1000 won) at the office. You need a photo at the peak as evidence. But actually, they didnt asked me to show mine, but really I reached the summit! I got 5 pics! :) And mind you, it's better to be in proper trekking attire, because I was not, especially the shoes, so I slipped several times on the snowy parts. Happy trekking!

One of 3 famous waterfalls in Jeju, along with Cheonjiyeon Waterfall and Cheonjeyeon Waterfallis but apparently the only waterfall in Asia to fall directly into the ocean.  Definitely worth the short climb down to get as near the fall for nice shots and a sea splash. If lucky, you might even catch a rainbow over the fall.  Walking shoes recommended to navigate the rocky boulders.  Do come early before the tourist horde arrive.  Adventurous hiking enthusiasts can continue to the Olle trail from the carpark entrance.

Not your typical stroll on a beach. This is more to walking on stones by the cliff. Please do wear comfortable shoes for walking at this location; not easy to walk on the uneven stones. Wind will be a little strong too, prepare a light windbreaker will help. There's certain times that you can't enter this attraction due to high tide (you can walk along the cliff) or strong wind. Please do check the opening time before heading there. The journey took us around 1hr to complete the cliff tour. There's a trail leading to a temple, but we did not go for it. There will be fresh seafood sold long the cliff, it cost us around 20,000 won for a plate of it. My guide told us that the price still can be negotiated.

Nice climb but plan ahead in case of rain, see weather forecast for best journey. We used Yeongsil trail, which  is the easiest  climb. Unfortunately we came during winter and did not have suitable shoes to continue our  journey. We stopped after 1km as trail is slippery from hardened ice, and returned to have soupy hot noodle at the base.Will do this again, hopefully  our next travel is on summer or autumn

Needless to say, Mt Halla was the highlight of my trip in Jeju. There was a good mix of clear sky and clouds during my hike up and down and the view is simply fantastic.
