There was not much to sustain interest in going further inside the cave so we decided to just go back. At least it was cool inside although the path was wet but nit muddy. Wear comfortable and non slippery shoes if you wish to see the cave.

We enjoyed this cave.  It's about 1 km to the end where the largest lava  pillar is located and then another 1 km back,  although the walk was relatively flat (no inclines) it was very uneven and slippery in places.  Wear shoes with good traction.  The cave is in a beautiful setting with many public toilets around.

Very educational walk through the lava tubes.  Be sure to bring a sweater and wear proper footgear (uneven ground).  If you are wearing any light coloured pants or shoes, be prepared to get them soiled alittle.  Basically its a   walk-to-the-end   and back type of attraction.  After the walk, you'll learn more about lava tubes and volcanic eruptions.

Really cool volcanic flowlines and terrain.  Bring a rain jacket with a hood or umbrella and decent shoes.  Although I saw a woman in heels, but wouldn't suggest it. ouch.Take flash off your camera and use tripod for good pics.Does not take long at all to get at end and back.

One of the finest lava tunnels in the world and listed as Unesco World Heritage. Only 1km of the 13,422m Manjanggul Cave is open to the tourists. Temperature inside the cave is low (around 11 to 21'c) so bring a cardigan or jacket if you afraid of cold. Do wear a covered shoe (best is sport shoes) as the surface of the cave is wet and water are ponding in some area and your shoes is definitely going to get wet. Also, the floor / surface is rough and uneven, not easy to walk fast especially for elderly who have weak knees or children below 2. Along the route there are board with explanation about different kinds of lava rocks in the cave (in English, Chinese, Japanese and Korean). It's interesting. At the end of the route is the Lava Column behind a platform where everyone will take a picture before going back. Oh..this is not the end, you still need to walk another 1km to go back to where you begin (that's where you exit too). So total journey is actually 2km.

My family explored this location during a family trip to Jeju Island.  My toddler twins are three years old and, with help, were able to navigate the entire length of the cave and back to the entrance.  The lava caves are fascinating and it's a good workout.  It is very damp, cool, and dripping inside - make sure to bring a windbreaker with a hood.  You can do it without (we had just sweaters) but it would have been better to be wearing that.  Plus, there are extensive puddles so waterproof shoes are a good option!  My only suggestion would be to increase the lighting a bit so guests can really appreciate the lava markings - the atmosphere with the low light is nice but I wanted to see more of the characteristics of the lava versus a non-lava flow cave.  Some people brought a flashlight and that seems like a great idea.  The price was very reasonable and there is a restaurant and clean restrooms.

It is a lava tube stretching 1km deep which means you need to walk 2km to get to the end and back to the entrance. It is a stunning cave and it's among UNESCO World Heritage sites. It is a popular site in Jeju and you won't be alone in the deep cave. It gets cold inside the cave and the floor is uneven so a coat and a pair of comfortable walking shoes/runners come highly recommended. The cave walk does not take that long, so it's a must visit.
Be immersed inside this lava tube! It's cold and wet, so prepare sport shoes and a jacket. Length: 1 km which you have to do twice (to go and come back)

Although I am not a Geography buff, I found Manjang Cave an interesting place to visit.  Only 1km was open to public.  Walking in was 1km and walking back to the entrance was another 1km, so total was 2km.The ground was very slippery and wet and lighting was not bright in the cave.  Good shoes and waterproof jacket will be advisable for visiting the cave.  The feeling of walking in a lava cave was a pretty awesome feeling to me.  The explanation of how certain formations came about were good and clear.If you have not seen lava cave before, I think it is worth a visit.

This place was soo dope! Take note that it was so nice to visit this place around sunrise so it was a good decision that we stay near the sunrise peak! Our airbnb owner was driving us to the sunrise peak 30 minutes before the sunrise. As a beginner, the track was good and a nice hiking for us. Definitely a must visit when you stay at Jeju Island. Note that, bring your hiking shoes and hiking outfit! If you come in the morning, you cant see the woman diver show or take a boat around, but it was nice!

It's a nice shopping street that is about 5 min walk from Dongmun Market and beside Jungang underground shopping place that is closed till August 2016. There is Tommy Hilfiger interesting souvenir store The Islander local designer and mid-range fashion shops shoes and stationery stores and cafes as well. Nearby at one end is the attraction Gwandeokjeong Pavilion. At the other end of the street there is also a black pork street.

For those that love fish, this market is a place to visit. Very interesting but not for me. You can also shop for shoes, clothes, chocolate, souvenirs and fruit. I found it a little on the dirty side but it might be because I don't care for fish much.

Every kind of locally caught fish and produce can be found in the Dongmun Market, as well as some imported items.  Don't miss out on getting a box of mandarins or Hallabong oranges.  Try the kiwifruit, too.  It's also a good place to sample Jeju's   street food   made by local vendors.  You can find all sorts of clothes and many household gadgets, accessories, rain shoes, Korean quilts, souvenirs...you name it, it's most likely in the market.  You can visit Dongmun during the day or at night.  Nearby, you can also see Sanjicheon Square, where local performers can also be found playing, singing or dancing for tips.  Some local seniors and maybe a few homeless persons frequent the area, adding to its   color.    The square is by a small tidal inlet, and features a quaint railing with traditional Korean characters on the railing.  Do check it out!

We visited the Manjanggul Cave on a very wet day.  The floor of the cave was wet and the stones slippery. Puddles of water lined the route. It would have been all right if the light was brighter but it was not. The lighting was dim and you can easily twist an ankle if you stepped into one of the many crevasses in the floor. The dim lighting did not make things any easier and you really have to watch where you are going. Wear proper walking shoes if you do not want to slip on the stones. I felt that the lava cone that was our destination was quite dazzling but I wish the authorities had spent a little more care in making the whole walk safer for those who are mobile but who are a little unsteady on their feet like the elderly. The video presentation that we saw after the walk was good. The exhibits were well curated and gave us an idea of other earth formations resulting from volcanic activity in the area.

The Manjanggul lava tubes caves are amazing and the walk is well worth it.  Dont forget to take your flash camera as you will not see sights like this again.The sides of the cave are smooth from the flowing hot lava and show striations along the sides from when the lava level was falling.  The size of the tune varies from small to very large.  Lighting has been set up to high-lite many of the features.  Wear good waterproof shoes as the floor is uneven  and there are many puddles from dripping water

The Koreans we were traveling with said that this was the largest folk village they had ever been to.  It is very large with many many huts buildings and gardening examples.  Sunscreen and good walking shoes are a must.  This is not a quick in/out place.  There are several restaurants inside.  There is a Jeju cactus fruit taffy shop inside that will give you free samples - so yummy we had to buy a few bags to bring home!This is also a popular tourist destination but the place is so big that it never felt overcrowded anywhere we were except the entrance.  There are waterfalls a maze flower gardens and many little shops tucked in here and there all over the place.  There are restrooms near the main entrance.If you want to experience an almost overwhelmingly large example of Korean folk history this is your place!

The 1k walk is really interesting and had good info in english. It's much cooler as soon as you walk down the steps and raincoats are useful as there are water drops and wear comfortable shoes for the rocky and wet floor. Most of it is quite dark but you can still get good photos. Definitely worth the visit

Really cool and Interesting lava tube under the ground of Jeju island. It shows a lot of cool facts about how it happen and also how the island is formed like it is today. The attraction is both on English and Korean. The test is easy to under stand on the sign and pictures there are. Remember to bring some good walking/waterproof shoes or boots because there are water every were and the terrain is uneven because of the lava it self.

Our last destination for our first day in Jeju is this temple. Before arriving to the worship place near the parking area you will find vendors selling various souvenir items. Upon entrance we walk through the garden where we saw trees with oranges (mandarin in their place). It was last week of March when we visited this place we were lucky to see trees beautiful big oranges. Continuing the path we pass big rocks display with signage written in Korean which I don't understand. We then continue to walk farther and took the stairs until we reached the temple. Just like other places for workship you are not allowed to bring your shoes inside the place. Near the temple is a fountain they say if you drink water in the fountain it will bring good health and good luck to the person.
It`s worth to see the waterfall going straight to the sea. Have good shoes - you'll need to walk on stones to get close to it.

Driving from Jeju city centre to Manjanggul Cave is straight forward and easy. Parking is also free for this attraction. We had to purchase a ticket prior to entering the cave through a steep and slippery rocky stair. The cave is wet and cold even in March. The grounds are contantly wet with water dripping throughout the cave. It is also not easy to walk on as the grounds are very uneven and filled with puddles of water. Walking through the cave was thrilling and filled with excitement. Round trip to and fro the cave took us about 1hr30mins. Would highly recomend to anyone visiting Jeju Island. Proper shoes are also recommended as it can be very slippery and slip and fall may happen. Kids and Older people may find this attraction tough and difficult to walk through.
About 5mins down the long flight of stairs and you get upclose with the waterfall. Helpful to come with proper shoes as you can walk closer the the waterfall on the rocks to get a good photo.

A popular hotspot and parking can be a problem. The waterfall is nice but not very spectacular. Can stand on the rocks bottom to catch a better glimpse of the waterfall but mind the slippery rocks. Wear a sport shoes with good traction or simply walked bare footed on the rocks.

You need to purchase a ticket at 2000won each and then take 130 steps down a flight of stairs to get to the waterfall. Comfortable shoes are recommended if you want to get closer to the waterfall. It is advisable to use your feet to check for the stability of the rocks before stepping on them as there were some loose and moving ones amongst the pile of rocks. The rocks nearer to the waterfall are wet so be careful if you want to get even closer to the fall. The waves crashing on the shore are also rather strong, so be more cautious if you?re moving nearer towards the shore.

You have to walk on a ramp in order to get into the museum because car cannot drive into the area of exhibitions. The venue is separated into indoor and outdoor. For outdoor exhibitions, you should be aware of the weather. If it rains, the ramp would be slippery, so visitors are recommended to wear water-resistant shoes for unusual events. There are plenty of cars exhibited, including antique cars and modern cars. There are descriptions beside every single car including where they produce, which car firm belongs to and when it is first produced. There are many limited-edition cars and some of them are even the only one in the world. There is also a shop located besides the entry of the museum, selling different car models and peripherals. I bought a wheel like key chain, it costs 10k KWD, which is relatively cheap compare to the models of cars.So, if you are a car fan or you want to have some souvenirs about cars, you are recommended to go to the car museum to buy your favorites.
address: 제주 서귀포시 안덕면 중산간서로 1610 세계자동차 제주박물관
입력주소: 제주 서귀포시 안덕면 중산간서로 1610 세계자동차 제주박물관

review: With a 2,000?? fee, this waterfall is well worth a visit! It's a short walk down from the parking lot - not hard to get to at all. You should, however, wear comfortable and supportive shoes because you need to balance on rocks in order to get close to the falls.

We went with my 63 year old mom, husband, and 15 and 6 year olds. It was great! It's waaaay longer, wider, taller and more interesting of a lava tube than at Volcanos national park in Hawaii! The largest accessible in the world. Bring a waterproof camera, hiking shoes or at least tennis goes, a raincoat or jacket. Won't wear white. I still can't get the ash stain out of my sons sleeve after he fell in a puddle. It's only a few dollars to get in. Do the quick museum first, if you want to know more about it. Cold, wet, dark, tired but Loved it!

We drove ourselves and although a little hard to find, it was worth the effort. The area was quite well set out with information and small local restaurant and gift shop area. Entry is free to Jeju workers but about 5,000 won - the steps down are step but well made. We walked about 2 kms to the end of the tunnel - it was damp, cold and generally well lit. Wear sturdy shoes and a warm coat, take a water bottle.  Worth a look.

Visited Manjang Cave in the month of June, which is Summer in South Korea. Entrance fee is nominal - 2,000 won per adult and it should be half price for kids.Temperature within the cave was 21 Degrees Celsius to around 11 Degrees Celsius, a good respite from the summer heat. Humidity is high within the cave, with dripping waters (natural) and wet grounds. Be prepared and carry with you a windbreaker, cap and good covered walking shoes. The entire walk is around 2km. Not entirely suitable for young toddlers, but kids above the age of 7 should do fine. Interesting rock formations within the cave, and a giant lava column at the end the walk. If you have not visited any lava caves before, this UNESCO site is a must-go when in Jeju!

This is, so far, the best waterfall I have ever been. You need to go down from a lot of big rocks to go near the falls. That is what makes it exciting. Wear comfortable shoes and I recommend to wear pants.

This is a lava tunnel, NOT a stalactite cave. There is one huge stalactite at the end of the tunnel, but if you are planning to see many stalactite formations, you would be very disappointed. Nonetheless, there are many interesting rock formations here. The horizontal and vertical lava flow marks on the cave walls and dimmed lighting give an aura of an alien tunnel. There is also a stone that looks like a stone turtle. :-) The air is slightly chilly and damp with occasional water dripping from the cave ceiling. I would recommend a light sweater or a light scarf to make experience enjoyable. And wear comfortable walking shoes, since the ground is very uneven(but interesting).

There are three main waterfalls in the south of Jeju and this was the first one we saw, it is the only one by the sea and is about 15 minutes walk from downtown Seogwipo. There is a nice little park before the entrance to the waterfall.We went in the afternoon and it was crowded with many people taking pictures. Would suggest going early in the morning (they open at 8am), better for pictures with the sun shining on the waterfall and less people. Bring proper footwear or shoes you don't mind getting wet as it is very rocky and you can get wet from the spray. Entrance fee is 2000 won and it is a short walk down some stairs to the waterfall.
The water was cool (it was a hot day), we went on a weekday so it was not too crowded. Take off your shoes and frolick.

One of UNESCO site, worth visiting. It is a good experience walking through a dark, deep and huge cave.  Very important to wear a proper walking shoes if you are exploring the caves as it is not easy to navigate the 1KM long rough path of lava stones.  Bring a jacket as the temperature is cold inside (14 degree celsius), and a torch light if you can to help you as some rock surfaces were slippery with puddles of water around throughout the journey. It is rather tiring to navigate in the dark as you will be focusing on the ground instead of enjoying the surrounding lava structures.

One of the real highlights for my visit to Jeju Island. It's absolutely fascinating and I've been to a few different caves before. It's different because it's a lava tube cave and there are a few different information boards in there to explain the different features which helped to understand how it was formed. It's very well and cold in there so bring a wet jacket and comfortable walking shoes (waterproof/ resistant if possible) with good traction. There is a small descent but other than that it's rather flat in there so most people should be able to do it, just watch out for the wet surface. If you go to Jeju, you must visit this cave.

Never been to a beach where the sand had a huge net over it. But then I'd never been to a beach in Korea. We werent too upset because we kept our shoes clean for the museum we visited next. The only sunbathers were foreigners, everyone else waded in the water almost fully clothed or stood on the lava rock taking selfies. It's pretty and there are places to grab lunch or an ice cream.
It?s very cold in the cave. So dress warm for this location. Try wearing waterproof shoes, lots of puddles.

it was just a super long cave that is really cold, perfect when you are visiting during the hot summers. Wear comfortable shoes because you will be avoiding water puddles, trekking on uneven rocky floors. Its just a super long walk in and out.

Free carpark. There?s a replica fountain of the real lava column which is found at the end of the tunnel. Entrance costs 1000 won. Descent about 80 steep steps into the tunnel. Temp change can be felt immediately. Floors are damp from the rain and the water drippings from the ceilings. Best to have a hoodie and raincoat or an umbrella. The tunnels are very dark and damp. Go slowly and let the eyes adjust to the dim conditions.  There is a marking at 850metres which is great as it is difficult to gauge the distance while walking in the dark. Then you will have 150 metres more to go before reaching the end of the tunnel open to public. The world?s largest lava column, 7.6m in height is located at the end. Advise: wear sensible shoes with good grip as the floors are damp and slippery ; warm clothing; carry a torch- or use your phone?s flashlight. It makes the trek so much easier. Lastly, restrooms located at the surface level are decent though damp and a bit stinky.

Falls is very beautiful.  You walk down 100 steps or so, then across big rocks to the bottom of the falls.  Wear tennis shoes or flip-flops for rock hopping!  Lots of water spray, and nice wading in the cool water as it runs across a few rocks to the ocean.

Bring your jackets, better to be water proof! Cave temperature is around 10 plus degree or lower. Also ground is uneven so wear good shoes and walk slowly. But overall fascinating to see how geography works

Believed to be formed about 2,00,000 ? 3,00,000 years ago, this UNESCO protected heritage centre, the Manjjanggul Lava tube tunnels said to be one of the longest ( around 7.5 km) and well maintained Lava tube tunnels in the world. Though there would not be much to see around, the sheer excitement one experiences just walking into the dark ,rocky ,slippery tunnel is worth the money paid for.Important things to remember.-Those who are having difficulty in walking should avoid getting down the tunnel as the floor is rocky,slippery and uneven.-A good pair of shoes is a must. No high heeled footwear please.-Carry or wear warm clothes as the inside temperature would be much lower than outside.-Wearing a cap/hat would be also good as water would be dripping on your head as you walk.-The Tunnel is open for 1 KM for the Public and with minimal lighting. Carrying a low intensity torch would be best.

Beautiful Falls. Also its rare to see falls directly in ocean apparently only one in Asia. It said that the dragon's spirit is contained in the water which can cure diseases and bring rain during drought. Easy to access. Make sue you wearing comfatable Shoes, it does get slippery. We had some lovely click out here, spl couple ;)

A must see when in jeju. Jeonbang Waterfall is the only waterfall that falls directly into the ocean. It?s a beautiful sight to see. However, if you are handicapped it is not accessible, as there are stairs. Make sure to wear gym/grip shoes as there are lots of rocks/ slopping hazard. There are also (henyo) female scuba divers that harvest abalone and various seafood that are available to eat nearby. Definitely check it out!

I have visited a number of limestone caves before and this is the first lava tube cave I ever visited. I found it fascinating. Be warned that the floor is undulating and wet and one needs a pair of hiking shoes and a rain jacket to really enjoy this place.

The lava tube is different from other lime stone or erupted caves I seen before, this one is very big and the its formation and feature is fantastic.  Try to avoid the high crowd and prepare jacket, poncho and hiking shoes.  We took good camera and tripok to take picture.

I have never seen anything like it. The walk was unbelievable! A must see and do in Seogwipo. Great for travellers who love nature, hiking (must wear comfortable shoes) and photography. Highly recommended.
A UNESCO Heritage site, but basically an underground hole. Make sure you wear good hiking shoes+you may get wet.

You need to bring jacket that day we went even if its summer still cold inside, wear rubber shoes easy for you to walk, though there's not much inside to see, young kids will not enjoy for sure they will just be tired walking very long cave.

Good sight seeing place and jungle trekking. Wear sport shoes for easy walking if you plan to walk   round the sea  . Weather was just nice for walking in April. Crossing the bridge and standing there watching the big sea was feeling awesome.

Went there to see how the locals interact, to feel and absorb the local vibes. Nice to see how the locals live and behave. Pleasant to stroll through the stalls. Went there in the morning and saw many fresh local produce like seafood, meats, fruits, vegetables, household items, clothes, bags, shoes .......just about everything. We also saw many stalls selling street food - bungeoppang ( fish shaped bun-filled with sweet red beans) , eomuk ( fish cake ), hoppang ( steamed buns) , tteokbokki. ( stir fried rice cake) , gyeranppang ( egg bread ), dak-kkochi (korean chicken skewers ). Had a great breakfast on these streetfoods. We also saw lots and lots of hallabong too. Very juicy and sweet these Jeju?s iconic mandarin oranges. Not to be missed one must try the hallabong fruit juice and hallabong icecream. We also bought some local korean snacks , kimchi and souvenirs to bring home.

The stacked cliffs of Yongmeori are beautiful! This was one of my favorite sites in Jeju. It's a very windy walk but in the summer, this provided respite from the humid heat. The rocks are uneven and bumpy, so it is a good idea to wear sturdy shoes.You have to pay a small fee but it's very much worth it. Along the walk, there are women selling raw seafood meals for 10,000 a pop. It's a very simple set-up: plastic stools and chairs, some garlic, gochujang, and soju if you wish.

Since my hotel is located at one end of this shopping centre, I visited this place every day during my stay in Jeju. Being underground, it was great to shield the winter cold especially in the evenings.The shops essentially sell similar products - clothings, cosmetics, shoes, accessories, bags, hats, etc. There are few eateries and fast food chains too. This shopping street tends to be crowded in the evenings. There are free toilet facilities at one end, i.e. exit 1.

You can go underground and experience the cold temperatures close to 12 degrees.. its like walking through an igloo.. Cold air everywhere and some parts are wet due to the precipitation though the soil. Reminder to bring a jacket and good shoes as floor is slippery and area is dark! Very good experience!
Went on a rainy day but most importantly wear comfortable clothing and walking shoes that won't slip on rocks.. Also bring a sweater or wear long sleeve as it gets colder further inside.

We were taken to Manjanggul lava Cave as part of a day tour. I've never been in one before and this was pretty neat. Comfy shoes are a must. The feeling under your feet is a slippery one and one of many uneven ridges. The cave is dimly lit which does give it atmosphere but does pose problems if you are unsteady on your feet. The 1km tube takes about 25 mins to walk to the middle of where the volcano erupted. You can't go any further in. We thoroughly enjoy this fab experience and would highly recommend it. It is not suitable for people in wheelchairs or strollers. There are lots of information boards through out the lava tube giving you lots of nformation. The coloured lighting adds to highlight the different textures and forms of the rocks.

Visited this amazing cave recently with the kids. Aged between 7-13 years old. We all enjoyed it. Remember to bring along a jacket as the cave can be quite cold. It?s about 11 degree Celsius. Wear a pair of good shoes too as the walking surface is uneven and wet.
This is the longest tunnel with very dim light and the temperature is 13 deg C.You will need a proper shoe/sneaker not slippers to walk safely on the uneven ground
This is a fantastic place to see the awesome landscape of jeju. There is quite a bit of walking so wear comfortable shoes. It will also be rather hot in the summer as well.
Nothing much in this cave except it was very cold for me.. would suggest to go in with shoes. And iz a 1000m walk from the start till the end

Nice walk across it and seeing the island plus cliff wall and the fishing harbour bay. After the bridge a serenity walk with beauty scenery walk. Use proper shoe for the walk. The bridge also light up at night with colors.
Make sure to wear good shoes.  Also wear rain gear to keep from getting wet.   Walk slow and you should be fine.   Great experience and would recommend to visit. !

Lava flows which are cool-you walk along about 20mins or so then see the large lave flow at the end which i think is one of the largest in the world. The walk is in semi darkness but there are enough lights to see by without ruining the ambiance. No need for a torch. Bring good shoes as the ground is super uneven. It can get cold too so bring a jumper.
It was an interesting visit but make sure you are able to walk two kilometers in dim lighting and on uneven flooring which can be wet and slippery. Wear comfortable shoes.

It was almost 1.5 hrs drive from our hotel but was worth it. It's the only 1 of the 8 caves (I think 8) that is open to public . Amazed by how mother nature ends up creating such beautiful sites . You can keep walking for almost a km in the cave where lava used to flow when volcano erupted . It has some signs describing the various locations. Tip: wear shoes and take a jacket if travelling with kids as it gets really cold inside

it was a hot summer day when our tour guide took us to this park. It has a very large variety of plants and bonsai. Some of the bonsai plants are more than 100 years old!! The most interesting bit in my opinion was going into the lava tubes which are like under ground caves with unusual rock formations. Wear comfortable shoes. Its not strenuous but best to be comfortable when walking.

It is worth a visit when you are in Jeju Island.We enjoy the two kilometres walking vv. please make sure that you have a comfortable shoes no  as the surface is really from the lava. This cave is one of three unesco heritage sites in Jeju Island.Nice and cool inside the cave and interesting marks of lava. We enjoyed it very much.
Enjoyed the walk in this cave. Quite cold inside and wet. Got to be probably dressed and have good walking shoes.
Bring your jacket: is super cold as walking into cave. Entrance fee is KRW 2000. Wear sport shoes: cave floor is slippy.

A good wet wet weather option. Make sure to wear proper walking shoes as the walk to the inner pillar was 1km through a dimly lit and oft wet underground tunnel. The stairs leading to the tunnel was steep and the temp in the tunnel was lower than outside. Maybe not for those who's afraid of the dark.

Yes, it's just a cave. Nothing much there besides a long, large, cool and dark cave with uneven walking path. The walk path is uneven and wet. Please wear good walking shoes and that will be good if you have flashlight. I will not recon to bring kids or old folks to this attraction. I saw only 1 security camera at the entrance but none in the cave and no workers in the cave. So, if someone injured or any emergency help, I guess no one can help you except other tourist.

We were very excited to visit Manjanggul Cave, and it did not disappoint.It is quite a large cave, and if you walk slowly and look around at the cave carefully, you can see the changes of the lava formation colours and shapes.Make sure you walk the entire length to check out the lava tube, I mean - when will you get another chance? Also make sure you wear comfortable shoes, as my recommendation of walking slowly is not just to check out the different sections, it also means you won't trip, as the ground is pretty uneven and the cave is quite dimly lit!

We were at Seongsan Ilchulbong in the afternoon before we went to Manjanggul. It was a god decision as it was a brief respite from the scorching sun.That aside, this place is itself a gem. Well maintained and interesting facts have their own boards for the visitors to read. Light jacket is highly recommended if you don't like cool places. Temperature is similar to if you blast your AC unit in your room. Very nice. Wear good shoes. Slippers and heels / platforms not recommended although we saw several girls wore them. You'll be walking on solidified lava. Hence, the walking surface is very unkind to ill-equipped feet. :).Overall, very good experience.
Very nice, also very cool inside. Walk is pretty light but the floor is uneven so wear your walking shoes.

This was an interesting place that was well preserved. Wear a good pair of walking shoes as the place is quite dark with very uneven floors so watch your step. The air in the cave is kept at a constant temperature of about 19-20 degrees all year round, not a problem as we went in winter. Very good if you have not seen anything similar to this before.

This is the first UNESCO world heritage that we visited in Korea. Walking distance about 1km, so be prepared to wear the comfort shoe. Some area a bit dark so be careful. Overall nice experience to visit this nature cave.

This is a most unusual feature on the North-East coast of the island of Jeju, South Korea. Although there are a few around the world, these tubes are some of the best preserved ones and it is a Unesco World Heritage site. It is also accredited as a Global Geopark.You can walk 1km of the tube at Manjanggul (there are over 7 km but not open to the public)- it is damp and dark so go prepared with shoes that won't slip and also have an extra layer. The temperature drops quickly: it was 28C outside when we visited in late September but only 15C inside. However, they are very 'manageable'.The caves are well-preserved and present themselves as a long tunnel which displays various features. Though it is dark and so difficult to take photos, you can clearly see the lava flowlines and the lava shelves whilst the floor is ropy lava. At various points along the walk, you are directed to other features such as lava columns and lava stalacmites. Only one entrance of the 3 existing ones is used by the public.Well worth a visit, and especially so if interested in geography/ geology.
The place is nice and well maintained, it was a bit cold down there so i would suggest a light sweater and comfy shoes as the floor was uneven with lava stone and made it hard to walk
nicely labelled signs to explain the lava tubereally awesome to see the marks left by nature it's about a slow walk of about an hr, wear good shoes and a jacket as it gets cold
Must visit.  Remember to bring a light jacket with comfort and non slip shoes.  It is about 40 mins walking, but worth it.

Manjang Cave is one of the finest lava tunnels in the world. It is one of the UNESCO heritage. There's a good 1km walk from the entrance of the cave til you get to the end of the tunnel to sight the beautiful stalactites.  The tunnel is of course much longer than that however access is only allowed up to the 1km mark. The path is dark, chilly,  rocky and slippery. Please wear good shoes and bring a jumper and mini torchlight if you wish.
It's quite a long walk to the end and return but I enjoy myself. wear suitable shoes, its rocky, wet and limited light source.

Its definitely a worthwhile trip to make and just walking through the Lava Tube is quite an experience.  It is not everyday one has the opportunity to walk through and see the various formations, the caves formed, columns, the different textures formed, etc.One needs to be relatively fit to do the walk with comfortable shoes as the location tends to be wet. Elderly should have a walking stick which will help and carry a torchlight.  Its a few degrees lower underground.

it's definitely a unique place to visit but you should wear proper shoes as the 2km walk to and from the entrance has lots of rocky areas...the cave was dark,cold and wet but worth the visit if it's part of your tour.

It's a natural wonder.  Amazing how lava can create a tunnel as large as this. Must visit when in Jeju.  Wear a pair of walking shoes and an autumn jacket as temperature falls to around 15 inside the tube. It'll take you at least 30 minutes to walk 1km in and then another 30 minutes out.  So,  it's pretty chilly if you are without a jacket. Floor is wet therefore walk carefully & enjoy the unusual sights especially the walls & ceiling of the tube. Walk until the end as there's a lava column in there, the only one.

It was an interesting experience to walk through the 1km long tunnel if you enjoy understanding and seeing the various structures and rock formations formed from the lava flow. Wear comfortable shoes with good grip, tunnel is rather slippery and rocky.  On a side note, I think I enjoyed walking through the Manjanggul Caves better than the DMZ Third Tunnel. :)

It is really long cave. Pls wear sensible shoes and high heels are NO NO there.I think it is nice for the first 15 min but after 15min it all looks the same. So unless you really knows you rocks well, or else it will be just a walking trip

It is a lava tunnel. It's interesting to see but not a must-see. There were some stairs to descent into the tunnel at the entry and it gets pretty dark inside. Your eyes will need to adjust, and there isn't any place to grip along the wall. Please wear comfortable shoes and some layers since it gets wet and chilly inside. Walking paths are uneven on some areas, and most are not well-lit. The tunnel is purposely not well-lit to preserve the natural habitat of its resident animals. A round trip from the entrance will take about 30-40 mins if you're strolling through the tunnel. We visited this cave as part of Yeha East course tour. If you have interest in geological formation, stalagmite, and nature, you may find it interesting.

I'm from Hawaii, but this cave was very impressive, not to mention a welcome reprieve from the heat and humidity!Walking on wet lava rock is not for the faint-of-heart, so wear a good pair of tennis shoes that can provide some traction, because it is slippery!

If you love nature and have never seen any volcanic formation before, it would be worth the visit. Personally,  i enjoyed walking inside the cave and having a look at the volcanic formation.  It's like you can almost imagine how the lava flowed inside the tunnel a few thousand years ago :) i was in awe of how powerful mother nature can be. It was quite cold inside. Wear layers and proper shoes.  Can be quite slippery as well.

If you have an opportunity to visit these lava tubes, then make sure you do!   We have lava caves in New Zealand and I have seen the lava tubes on Hawaii, but these are giants in comparrison.  The grounds of Manjang Caves are well kept.From the carpark it is only a 3 or 4 minute walk along a concrete path to the entrance of the caves.   We were expecting big, but these caves are huge!There are a number of steps leading down into the mouth of the cave and then you are inside this amazing formation.   It was quite an eerie feeling as we ventured deeper and deeper inside the tube which measures approx 5meters wide and up to 10 meters high.   The temperature is quite pleasant inside the caves and it is a little damp.   Even though we all had good walking shoes on, we still had to be quite careful of where we walked on the uneven, slippery  floor.   It is true that there is not a lot of light inside the cave, but we felt that the dim lighting added to the atmosphere.   In hindsight, a torch might have been helpful.All in all, definitely well worth the visit and would highly recommend to all. I would recommend that this is probably not a safe place for the elderly and very young children.  My elderly parents waited for us at the main building where there was a restaurant, shop and toilets.

I saw one picture in instagram and decided to go Jeju olle train route 8. Actually, Route 8 is restricted, but you will see everyone just walk into. It is called 'Gaetkkak Columnar Jointing (媛二쇱?\由щ?)' It is better to wear comfortable shoes since you have to walk on rocks, but you better dress nice if you want to have a good picture. I saw many girls dressed up and walked on the rocks which looked extremely tiring but worth it. You might need to line up to take a photo, and I also waited to take a photo at specific spot. Now I have really cool pictures ;)

I really enjoyed my visit here. I've never visit a volcanic cave before but its an very cool place (literally!). The temperature in the cave is much cooler than outside, although be careful, because they keep it quite dark so it can be difficult to walk on without good shoes.

I haven't been anywhere else in the world where there has been the option to walk a couple of kms through a volcanic cave. The experience is quite surreal. From 30+ degrees on the outside you soon plummet down to perhaps 10-15 degrees, damp and dark. The rock formations are stunning and they've done a good job to keep it natural without too much human interference.Bring sensible shoes.

I find walking in this lava cave is interesting as it is so cool inside and surprisingly there is no bad smell as it is rather wet. The cave produces it's on air conditioning as the temperature inside is around 15-17 Celsius. Some areas are well lighted and some are not, proper walking shoes are needed as there are many uneven areas along the path provided. Good experience for the ones who loves outdoor!

Despite the heat, its very cooling inside the cave. Took a walk and I find that it was smaller than what I expected. Path is quite rocky and its good to wear proper shoes instead of sandals or slippers. It can be quite slippery too. Its good to visit but if you are tight on your schedule I think you can give it a miss :)

As there are not much railings inside the cave to guide the tourists while walking and steps are uneven, make sure to wear comfortable walking shoes. It is beautiful and a must visit when in Jeju. I joined a tour for this visit as it is quite far from where I stayed. Tourist spots in Jeju are not close to each other and I didnt quite see a lot of public transport the in the area.

An amazing cave; one of nature's wonder!  Must wear a good pair of walking shoes, and be prepared to walk some distance. Enjoy the strange and mysterious dark tunnels. Dimly lit, but well kept with small platforms and bridges, this UNESCO heritage site is one selling point selling for Jeju! Worth paying a visit.

A very wide (23m), high (18m) and long cave (7+ km) one can walk along by yourself (about 1km is open to the public). The temperature inside is perfect, when there is a heatwave outside (which was the case in August 2016). It is doable with a small kid, however you can't bring a stroller as the surface is too uneven in the cave. Also bring solid shoes, it is slippery. Some visiters had flipflops or even some kind of high heals - truly not recommended.

A lava tube showing the flow of lava and various natural formation such as the lava shelves or columns. Inside the cave is chilly (around 11c when outside is around 25c), dark, wet and slippery. Bring your jacket and sturdy shoe for this visit. Heels is a definite no no. Forget about your camera (too dark for photo taking) and just enjoy the brisk walk. To and fro takes you around 45mins-1hr.

You cannot pass up going to this park with many trails to accommodate your experience level.  We took on of tge shorter trails but it was one of the steepest.  The views are spectacular and well worth the hike.  A must see if you are visiting the island.

Woke up early hoping to catch the sunrise. We stayed at a pension just 5 min walk from the entrance to Seongsan ilchulbong. It was a wonderful experience to climb in the darkness of the predawn hour. We were surprised to see so many people waiting the start the climb when we reached?? it was raining the night before so the ground was rather slippery. Thankfully the rain had stopped when we started the climb. According to a local there are 500 steps to the peak. It's  doable though it does require a good amount stamina / more time (we were pressed as we wanted to catch the sunrise). The route is easy to follow - steps all the way; there're toilets along the trail too. It was cloudy on the day we climbed so the sunrise wasn't as we'd hoped but still spectacular regardless. On the way down we took a short detour down a flight of steps to a lagoon-like region where the haenyeon dive for seafood. The view there is spectacular especially before the tide rises in the morning. There is a restaurant that sells seafood caught by the haenyeon that was very yummy  we actually took some really nice pictures there. Would return in a heartbeat just for the refreshing climb!!

We were hoping to climb up to the summit. However we ere told to be there before 9 am. We hiked the Yeangsil Trail instead. It was a great experience. The trail was as per the Trod advisor reviews. Make sure you have the right shoes with the right traction. It was not that hard except for some parts of the trail. We enjoyed it very much. We bought some snacks on the trail but had to carry the trash back to our hotel!! The trail is well kept and marked. Will go back again but before 9 am so we can go to the summit. The views were fantastic . We saw a couple of deer. It was worth the visit. Make sure you arrive before 9 am if you want to go to the summit.

We visited Yakcheonsa Temple on our Jeju Olle Trail Route 8. This temple looks delightful because of its architecture and beautiful surrounding scenery. The views from the second floor were amazing! We even had a chance to ring the bell and make wishes here! A recommended place for photographers to get vivid pictures. You can also experience a temple stay activity in this Buddhist temple.

We rode most of the Olleh trail routes by bike and it was awesome.  We made a film about it (titled Jeju: A Bicycle Adventure) and met heaps of interesting people to interview.   I'd definitely recommend it as a not-to-miss part of visiting Jeju Island!   I'd like to walk some of the Olleh Trail routes next time to experience it differently and more slowly.

We participated in the 2020 Moonlight Walking Tour and it was a really great experience! They prepared a music show and guided us through the whole trail without any issue. The view from the golf course is especially stunning!

We hiked the mountain a bit late but still was very interesting. There are many trails to hike just make sure to be back to the bus station before 5:30. We missed throats bus and a Korean guy who works there showed his hospitality. He took me and 4 others to the next station and civilization ( 30 Klm away). Be light when hiking you will get some portable water and a shelter to get God about 3 Klm from the beginning. It was a very nice experience It an be very foggy

I have spent years reading about WW2 history so it's a sobering experience to walk the same places as the men and women who fought and died in that conflict. Altteureu Airfield was a WW2 Japanese airbase that sits in a strategic corner of Jeju Island  midway between China and Japan. In the 1930s bombing missions were launched from here to Shanghai  later it was a training base. There are 19 remaining concrete hardened shelters sized for a Zero fighter and Jeju has done a good job with preserving the site (even though most of it is active farmland)  adding a large parking lot and bathroom  and placards to explain the history and locate the structures. It's right on the Olle trail so there are many hikers passing through and it's easy to find from the shore road by car.

Enter the national park through the Eorimok trail and get down through the yeongsil trail. There are different scenary when you arrive at each check point. Can't describe more by words. Experience it yourself and you will know that those endless staircase that you climbed up is just so much worth for the view up there!

With a few different trails to choose from, climbing Hallasan is an experience I'd recommend to anyone visiting Jeju and wanting a close experience with its nature. Careful preparation of equipment is still necessary, as the easy trail was quite slippery even while wearing winter shoes. The change in scenery when ascending the mountain was magnificent, even though the snowstorm at the top prevented us from seeing the scenery at apparently one of the best sightseeing spots in all of Jeju.

What a way to experience another side of Korea on an extinct volcano. The view at the summit was amazing. Suitable for ages, but a certain level of fitness is definitely required. The park is well maintained and well kept by the government. However, if you are looking for something more unpaved or natural this might not be the right trail as everything is already nicely laid out. (You will never get lost)

Went on a day hike up and down the Seongpanak trail! It was a gorgeous day, about 18C and I couldn't have asked for better weather. It took about 10 hours round trip. Started around 8:30am and made it down by 6:30pm. Luckily the sun didn't go down until 7:15ish so I had plenty of light to guide me.Now, I am not a hiker by any means and this was one of the toughest hikes I've been on. To be honest, it wasn't because the trails were all that difficult - it was actually quite pleasant through the woods and there were 2 rest stops along the way. The first stop is basically a bathroom break and the 2nd had some food available before heading up the last (somewhat steeper) trail to the lake up top. Oh, by   food   I mean some cup ramen and snacks. They also sold water and sports drinks. It would be helpful for you to bring food of your own. They also have no garbage cans so you need to carry and dispose of your own trash once you get back down.The reason why this trail was difficult for me was because I simply wasn't ready for a 20km hike! By the last 5km of the descent, I felt my feet and legs were going to fall off or give in to becoming jelly due to all the stairs and rocks. Make sure you have proper shoes! All in all, I'm glad I did this hike - it was worth it when I got to the top and was able to experience amazing views and clean air. And the flowers!! It was simply beautiful. Just expect to have sore calves for a few days following :)

We were lucky to start the hike with a beautiful warm Autumn day and clear skies. We started around 7 in the morning at the Gwamneumba campsite, getting a taxi ride from Jeju city was easy and cheap - about 10500 won gets you right in front of the gate. We chose to go Gwamneumsa - Seongpanak, as research suggests that most people who did it preferred to avoid masses of people.. Gwamneumsa also boasts the best views, and it sure lived up to it.The Gwamneumsa trail was lovely at first, most tranquil. But then shortly afterwards, it started getting quite difficult having to balance hopping between and stepping up uneven surfaces of lava rocks..Great views came 2/3's in and at the very last part of the trail.. There's also drinking water available at a small fountain in front of a bridge 2/3 way in. The bathrooms on this trail were pretty gross, one of those toilets that pile waste at the bottom - only that the bottom wasn't very far down.. I would say the bottom was less than a metre, many outdoor bathrooms have their toilets down 20m!.. But consider oneself to be lucky to have bathrooms!We reached the summit around 1pm, having taken countless 2 minute breaks along the way. We were quite slow and took it easy. The lake at the top looked much like a drying pond, I think views would probably have looked better in the Spring. There's nothing much else there, a resting area, a helipad and a wifi tower.Next - Climbing down Seongpanak trail.. The first check point on the Seongpanak trail sells FOOD! We didn't know that, as many sources state there are no food stalls on the mountain.. There's 2 minute noodles, chocolate, bottled water, pocari sweat, tissues, etc. Then on the checkpoint after that you have a small fountain of drinking water.The rest of the trail was a nightmare. We didn't have the correct hiking gear and very underprepared trekking in sneakers and boots. Many say that Seongpanak is easier because its a slope, but having to balance each step as we walked on lava rocks was most tiresome. 99% of the time you're just looking down at your feet making sure it lands on a rock, and you're doing it in a hurry because you're trying to reach the end before the sun sets! And you'd probably be doing that for about 6km.It would have been much easier to go up Seongpanak and down Gwamneumsa, as it is much easier to go down by steps rather than on a slope with uneven rocky terrain.Make sure you have the correct hiking gear - sticks and shoes. Our legs ached! Mostly caused by keeping our balance on the uneven, rocky terrain. My partner ended up with a crook knee, micro ligament tear. We reached the exit gate at 5:30pm! Taxi ride back to Jeju city was about 15000 won.I give this 3 stars because a lot of effort is involved for minimal reward. Yes it is a mountain, and I have hiked other incredible mountains with magnificent views like huangshan and wulingyuan. My expectations were very high as well, the most you get are views of the city, mountain fauna ( though very beautiful), and the drying lake. Do it for the enjoyment of experience and go the other direction, climbing down Gwamneumsa would be so much easier as there are better stairs, not just kilometres of rocks on a slope! And with the right gear! ;)Enjoy!

We were dropped by a taxi at the beginning of the Seongpanak trail (a little way up the volcano), but you can catch the bus there if you prefer and there is a bus stop right near the entrance. The track is 9.6km (19.2km return), and took us about 6 hours return walking at a medium pace, including breaks at Sokbat shelter (4.1kms up - toilet facilities only) and at Jindallaebat shelter (7.3kms up - toilet and small kiosk). We had initially wanted to walk up the Gwaneumsa trail and then down the Seongpanak one, but were too tired to get up before 6am to achieve it in one day. Walking the Seongpanak trail up and down was a great experience in itself, even though it is apparently not as scenic as others. But, because it's one of the easier ones, it is packed with tourists, most of whom are not seasoned walkers, so be prepared for being held up a fair bit (and witnessing some pretty avoidable but hilarious injuries!).The trail is quite an easy one in comparison to other hikes we have done - no really steep bits or actual climbing - more of a gentle incline, with boardwalks in parts, dirt paths and as you get higher, rough rocky paths. The only strenuous thing about the trail is that it is long? It will take you all day, and you have to start early so you reach the Jindallaebat shelter before a certain hour (changes depending on the season, but in September it was 12:30pm) or the ranger won't let you continue - for obvious reasons, there's no lighting at night to climb back down, so he doesn't want to come and find stupidly lost tourists! You can check the times on the official Hallasan website. You don't really need proper hiking boots/other equipment for this hike (we did it in light walking shoes), but if you have weak ankles I would probably recommend wearing hiking boots with ankle support, especially for the walk back down the rocky paths. Take plenty of water and snacks - don't rely on the shelters like the Koreans do, they may sell out/be extremely busy, and you have to get to Jindallaebat by 12:30! We just bought some muesli bars, fruit, WATER and energy drinks like gatorade/powerade at a 7/11 before we left Jeju city in the morning, and were almost the only ones who had thought ahead! On the way back down, the Jindallaebat shelter will be quieter, so it's the perfect opportunity to then buy some of their hot ramen noodles or a chocolate bar. I would also recommend bringing a light rain jacket, and a waterproof backpack/cover for your backpack - it showers sporadically within the fog. I also took a plastic bag to put my camera in to keep it dry.When we began our walk, it was quite chilly at the entrance and the local walkers laughed at us wearing shorts - but by the time you get a few kilometres in, you'll be stripping off layers of clothing, so totally wear shorts if you want to - it's quite warm in the sun on the summit, so everyone will be peeling off their layers anyway! There was a thick fog hanging low over the volcano for about 2/3 of the walk, so it's a bit muggy, but the side of the mountain is lush and green, an eerily quiet forest. As you get higher, suddenly you notice you're climbing above the fog - feels like you've popped out above the clouds, on top of the world! The last part of the track is quite windy, and you can see how the wind has beaten its wooden steps, which are strewn everywhere. Be careful in the last part and beware pushy tourists! But, once you get to the summit, at Dongneung Peak (no facilities on the summit, by the way), the view is breathtakingly beautiful - like nothing I've ever seen before! The crater when we were there was overgrown with vegetation, with a small crater lake. Such a wonderful experience, and most definitely a highlight of our trip to South Korea! You must hike Hallasan during your stay at Jeju-do!

we were definitely not prepared for this - in terms of experience and equipment!started off at about 9am on the Eorimok route. the entrance was a 10 min walk from the bus stop. then, it was off on the hike!initially the trail was straightforward. then it gradually went into a steep ascent. the path was quite rocky and unstable. but there were sufficient rest stops along the way. also people going in the same and opposite direction to you so you will not be alone (unless you hike in the middle of the night)there were also multiple signboards along the route providing interesting facts about Hallasan and also maps showing your current location and remaining distances to go to the next point.there was almost a natural portable water point where you can refill your bottles. remember to stay hydrated throughout and take breaks when needed.needless to say, the views along the route were truly breathtaking but the higher elevation you reach, the colder it becomes. also, the winds were very strong!we reached the Witseoreum shelter at about 12pm and had lunch there. The locals actually brought hot water in their thermos flasks and had cup ramen there!after lunch, we started our descent on the Yeongsil trail and reached the entrance of Yeongsil at about 2pm and there was a 2km walk out of the entrance to the bus stop.by then our legs were aching and heavy, but we pushed on. overall the hike took about 5 hrs.in summary, we should have worn more proper hiking footwear, wear thicker clothing (as higher you go, the colder it gets) and more food and snacks!we decided we will come back to attempt the summit next time.

We went up the Gwaneumsa Trail and down Seongpanak and thought it was a great route. Seongpanak has much better views that are easier to see while walking down, otherwise your back is facing the beauty on the way up. Both trails are majority rock. Meaning, nearly the entire hike is trying to find rocks to climb up/down. There are some wood paths, bridges, and stairs, but mostly rock which is hard on the arches of your feet. I used regular Adidas sneakers which worked, however the bottom of my feet began to ache on the way down. On the way up Gwaneumsa, we couldn't refill our water at all, then at the top - NOTHING! It wasn't until 2 km down Seongpanak (6 hours after we began the hike) that there was free water access. Nothing was sold on this hike, even though I read about ramen and drinks being sold. I was DYING for water. Bring tons!!! At Gwaneumsa there is a store to purchase beverages and 2 servings of gimbap for 3,000 won, as well as walking sticks for 20,000. I didn't use one but many did and it seemed to help balancing on all the rocks. I began the hike at 7:00am and was down by 3:45 - this included a half an hour break at the top and 2 min stop at each base camp (there were about 4 or so on each route.) I'm not an experienced hiker at all and really doubted my ability to do this, but it IS manageable! Today I can't walk but it was totally worth it.PS - for those interested, drones are NOT allowed to be flown at the top however there was absolutely no indication of this in English anywhere.

We went on the first Monday of the month, and the mountaineering trail was closed, so do take note when planning. However, the first portion of the trail was still available for free, which was still amazing and less of an exercise. The view from all spots were breathtaking, making this spot a must-see when you?re in Jeju.Do catch the woman?s diver show at 1.30pm and 3pm, located down the trail. It was an interesting experience to see the elderly women dive down to retrieve the seafood in the ocean, and you can buy and eat some of their fresh catches at the shop nearby.Highly recommend for a magnificent sightseeing experience in Jeju!

We visited this place out of curiosity and was quite surprised how peaceful it was. It was a weekday when we were there but it might get a lot more crowded on weekends.Give this place a chance if you would like to experience a walk, albeit on man made trails, in the forest as it was quiet, peaceful and there are many great photo ops.

We visited Mount Halla National Park yesterday, Aug 25th, and it was an excellent experience and great views!It is very easy to get there by the 740 bus from Jeju Bus terminal, now here is the tricky part.. there are several entrances and trails. All of them are intense hiking. Use comfortable shoes, take lots of water and snacks.. there is nothing to buy up until the very top, which is noodle soup, water and chocolates......We took the Eorimok trail to go up to Witsae Shelter and took the Yeongsil trail to return down and my recommendation is:Take Yeongsil train, the view is by far much better than the one from Eorimok trail.In order to get there:Take 740 bus and get down on Yeongsil ticket office (@45m) and from there take a taxi to the main entrance (there is a taxi that goes up and down all the time and charges 5000). Please take the taxi, otherwise you will end up walking uphill for @2km. Once at the entrance... just follow the signs to Witse Shelter. Take lots of pictures along the way!Again ... it is uphill .. from @900m to @1750m, with lots of stairs and rock trails on both trails. Up and down in @5 hours is an ok time.Enjoy !!

We visited Hallasan National Park in mid-November. We did the Gwanwum-sa trail up to Hallasan peak and went down the Seongpanak trail. Although Gwaneum-sa is more challenging on the way up, we totally recommend this route as Seongpanak is way more transited. The trees' autumn colours were beautiful and although at the top it was below 0 degress and misty (making it hard to see the volcano cone and lake), it was an amazing experience. Would definetely repeat!

We visited Hallasan National Park in mid December. We ascended via Gwaneumsa trail (8.7km) up to the peak and descended via the Seongpanak trail (9.6km). Gwaneumsa is shorter but more challenging on the way up, it is easier on the knees. We started at 07:30hr, which is the sunrise time. The initial hike was relatively flat, walking on uneven big rocks. There were signs throughout the trail, indicating where you are, distance and estimated time to the peak. Snow started to appear midway and we had to put on crampons on our boots. We took about 3 hours to reach the shelter and another 1 hour 45 minutes to reach the peak. Unfortunately, the weather was cloudy at the peak with low visibility. It was very windy and cold. We joined the queue to have photos taken at the iconic landmark.We started our descent at 12:45hr, arrived at the shelter at 15:15hr, had a short break before descending the remaining 4.1km. We took about 4 hours for the entire descent, exhausted by then.This is the first time my friend and I hiked in snow during winter. We took longer than expected as we were extra careful and also took many photos. Overall, it was a great first time experience hiking on snow.Tips for winter hiking:1. Start as early as possible so that you are not pressured to reach the shelter before 1200hr.2. Wear comfortable shoes, preferably water resistant or waterproof.3. Be extra careful when stepping on the big rocks during the initial trail. They are uneven and may twist your ankles. 4. Crampons are necessary, while trekking poles are optional.5. Wear layers of clothing so that you can add/remove when necessary.6. Wear beanie hat and neck covering to protect your ears/neck from the cold, especially at the peak.7. Bring your own food, snacks and water/energy drink. There are no food stalls nor toilet at the peak.8.Toilet facilities are only available at the shelters, hence relief yourself before proceeding.Hope you enjoyed the hike.

We travelled from Seogwipo by bus to Jungmun Elementary school.  Thereafter, we were supposed to hop on another bus to the stop nearest to the entrance of Yeongsil Trail.  However, we did not read the bus schedule careful enough to notice the change in the schedule during winter.  The bus starts later and ends earlier during winter.  We ended sharing a cab with the other 2 tourists who happened to be there earlier than us and were heading to the same destination.  The guy who mended the convenient store near the bus stop was so nice that he helped us to call the taxi.   It was a blessing in disguise since the taxi actually sent us right to the door step of the Yeongsil Trail entrance in which otherwise, we would have to walk up for about 2 km to the starting point of the trail.  Should you travel with baggage, the park office (which I guess so) can keep them for you.  I?m not sure of the storage capacity or if lockers are available, or this is just an additional service provided for those who happen to travel there with their baggage.It took us slightly more than 3 hours to hike up to Witsoreum Shelter since we?re quite slow and took plenty of photos.  The Koreans took 2 hours only.  The wind was very strong, so do take care of your scarf or anything which is light.  Witsoreum Shelter is where you can opt to go back down with the same trail or by another trail, Eurimok Trail.  However, the other trail was closed on that day.There?s a canteen and restrooms at Witsoreum Shelter.  The canteen sells instant noodle and simple snacks.  After eating and disposing the residue of the noodle, you have to bring the trash back for disposal.  Plastic bag for keeping your trash is provided but I find it rather thin.  However, we brought some plastic bag along with us for this purpose as well since we had some snacks while hiking up.The fog was building up when we left at about 1:10 am.  It took us about an hour and 40 minutes to descend.  Overall, this was a good experience.  We were just on time to catch the last bus back to Jungmun Elementrary school (if I recall this destination correctly).

We took up this challenge in early April, just stepping into Spring. We took the bus from Jeju Express Bus Terminal, took about 40 minutes to reach the Eorimok bus stop. Before taking the bus though, we highly recommend to check with the Tourist Information Center just outside the bus terminal on the last returning bus. Thankfully we checked, the last bus in March period was 4.55pm at Eorimok. Summer periods probably have a later last bus back. This bus serves the Yeongsil trail entrance as well.There is still a ~20 mins walk along the road before reaching the entrance to the Eorimok trail. Impressive mountain views once you reach the park entrance.The Eorimok trail starts off deceptively tame for about 500m. Once you get the past the wooden bridge, the tough hike starts. For the next 2km, we experienced the toughest climb of the entire trail. Steep and large steps at times, with large, uneven rocks littering the way up. The view is mostly green at this point.Near the end of the first 2km, we started to see melting ice along the trail. Certain parts were still iced up; we had to climb on top of the ice to traverse. Due to the melt, it was quite slippery. A hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended, though we had not brought any for our trip.After 2km, the trail leveled off into a plateau, a welcome rest after a seemingly endless slog. Strong winds and rain pummeled us that day, but all the more made the challenging climb more exciting and enjoyable. The rest of the way to the Witse Oreum was of average difficulty, and the landscape was foggy and snowy/icy. We encountered many instances that we had to walk on the ice so be sure to be equipped with good shoes to reduce the chance of slipping on the ice.We finally reached the Witse Oreum after about 3 hours, and bought and slurped down the ramen and its soup, as well as a chocolate energy bar. They also carried stuff like crampons and plastic sheet raincoat (we bought it for the heat trapping characteristic rather than for shielding against rain, we foolishly did not expect snow and ice in April tbh :P).We originally wanted to go down via the Yeongsil trail which meets the Eorimok trail at the Witse Oreum, but a pair of local, seasoned hikers who turned back for Eorimok warned us that the Yeongsil trail is still mostly frozen over and is very difficult to traverse at this time. Due to the lack of proper equipment, we heeded their advice and went back down Eorimok instead.The trip down was much faster, but hurt our knees more due to the impact. Tread with care as the uneven terrain may cause slip and falls.The journey down took approximately an 1.5 hours.Overall it was really challenging but fun.Things to note:1. Take note of the last bus timing or you may have to hitch a ride back to town.2. And of course, cater buffer time to reach the bus stop, there is still a 20 min walk to it.3. Hiking gear, especially proper shoes and a hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended.4. Early April features unmelted snow in the terrain, wear proper clothing.5. The same bus goes to the Yeongsil trail, may want to try hiking that as well (on different days of course)6. The Eorimok is pretty challenging for a novice like myself, heard from locals that the Seongpanak trail on the Eastern side is more relaxing but longer.7. The Eorimok trail does not reach the summit, if you want to reach the summit, try the Seongpanak or Gwaneumsa trails instead.

We took the Hallasan Yeongsil trail up to Witseoreum Shelter and back in early January (winter). The views were fantastic and the hike was just the right distance for us (1.5 hours up, 1 down). It was challenging but didn't wipe us out. Make sure you stop and have some noodles at the shelter, as dumb as it may sound I found this part to be the highlight of my Jeju experience. It would pay to do a small amount of research if you are planning to go as there are multiple trails of different lengths and difficulty. The Yeongsil trail is fairly easy apart from one steep section with ropes which were tricky in the snow (mainly going down). Most of the trail features steps when required, is well signposted and has guide ropes along the ridges. Also, make sure you head out early: we did and shared the path with only a few hikers but on our way down came across masses of people trying to go up. Most of the late arrivals didn't have snow crampons and/or not enough fitness/experience for this hike and many seemed to be turning back once it got steeper. I don't think they would had a very good time. You can buy cheap crampons at the bottom at the trail entrance and apart from warm clothes the only equipment you would need in winter (maybe hiking poles if bad knees or unsteady). In warmer months, some good boots, snacks and water would be fine.

We took the eomorik trail up - the first 1/2 or so was a tough climb, but through the woods so it was shaded. The second 1/2 was in open space - mostly on a Boardwalk type pathway. The path is clearly marked throughout the trail and there are signs to indicate how far you've come and how much you have left. The view was just average. It took us two hours to reach the top and we are not experienced hikers nor were we wearing hiking shoes, but we only took one short break for 10 minutes so we were always moving. We took the yongsil trail down and this was much more scenic with beautiful views of the mountains and rocks. Most of it was not shaded and most of the trail had steps so it was easy going down, but the look on people's faces as they were coming up showed how tiring it was to climb all those stairs! It took us about 1 hour and 15 minutes to get down. There were no taxis when we reached the bottom so we had to walk 30 minutes to the ticket booth to catch the bus. Since we just missed the bus and they don't run very frequently, we got a cab to take us back to our car at the eomorik entrance which cost about 10,000won.

We started at 8.30 at Yeongsil and exited at 1 pm from Eorimok . Lovely walking and climbing experience. Fresh air, lot of greenery, lot of birds. Just us and nature and fellow hikers. It was fun. Very exhausting but refreshing.One must have good pair of shoes. It has lot of rocky patches.Carry water and some snacks. Sunhat is must. The trail is well guided with sign boards and emergency numbers. It becomes windy on top so a jacket is useful.Must visit place.

We made a side trip to this attraction and thanks to our guide, we were able to experience a very refreshing afternoon hike and enjoy the beautiful colors of autumn.  There is a walking trail and it's  an easy hike even to non-hikers. It was late October when we visit and i just love the foliage in this mountain.

We initially came here the day after a typhoon, and when we arrived, all the trails were closed due to wind damage. It was unfortunate, but we got some BEAUTIFUL pictures on the road along the way back of the fog hanging in the trees in stuff. It was sort of a spooky, peaceful atmosphere and we barely saw another car. So even if it's kind of a crummy, foggy day, you might get some really pretty photos. We came back the next day (after confirming the trails were reopened) and decided to do the Yeongsil trail. It's not terribly strenuous, and a lot of it is on wooden stairs/walkways. The worst part is going up all the stairs about halfway through the hike (which is basically the rest of the hike), but if you're like us, you will probably be stopping frequently to take pictures. Bring lots of sunscreen/protective clothing because a good chunk of the hike (maybe even half of it) is completely exposed with no shade. We stopped and had some obligatory ramen at the top (along with some mochi cakes that were kinda like protein bars we bought at the market that morning), then hiked back down the same trail, because that's where our car was. I wore my heavy-duty hiking boots for this, but if it's nice out you can probably do it in a pair of Keens (or similar), or even a decent pair of sneakers with a good tread (there are some parts that are slippery and rocky, so something like Converse sneakers or flip-flops are probably a bad idea. I say this as an experience flip-flop hiker, lol). Go as early as you can, because there will likely be lots of people out. I think we started around 9:30 -10AM and there were a fair few people, but not so much that it was blocking or slowing down traffic on the way up or down.

We hiked up the Seongpanak Trail and hiked down Gwaneumsa Trail.  These are the only 2 trails to the summit and hence it is the best option to get the best of both trails.Iit was a huge satisfying feeling to reach the top and then to descend safely.  It was not difficult if we were more prepared.  Here are some pointers to note:(1) We went in Spring and therefore we were not expecting any snow.  However, probably due to a snow storm 1 or 2 weeks ago, some areas were still covered in snow.  As we didn't bring any hiking sticks nor cramptons, the descend was difficult and dangerous.  I slipped many times.  There was even one path which was totally covered with snow and we had to detour to the side which was hard given the little space and all the snow.  As we descended via Gwaneumsa Trail, it was more steep and therefore the snow made it such a challenging task to hike down.(2) There are no water point.  We thought we could get some water from toilets but there are no taps in toilets too.  We ran out of water towards the end.(3) No food.  Do bring your own food as you would not be able to buy any on the way up and down.  We  brought our own snacks.  Also be prepared to bring your own rubbish down the mountain.  There are no rubbish bins for you to discard your rubbish.(4) Do allocate more time for the hike.  We thought we could do it within half a day but we spent much longer time.  By the time we reached the bottom, it was already 4 - 5 plus.  Even though we were relatively fast and hardly stopped, we still require that much time which probably was also due to the snowed paths (lots of snow).It was a unforgetable experience and we were so happy we did it!  Will we do it again?  Definitely!

We hiked the Eorimok (up) and Yeongsil (down) trails. *If you're hiking in winter, you definitely need crampons.*These trails were stunning. On the Eorimok, we experienced surreal forest setting shrouded in misty clouds and stunning landscapes. At the top of the trail, there's a great place to snag some cup Ramen and Choco-pies. Bring a few cheons and you'll be fine. Two-thirds of this trail was in the forest and the last third was along a large plain created by a lava field. Expect to be amazed by vast skies.The Yeongsil trail was just as satisfying. There are sheer drops and exposed cliff faces. Most of this trail was composed of wooden stairs. If you're planning to bus in and out, make sure you start early. The buses fill up fast and the last bus back to Jeju-si from Yeongsil runs at 16:15 during the winter (until March). Also, if you're not exhausted, the walk to the bus stop from the trail is not too far (maybe 2km at max). Don't waste you money on shuttle service.

We climbed the Eorimok track on the way up and Yeongsik track on the way down. I must say Yeongsik is SUPER SCARY, because the snow is so deep the safety rails were buried under snow, so parts of the trail we had to walk on snow steps next to the cliff.... For totally unexperienced climber like me, it was quite intimidating. If you go in winter, and are not very confident in your skills (like me!) make sure you have crampons and hiking sticks. The convenient store at the entrance sells crampons (around 7USD). My friends were totally fine with those simpler crampons, but I prefer the wire-net style one (the one my friend lent me was from Columbia brand).Hiking sticks are helpful because where it's supposed to be stairs would turn into slides because of the snow -_-Good luck and enjoy!Amazing view. Must note the bus timetable, as we missed the last bus (around 5pm) and had to take taxi (at Yeongsik trail entrance there's an office which can help you find taxis. But it took >1 hour for ours to come...)

We climbed Seongpanak Trail on the Saturday of a 3-day weekend and it was crowded as hell. On the way up it didn't feel like a hike but more like a line of people marching. It was not a huge deal for me. I've never seen a mountain for hiking so well equipped. There were 2 rest areas, one about a fourth of the way up and another 3/4 of the way up. The one 3/4 of the way up is where many people have their lunch and can buy snacks/ramen (less windy). The toilets are horrendous and I had to tie a scarf around my face but it was so strong. About halfway up a mountain you can take a left and for a 20 min walk in & out you can see a nice lake (it may be foggy).This was DEFINITELY a worthwhile experience. The hike was quite easy because there were many man made walkways. When you are approaching the summit it can be very windy. I had to grab the rope a few times to prevent myself from being blown away (I am only about 50kg). We went in October so it may be less windy and cold in the summer months. The clouds move quickly so we were able to see and take many great pictures. Please do this if you enjoy hiking and want to stand among the clouds!

Visited in October to see beautiful autumn colors revealing itself. I recommend to start early morning if you want to hike to the summit.  The cut off time for the summit can be anytime between 11am to 1pm depending on the season. There are 4 different trails around Hallasan Park - Gwaneumsa and Seongpanak takes you to the top. As Gwaneumsa is a bit boring I recommend to take it when you go up.
