OUR TRAILS: Yeongsil trail (up) - Eorimok trail (down) Based on advice from friends, we (four of us) opted for the 'easiest' Yeongsil trail to embark on our climbing adventure.. (personally, my friends and I do not think the hike up was that easy). To save ourselves from walking woes (about 2km from bus drop-off point to start point), we got a cab (from Seogwipo; about KRW25,000) to drive us right to the start point, where a cafe is located. Upon arrival, the temperature was about 6 degrees with strong wind (downtown Jeju was about 13 degrees). We immediately purchased head scarves and gloves for the climb.The beginning of the trail started out easy but not much of colorful scenery (thou it was still autumn). The steps got steeper and steeper at about altitude 1,300~1,550m. These was the part where I guessed we stopped several times to gasp for air. And that was only halfway of the climb! After the steep climb, we reached the easiest portion of the entire climb. The boardwalk to Witsae-oreum Shelter. A place where we could no longer differentiate the sky and the sea, it was a great place for us to take a group photo (with Mt Halla peak as the background). When we reached the shelter, all of us dashed for quick toilet break and joined the queue to purchase some instant noodles and energy drinks. The very optimistic us then rest our feet till 4pm and made our way down the Eorimok trail. Going down the trail within 1.5hrs (before the sky turned dark) was crazy. There were just too many steps or uneven routes to descend. However, the consolation was the different colorful scenery from Yeongsil (many oreums could be seen). Our fastest speed at our physical condition then, we took 2 hours to descend (I guessed we were the last batch of humans) and the sky has already turned dark when we finally reached the exit at Eorimok trail. There was no more bus nor taxi but thank god for the kindness and efforts of the nearby workers; they drove us to the foot of the mountain and got us a cab. Without them, we would never return back to our guesthouse safely. God bless them!LEARNING POINTS & OBSERVATIONS 1) Yeongsil (grand) and Eorimok (colourful) trails offer different sceneries. 2) Always double the time/ distance, advised by a Korean. (LOL). They are fast walkers and climbers. Few occasions, we managed to reach our destination after 2x their estimation.3) Saw many Korean seniors and children ascending/ descending Mt Halla. They lead a healthy lifestyle!4) Do not stop for photo taking. Take few shots and proceed with the climb.5) Lessen individual's weight for the climb. Forget about DSLR and tripod! LOL.6) Apart from a solid windbreaker/ jacket, small haversack with water, museli bars, gloves, scarf and hp are a must. Hiking sticks are recommended.7) Experienced strong telecom signals up in the mountains.8) The only toilet (after the starting point) available can be found at Witsae-oreum Shelter only (No tap for hand wash).9) Rubbish (@ Witsae-oreum Shelter) can only be thrown at the exit only. 10) Not to proceed further and U-turn if very tired. Because descending can be more demanding and tired too.11) @ Witsae-oreum Shelter, all climbers have to proceed down the mountain by 4pm (October). Please refer to Mt Hallasan's website as the information are very accurate and informative.SUMMARYWe took more than 6 hours exploring these two trails. Of course, time would be lesser if we did not make many stops along the way.  We were gasping for air while climbing up Mt Halla but the overall scenery was really breathtaking. Despite suffering muscle pains for the next 5 days, all our efforts were worth it.RECOMMENDATIONHighly recommended if individual is fit, adventurous, loves beautiful scenery and has time on his/ her plate. Personally, I recommend to teenagers and above. : )

Not many things beat the sound of a waterfall, and this one is no exception. Situated right where the river meets the ocean, it is a beautiful sight to see.There is a parking area right by the entrance to the trail. The entrance fee is ??2000 per person, and you should be careful when walking along the rocks - they tend to get quite slippery.Note: definitely not wheelchair accessible!

No required permits and other fees before climbing. The jump-off, either through Eorimok or Yeongsil, can be easily accessed by public bus, so there's no problem going back to the city. We went up through Eorimok trail, 2-3 hours hike, then descended through the scenic trail of Yeongsil. Cold at 2C at Witsaeoreum Shelter, a cup of spicy noodles or a cup of coffee will be sure of great help.

Needless to say, Mt Halla was the highlight of my trip in Jeju. There was a good mix of clear sky and clouds during my hike up and down and the view is simply fantastic. I loved everything and every minute spent on this mountain.I went up via Eorimok trail and down via Yeongsil trail. Both trails DO NOT take you to the peak but to Witseorum Shelter. There, you can buy cup noodles, coffee and energy bars etc. but there are NO DUSTBINS - you must bring all your trash down with you. It was crowded when I reached the shelter around noon.I will not lie. You do need to be reasonably fit to hike up Mt Halla. You WILL have to do lots of climbing on rocks and proper walking paths probably make up 10% each on both trails. Many people recommend wearing proper hiking shoes but I went up and down wearing sports shoes and had no problem. It really depends on your personal preference and level of fitness.One last thing, toilets are only available at the start of each trail and at Witseorum Shelter. And make sure you have plenty of memory space on your camera for photos!

Myself and wifey and our 2 boys aged 12 and 15, decided to walk this mountain, and arrived just after 9.30 in the morning. This trail is supposedly the easier of what are now 3 trails that take you to the summit. Because it wasn't the weekend, there were fewer people, and this was a big bonus, as the whole way up is sectioned off with guide rope, and is either wooden stairs or stones and rock. The few times we came across people, you were held up a bit until you came across a widening where you could overtake them. I can imagine this being very irritating on a weekend, and also you lose that feeling of being out in the wilderness.On the way up we met small groups of older Koreans, who offered us cucumbers and oranges, and we greeted all we met with    hello   or    how you doing ?   in Korean. This was mostly met with a smile and a happy reply.The downside with this trail, is that you are surrounded by trees the first 8 km up, and it is not until the last kilometre that you actually begin to get an appreciation of the views. In some ways it is quite beautiful, but like I said to our two boys, the bottom of the hill is nearly like the top, because you can only see the trees- okay different formations, but no view.At the top, you have the crater sectioned off, and you can peer down into it and take pictures. Because of the distance, we rate this quite a hard going trek,and there are many loose rocks that you could easily twist your ankle on, wifey did!!We used 3 hours up, a little more down, because we had to stop for a while, so wifey could swear at me when she twisted her ankle!!

My wife and I hiked the Seongpanak Trail up Hallasan in late May 2015. The trail starts relatively easy but gets more difficult after the first shelter. Make sure you have the rights shoes as the rocks can be pretty hard on your feet. This is a long climb, and for most of the trip you will be in a forest. Keep your eyes open and you may spot some of the elusive small native deer, we saw three on our trip. I am not in great shape, so it was a tough climb for me and took us 9 hrs. round trip. The rocks are really hard on your feet on the way down. Leave early since if you don't make it to the last shelter before 1 PM they will not allow you to ascend to the summit. The last shelter sells ramen and water and a few other items, but be aware you are expected to pack all of your own trash off of the mountain. There are some stores and shops in the parking lot at the entrance to the park, we bought some kimbop for lunch and packed it up with us. This is the tallest mountain in South Korea and the summit provides wonderful views at over 1900 meters high. Climbing Hallasan was a   bucket list   item for my wife, who was born in South Korea, and a memorable experience.

My husband and I climb Mt Hallasan today. Though my feet are sore, i thoroughly enjoyed my hike. The trail was really well marked and in good condition (Both Seongpanak and Gwaneumsa Trail). We entered via Seongpanak Trail (9.6km gradual inclination - trail was a mix of wooden steps and rocks). It was fairly easy till Jindallaebat Shelter, and then it gets tougher but doable. We started at 8am and reached the summit at 12 pm (we?re not athletic and not super fit). We then descended via Gwaneumsa Trail (8.6km) at 1 pm and arrived at the trail head at 5.30pm. Gwaneumsa is more scenic as many blogs have mentioned so am glad we descended using this trail but Seongpanak trail is easier and is nice as well.Useful info:We took the public bus from Jeju-si city and back. Journey was about an hour one way and we found our way fairly easy with the Naver Map app. The public bus from Gwaneumsa trail entrance only runs on weekends I believe. Bring snacks, lunch and water for your climb. A windbreaker is advisable if you come from the tropics like me.Good shoes are recommended as you?ll be walking on rocks a lot of the time. Bring a raincoat too as there aren?t many shelters.Start early, you have to arrive Jindallaebat Shelter by 1230hrs (you cannot proceed after that) and you must begin your descend by 1430hrs.

My family with two boys 10 & 12 hiked up the Yeongsil trail to Witseoreum and back down by visitor center near Eoseungsaengak trail. We made a mistake of getting dropped off at the ticketing office by Yeongsil trail and not at the entrance of the trailhead.  It added another hour to 4 hour hike. But the walk was nice nevertheless and we saw a snake and a giant snail to compensate for it.         Trails were very well maintained and clean. But be prepared for ankle twisters and knee pains. I sure wished I had my walking sticks with me. I had to drink some Hite(Korean pale beer) afterward to relieve some pain on my knees. My two boys had no problem for them being young and all.  A little one did the whole trail on sandals but I don't recommend it as there are sections of trails made up with volcanic rocks. One wrong fall and one can easily get a nasty scrape.  Oh yeah, don't forget to bring, snacks, bug repellent, bandaids, medical tapes for your toes and heels.          I enjoyed the cupnoodle at the Witsoreum.  It was only $1.50. I think coffee was $0.50 or 0.60. There are few other snacks offered at incredibly low price considering the location. They give you a plastic bag to carry all our garbage down the mountain.         One thing I really love about this place is the variety of landscapes. It felt like going to several different national parks at once.         Few things...there are no bathrooms between trailheads and Witsoreum.  Be sure to use airgun a the trailheads to blow away the ticks and other insects off your body and clothes.

My family and I visited this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument cave on a late afternoon for 2 hours. There were not many visitors and we didn?t find any tour buses when we reached here.   Getting there & fees: Manjanggul Cave is located in the north western part of Jeju-do. To get (drive) to Manjanggul Cave, key in GPS coordinate 7834818. There is no parking fee at the huge car park. Entrance fee is 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.Manjanggul Cave Museum: Upon climbing up the stairs from the car park, you will reach the Museum and a cafeteria/restaurant on its right. You could go in and have a look at the interesting exhibits, including how the Manjanggul Cave was formed from the volcanic activities.Manjanggul Cave: To get to the underground Cave, we followed the sign-posts ? it?s within 5 minutes? walk from the Manjanggul Cave Museum. Trek the entire 1 km stretch that?s opened to public and you will end with a colourful lit lava column - created from the dripping of lava from a hole in the ceiling ? which at about 8 meters high, is the tallest lava column on Earth. Nevertheless, there are a few things you have to take note while you are in the Cave:(1) The entrance to the Manjanggul Cave is also the exit ? there?s no exit at the end of the 1 km trail, which means you are walking 2 km return (2) Make sure you bring and wear a jacket or sweater with you because it?s freezing cold and chilly inside the cave. (3) Wear a cap or the jacket or sweater can be waterproof because you get water ocassioanlly dripping from the cave top onto you (4) The surface (floor) of the Cave is full of solidified lava flow terrain (i.e. extremely uneven surface) and water puddles, so you have to wear a pair of good walking shoes and walk carefully. Hold on to the railings of the stairs.(5) You probably don?t need a torchlight because the Cave is illuminated just enough by ground lightings. Some parts of the cave even have colourful lights shining at the dome shaped ceiling (cupola) (6) If you would like to take photographs inside the cave, you would need a tripod and switch to manual mode for long exposure (I used 4 seconds to 10 seconds exposure on my digital SLR).   There are displays at certain parts of the cave in English explaining the geology of the cave and the formation of the interesting structures (e.g. stalactites). In particular, there?s one structure ? ?Stone Turtle? ? in which the shape looks like Jeju-do Island, and which you could reach in about 30 minutes of one-way walking as it?s about 400m from the entrance. Along the Manjanggul Cave wall, we saw varied patterns of lava flow lines, some are straight while some are wavy. Really interesting! I have been to over 10 limestone caves around the world, but this is my first visit in a lava tunnel cave or lava tube cave (and Asia?s longest lava tube cave for that matter). You have to experience being transported to another world in this ?out of this world? cave for yourself ? don?t miss it!

My family and I drove to this awesome natural attraction and walked along the layered rocks and cliffs produced as a result of a volcanic eruption on a beautiful non-windy and sunny morning. Safety concerns: Yeongmeori (Dragon's Head) Coast is opened from 8 am to 6:30 pm from May to September. It will be closed when the weather changes in a way that impacts people?s safety (e.g. high tidal waves, strong winds), so it is better to call to check before going. Also a rainy day means that the rocks and coast will become slippery and you may have problems taking photographs. in any case, you definitely need a good pair of walking shoes.2 walking trails: You have to take note that there are 2 trails and entrances to Yeongmeori Coast. Both trails meet each other but are not connected due to safety issue, which means you have to pay separate entrance fees. However, I saw a white bridge is presently being constructed that links the 2 trails, but it remains unclear as to when it will be opened. Between the 2 trails ? Trail 1 and Trail 2 (described below) ? I found Trail 2 to be  safer for walking and has more spectacular sandstone rock formations and cliffs, and because of that my family and I spent about 3 hours admiring the attraction and taking photographs.  Trail 1: This trail is where the tourists go, and starts after the Hamel Castaway Memorial and the Hamel vessel. You park your car (along with the tour coaches) at a car park that?s next to a mini theme park (with the Viking amongst others). You then walk along the seaside promenade next to sandstone layered rocks along the sea, which takes about 1.5 to 3 hours return after the ticket booth (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children). Since certain stretches of the promenade are narrow, you have to walk carefully so as not to fall into the sea and onto the rocks.Trail 2:  This is a shorter trail that in theory should only take about 30-60 minutes return after the ticket booth. You park your car just beneath the temple. Parking is free. Cross the road and look for 3 bronze circular structures with inscriptions of ?Jeju Island Geopark?, ?Global Geopark Networks? and ?New 7 Wonders of Nature? and a green signage ?Yongmeori Coast Entrance -> 300m? From there, you just walk down the steps and follow the path which will take you past several shops. After about 10 minutes? walk, you will reach a ticket booth. After buying the tickets (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children), turn left and you would come to the top of a narrow and steep passageway to the coast. Take your time to carefully choose the big rocks as your steps for your descent (and then I realised what the term ?stepping stone? means). There are no handrails. Once you reached the bottom after about 6 minutes (longer when there are many people), turn around and look up at the challenging and difficult passageway and appreciate your achievement! Looking across the sea, we saw Mount Hallasan. Instead of going left, I recommend you go to the right and once through a archway or hole in a rock wall, and you will soon encounter the spectacular irregular layered and wavy sandstone cliffs that often contain ?pot-holes?. The rock formation at certain places was carved out by  a blade that cut itself into the layered rocks, creating v-shaped clefts. And when the waves crashed into the rocks, it sounds like roaring thunder ? awesome!  There?s a short cement bridge where standing on it allows you to take a superb photograph of the rock formation and the narrow stretch of turquoise-coloured sea. It is also around this same spot that you can take another superb photograph of the cliffs with Mount Sanbangsan in the background. There were 2 ladies (I didn?t think they were the famed ?Haenyeo? sea-divers) at the shoreline with 3 basins of sea animals - sea snail (sora), sea squirt (myeonggye) and sea cucumber (haesam) ? who would be happy to enable you  to experience Korean culture of eating raw seafood by the shoreline. I didn?t like to eat raw seafood so I didn?t try.Overall, my family and I think that Yeongmeori Coast is one attraction in Jeju that ranks it as among the top 3 attractions in Jeju. Don?t miss it! It will blow your mind away!

Mt Halla is known as Korea's jewel. It is its highest peak. And well worth the trip to Jeju. We left Seagwipo very early (around 7 am) and took bus 182 (181 also goes there) to Seongpanak because we wanted to climb up to the peak. We got to the mountain around 7:45 and started the hike. The weather was super nice when we left, and we planned it that way, because we wanted to at least get some nice views of the city, and while at the summit. This is a long day of hiking, so be prepared. Bring snacks (and a trash bag, because you have to carry everything back down), and water. There are 2 checkpoints along the way that have bathrooms. The last checkpoint sells ramen for about 1500w with hot water. This is the checkpoint you have to get to before 12:30. We made it there around 11, and up to the summit before noon On the Seongpanak trail, there is also a lake with an observatory that's worth the detour.The last part of the hike up to the summit is pretty steep and rocky, so watch your footing, especially because you might be tired from walking up. Wear adequate footwear, make sure they are sturdy and comfy!Unfortunately, we didn't get that lucky with the weather as it because overcast as we were getting up there. I guess it really depends on your luck (the next day, it was super clear! Damn you Mt Halla!!) hahaha.We took the same trail down (from the summit, there is another trail, but no buses stop there. And this is where your comfy shoes are a must. The hike up was not bad, but the hike down, was torture! Our feet kept hitting the front of our hiking shoes, so we were bruised and hurt by the time the hike was done. We were also sore for the next 2 days (and we're pretty sporty, but we rarely walk for 8 hours) Overall, it's a great hike. The trail up is covered by trees, so it is cooler than it seems, but there are still some great views, especially with the fall foliage. We'd be surprised at the range of people walking the trail, old and young love to hike up this trail, and we understand why!

Located at the eastern end of Jeju Island. It will be about 1hr - 1.5 hrs drive if you stay at the city centre to this stunning place. Advisable to travel early in the morning if you want to avoid the tourists. I drove from Yeha Guesthouse around 7am and arrived in Seongsan Ilchulbong about 8.10am. The area was still empty with only those coming with their cars and still lots of parking lots. However if you arrived around 10am onward, rest assured the parking space will be a challenge. The entrance fee is KW2000 per adult. If you intend to hike until to the top, please wear proper shoes as the stairs can be pretty challenging and steep on the way down. The hike will take about 50 minutes if you walk slow and steady. Can be shorter if you climb faster. During the winter season, you are lucky if you can watch the sunrise. When we were there, it was cloudy and the sun is rising behind the cloud, but still the view up there is beautiful. If you don't want to climb up to the top, you can still enjoy the beautiful scenery around the area. If the time permits, you can also catch the Jeju Woman Diver (Haenyo) in action on your way down from the Seongsan Ilchulbong performing at two timing 1.30pm and 3.00pm respectively. There is a separate trail that leads down to where the action is. I wasn't able to watch it as we are rushing to go to Udo Island.There are Starbucks & Dunkin Donut for you to stop for a cup of coffee while enjoying the views and few shops that sells souvenirs. However the price may be a bit expensive as compared to Dongmun Market.Return visit : A must...for a sunrise views!

Living in Hong Kong we're pretty used to tough hikes - this one is a little difficult but manageable for anyone who is reasonably fit or has some hiking experience. Whilst the incline on this hike is never that steep and the first part of the trail is easy with paved walkways, the terrain for the second half is pretty hard going with lots of rocks and boulders. We managed in trainers but hiking boots with a sturdy sole would probably be better, and some may feel more comfortable with poles. But it's ABSOLUTELY worth the effort for the view. The crater lake is quite impressive but more stunning is if you look back on Jeju from above the clouds. Took us about 6.5 hours up and down but bring plenty of snacks as there is only one point where you can buy water and some dubious looking packet noodles. Oh and there are no bins so bring a bag for your rubbish. If you are in Jeju and like hiking, you must do this as it's a great sense of achievement when you can say you've hiked S Korea's highest peak!

Lava tubes are different all over - so these have their own special yet similar features. The overall experience was well worth it and I certainly recommend the visit. The trail is reasonable well developed with stairs down into the tubes. Though basically light, I thought the selected illuminations added to the features and overall feel of the caves. It is not overly spectacular in showing off the various formations and features, but it still gives a good view of the tube walls. Be careful of the path as it does have rough spots and puddles. Moist, cool and over 2 kms of walking, I enjoyed the visit, although not the most impressive caves I have visited.

Jeolmul Natural Forest is a must-see in Jeju Island. I really love the lush greenery in the forest park. There are many trails, each with different length and level of difficulty. We only had slightly less than 2 hours in the park. Therefore we only managed to walk the Samwool-gil trail followed by climbing the Oreum Trail (many steps, may get slippery if it rain) and explore the relaxing garden/ pond area. If I come again, I will allocate at least half a day in this beautiful forest. The entrance fee in only KRW1000, and there was a small stall at the entrance whereby you can grab a coffee or buy something to eat. Do not miss it if you are in Jeju Island.

Jeju Island is indeed a unique island with so many gorgeous scenery, i had a great time travelling there in Winter, a low season with lesser tourist gives a different experience from visiting it in busy Summer. I have seen pictures about Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff (?ъ＜ⓒ\由) and was amazed by the neat shapes of hexagon stone pillars formed by volcanic lava, i totally recommend tourist to spend time walking around the nicely design olle trail in the beautiful, as well as to visit Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff during your trip in Seogwipo or Chungmun area. you don't have to plan for a long stay, a good two hours should be more than enough, as it was just a viewing spot rather than you can actually walk-in and visit. Don't worry about the transport, bus services are available (in fact it is very convenient to reach most of the travel spot around Jeju island), just drop by Jeju International Convention Center (ICC) and walk about 15 minutes to the park entrance, bus drivers in Jeju are very friendly and can basic communication woudn't be a concern. there is a entrance fees of 2000won in the park.there are steps to walk down to have a clearer view, description board with picture will explain how the hexagons shapes are formed, you can take amazing pictures and enjoy the sea view too.speaking of the weather, i have quite an experience, it was sunshine at first while i was taking the bus, and soon it become heavy downpour and even snow flakes begin to attack me during my walking! i think an umbrella or raincoat is necessary for either bright sunshine or unexpected rain. i gotta say, Jeju Island's weather is unpredictable! although this is not a spot to actually feel and touch the pillars, it can be quite boring to certain people who expected more attraction, but seeing the amazing cliff, the neat pillars, it was totally worth it to witness it by your own eyes, even the finest artist surrender to this piece of art, isn't it?

I've climbed Hallasan twice now, once in December and once in early March, and both times I took this route. This route is slightly longer than Gwaneumsa, but it's also a gradual incline with several easy portions. I took this route primarily because there is not a lot of public transportation available to/from the Gwaneumsa trail, plus I'm not sure I can do a steep incline the entire way up to the summit. For Seongpanak, you have about 5 km that are easy, 2.5 km that get harder, and then a pretty brutal last 2 km. Regardless, know that there are other hiking trails around the island and even around the volcano, but only the two mentioned above will lead you all the way up to the summit.Given some of the reviews I saw that are either inaccurate or not very helpful, I hope to compile a quick list to help you decide if this is something you want to do and if so, what you will need:1) It's definitely going to be an all-day kind of thing. You will be tired afterward, so you likely won't want to schedule too many other activities for the evening. Also, it's likely that you will be sore and tired the next day or two. 2) You need to start climbing no later than 8:30 AM. As several people have mentioned, you will not be allowed to access the last chunk of the way if you're not at the second shelter by 12:30 PM (this is winter time, so the schedule varies slightly from season to season... always check the Korean tourism sites).3) Even if it's sunny, there's a chance you might need crampons. In the winter months you will need them for sure, but even last weekend people were sliding down and falling repeatedly without them. I hear that it's even worse on the Gwaneumsa trail since it's a lot more shielded from the sunshine. 4) Bring food and water! The only place you can buy something is at the very beginning of the trail, and even then the options aren't fantastic. A little protein or fruit will go a long way whenever you're starting to feel tired, and it'll help you push through. Please make sure you do not leave any of your trash along the way; there are zero trashcans, so if you carry something particularly messy, you might want to pack a bag for the waste.5) Do not use the toilet in the first shelter! It's the worst smelling bathroom ever, which is rare for Korea since things are usually so clean... I suppose it's the septic system. I suggest using the toilets at the parking lot and at the last shelter (there are two). The first one is seriously a nightmare. 6) It's not an easy hike, but it's doable even for people who don't exercise strenuously. I've seen people carrying babies all the way to the top, and I've seen small children and old people make it, too. Definitely wear the right clothing, though, and especially the right shoes. If you're hiking at a time without snow, you will spend hours circumventing rocks of all sizes and ankle support will be extremely helpful for this. Anyway, thanks for reading, I hope you have a fantastic hike!

It's got a high ranking but I was disappointed,  this was the 3rd waterfall I'd paid an entrance fee to see,  it's nice to see but nothing spectacular we hooked it onto the end of olle trail 7 after cheongjiyeon falls.

It?s our 2nd time in Jeju Island so we decided to do it. We took a bus to Seongpanak and started our hike there. It took us 5 hrs to the peak. It?s not an easy hike at all. Wear comfortable shoes, hiking shoes or sneakers with very good soles. The trail is full of rocks. This will definitely hurt your feet. Don?t wear jeans. Wear something more comfortable. Also bring as much water as you can. In the map, it says there is a Water Station  but they are gone now. You have to be by the second shelter at 12:30 or else they wont allow you to go to the summit. Everybody must descend by 2pm.Going down we took the Gwaneumsa Trail which is shorter but more difficult trail. However, I would recommend this trail cause it?s more scenic. It took us another 5 hrs.

It was a short drive from Seogwipo where I stayed with my son In late Dec. The trip was highly recommended by the Shilla hotel staff and I could understand why after having spent an hour on its rugged coastline. Awesome selfie spots at every turn! Another highlight was the women divers selling their harvest (sea cucumbers) on the coastline. It was a stimulating walk, with crystal clear waters lapping at our feet. We went when the tide was receding as advised by the hotel staff. So do check before venturing down. 2nd tip: go well bundled up as it can get very cold in winter. As a reward, we headed to the Hiddink cafe at the end of the trail (next to car park) for a hot cuppa. It felt like we had stepped into a Dutch village, replete with tulips and clogs. As you can probably guess, Korea is still besotted with the Dutch football coach.

It is quite expensive with 12.000 won per adult, but you could easily spent 2-3 hours and it is nicely set up. Of course the glass castle has a lot of romantic photo ops for newlyweds. But also their little hiking trail is nicely decorated and I loved all the wind chimes. You could do glass blowing or get your picture in glass. They have snacks and a coffee. Overall a nice little theme park.

I'm an American living in South Korea. On the west coast of the United States there are many hikes and every weekend I was on a trail. So, when I saw Hallasan I thought it would be a peice of cake. I was very wrong. It doens't look hard but the trail is cut straight up, (no switch backs). After reaching the top you know that you climbed a mountain and it feels good. You look back wondering how many steps you climbed.If you're going bring plenty of water and start early. Now I've been up about 5 times and I feel like I don't need to go again.There are tails to the top from almost any direction.It's worth doing at least once.

If you live on Jeju you have to do it at least once. I'm from the West where the mountains are huge so, when I saw Hallasan it looked like a piece of cake. How wrong I was. Mountain trails in the West take you up by switchbacks but the tail up Hallasan goes straight up  and straight down. There are no switchbacks. Only about a million steps to climb. I'm not saying that there is anything wrong with that......just be prepared. Start early and take water.When I went up I thought I was going to die. It didn't help that there was this grandpa in flip-flops who passed me on the way up and then he passed me again as I was still on my way up and he was coming down and then he passed me again going up as I was still on my way up. How embarrassing was that?????? Very embarrassing!As far as the climb went, it was great. I felt like two cent going up but once on top I felt like a million bucks. Clean air and blue sky. Views of the whole island.One good thing about going down is that it's all down hill. I do a lot of complaining about it but I've been up there five times now so  there must be something I love about it.If you do go up and you see that grandpa tell him hi from me. He passed me so many times I feel like I know him. ;)

If you are fanatic about nature then you would probably really like this park. However if you enjoy nature but are more swept away by breath-taking scenery then in my opinion you will be really disappointed. We did the Seogwipo trail and for the effort involved the reward was just not enough. The trail took around two hours each way, and part of that was over some extremely difficult terrain. It's not that step, but walking over really large stones and boulders for over an hour can get really tiring, especially when there is no view to distract you, you are just surrounded by trees, There is nothing to see at all for the most part! At the end of the trail, the mountain lake and view of the valley is nice, but nothing that special or amazing. We were there in low season and even then it was extremely crowded, so you never have the feeling that you are really hiking a mountain. I wouldn't do it again.

I woke up really early to get ready for this hike. I took the first bus 281 from the old bus terminal in Seogwipo leaving at 6am. We arrived at Seongpanak trail entrance about half an hour later. I did this trail mid January and you need crampon for this. Personally, I don?t like slippery surface so crampons really give me the confidence. But I saw people on the hike didn?t have crampons. Some other people hiked in their running shoes. Snow was thick but you basically walked on top so I guess You don?t necessarily need hiking boots. Unless you go off trail, the snow will be knee deep. It was such a nice feeling to see everybody get up and early to start the hike when it?s still dark out. The hike up was not very challenging and it took me about 4.5 hours. I?m an extremely slow walker. Keep in mind that there is cut off time. If you start too late and couldn?t get up to the last shelter on Seongpanak trail before 12pm, you are not allowed to go to the summit. The view at the top was so beautiful. It was very windy though. I took Gwaneumsa trail down since I wanted to change views. That was challenging. My knees hurt so bad even though I already wore knee braces. It?s shorter than Seongpanak trail but it took me almost the same amount of time. There was one part quite steep and I didn?t notice the rope which you can hold on to, I slid down and broke my trekking pole. Apart from being slippery, the trail is quite rocky and by the end of the day, after a beautiful sunny day, the snow started melting and made the trail very slushy. There was time I almost gave up, my whole body hurt and I started to get blister on my toes. When I got to the entrance of the trail, I took bus 475 for 10 mins to a university entrance station then changed to bus 281 to go back to Seogwipo. I guess you can take 281 directly from Gwaneumsa to Seogwipo but I didn?t know where it was so I followed the crowd. I totally recommend this hike.

i went to Jeju Olle Trail number 7. it was really awesome. i was travel alone and this place really good for refreshing your mind, relaxing, just enjoy the sound of the wave and the wind. trekking without feeling exhausted. and this place are one of shooting location for Jewel On the Palace :)!!!! must visited

I only went up this trail for 1.5 hours then came back as that was all I wanted to do.  I took my time and because I did that I saw deer which many people just walked by not noticing.  The trail is quite rocky.  You need good boots and cotton gear as you get quite hot. (All the Koreans dress up in this synthetic mountain looking gear and my husband who went all the way up said they were all nearly passed out on the side of the track from over heating!) Some people had these HUGE packs on their backs.  God knows what they were carrying! I had 2 bottles of water and dried octapus for sustenance and that was enough.  My husband who went all the way up used 7 bottles.  You can buy water at various places up the trail so you don't have to carry it all. There are a lot of people who do this ...or try...so it's best to start at 6am to beat the crowds.  There is also a train of sorts that you can pay for to take you most of the way up.  Not sure how much that costs.  There's a restaurant at the bottom surprisingly that's all in Korean,  no English, no pictures, which is odd for such a big tourist area. They have a beef soup, sushi rolls Kim bap and other stuff.  I'll upload a pic of the menu so you can get a translation before you go there.I'm not sure if you have to pay a fee to climb this track as we just walked up but on my return I did see a ticket box so maybe you do...

I loved my hike in Hallasan. We were a couple and we decided to take the 'most challenging trial' - Gwaneumsatrail (8.7 km).  There are four Hallasan trails on and around the mountain, but only two of these trails will take you all the way up to the volcano?s crater lip ? theGwaneneumsa trail is one of these, theSeongpanaktrail is the other one. It is important that you check beforehand which trial is open, because it depends on the weather forecast. In my case all the 4 trials were partially open which meant that the crater lip was not accessible unfortunately. There is a website you  check (in Korean) or you can simply do what I did and ask the staff at the reception of the hotel. Each trials is easily accessible by bus, however the buses are not that frequent - for example 1 every hour for the Gwaneneumsa train, so you might need a bit of planning. Our trail was accesible for 6 out of the 8.7 km and took us to the first shelter (1500m elevation) the hike took us.6 hours back/forth including a quick lunch break; the pace wasn't that high but we weren't that slow either. If you want to access the crater lip, one think that you need to bear in mind is that you need to make it to the first shelter by 12-13 depending on the season (November was 12.00pm).Another thing to remember is that there is no convenience store or food vendor available during the hike, so you want to pack some food (kimbap is a good option) and water. As the hike itself, I really enjoyed it, you will feel immerse in the nature and you will enjoy a nice variety of vegetation depending on the altitude.

I love this place, feel so peaceful with the wide space to walk around.  Admiring the natural landscape with pine trees, Eulalia flower and lush vegetation.  Perfect place for picnic if not for winter!  Kids can run wild or roll down the slope.  A great photography place.There are few trails to explore but we left in an hour as we have other places to visit.  A must go place in Jeju!

I hiked up Hallasan via Seongpanak trail and went down the Gwaneumsa trail. The hiking was almost torturous, for a person who does only some jogging as preparation to hike Halla, but it indeed worth every step towards the peak because of the heavenly view of Jeju from there. Expect rocky trails, crazy steep staircases and trails. Bring at least 2 litres of water (you can refill your bottles at fresh water springs along Seongpanak and after the bridge in Gwaneumsa trail). There's a small shop selling hot noodles, drinking water and hot coffee at Jindallae Bat shelter. Toilets are available at Sokbat and Jindallabaet and a few more somewhere along Gwaneumsa. Start early to complete the hike early. Be sure to bring your camera. Get walking sticks too if you can, I didn't but I could still do the hike :D I went to Jeju on a solo trip and did the hike alone, but a lot of other hikers were very kind giving me words of encouragement and even waited for me along Gwaneumsa trail. A must do if you get to Jeju! No entrance fee! :D

I hiked to the top today.  I had decided not to do this but at breakfast this morning a gal from Korea highly suggested I go, so I did. I took the Seongpanak trail up and back. I got there a little after 10 and was told that it was a bit late to make it to the top so I went out very quickly so I would make it to the Check station by 1 PM. If you get there after that time they won?t let you up to the top. I made it and got to the top. At 2:30 they make everyone come down. I came down slowly and at the end I was all by myself walking those trails as it got darker. I didn?t get down until about 7 PM. Because I was in such a hurry to get up it took me much more time to come down than it did to go up. As I was walking down a deer jumped right in front of me And then jumped away. I brought two bottles of water and lunch. That was perfect for me. There are restrooms on the way up but not at the top. They are outhouses. I do not have hiking shoes with me, just my slip on sketchers, so my feet are still sore from walking on those lava rocks with these shoes. This is also the reason it took me so long to get down, my feet were really sore At that point and I had to rest them during the descent. There is a Monorail track next to the trail. Today I saw them taking down some people who couldn?t make it down on that.

I have read a lot of reviews about Hallasan Mountain and before going there, you have to know that this is not easy to climb. Going to the top of the mountain is really hard and you should get some really good shoes, especially because at the end, it really hurts the ankles. I took the Seongpanak trail and it is 19.2 km in total, the view is not spectacular when you climb, it is beautiful when you are on top of the mountain but the problem is that it is so exhausting that I really could not enjoy the view as I could have if I was full of energy. I was lucky and so a deer in its natural environment. It is difficult but after doing this, you feel really happy. There is only a thing really annoying ; toilets are really really dirty with no toilet papers so take tissues with you (and a big bottle of water, two are too heavy for the back).

I found much of Jeju island to be very commercialized and crowded with loud tour groups. This is a great place to enjoy the natural beaty of Jeju with smaller groups of people. There is a small entrance fee.  The first half mile is along a wide crushed rock road. It is lined with young   nutmeg   trees. The trees are in the yew family. They are Torreya nucifera and are native to Japan. I  visited in October when the small edible nuts ripen. The nuts are encased in a thin husk that has a wonderful aroma. You will see people collecting them under the large trees.  Eventually the road ends and then you follow a loop trail that is about 2 feet wide it is covered with a hemp rope mat that felt lovely to walk on with bare feet.  The crowds end at the beginning of the narrow trail so you can walk through this section in peace and really marvel at the enchanting colors and smells of the forest and hear the songs of the many birds.  There were signs to watch for snakes but I saw none. The yews are huge.  Make sure to investigate the tree bark it is fabric like and soft. Also many of the other plants have English name labels which is nice. The trail is flat and should take a leisurely couple of hours or less if you rush.  I noticed a lot of people sitting on benches in the first section enjoying picnic lunches.

I didn't reach the summit but hiking the Eorimok and Yeongsil trails didn't provide amazing views as far as I was concerned, but it's definitely worth doing.Take the 740 bus from City Bus Terminal to Eorimok (krw1800, 45 min) or Yeongsil Ticket Office (krw 2800, 60 min). Bus leaves CBT at 07:00, 08:00, 09:00, 10:00. You don?t want to set off after 10:00 as you won?t get back! Last returns are 17:36 (Yeongsil) and 17:55 (Eorimok) April through October.I took the Eorimok trail up (there?s an easy 1km walk from the bus stop to the trailhead) and reached the Witseoreum shelter in 2 hours, including stops. The first 2.4km are quite tough but it gets much easier the further you go. If you?re worried about your ankles then wear hiking boots but trail shoes are fine. The descent down via Yeongsil was a leisurely 90 mins but it feels like it would be a slightly tougher climb compared to Eorimok. There?s also a 2.5km downhill walk from the trailhead to the bus stop, so bear that in mind if you decide to start from Yeongsil. The scenery is much better on Yeongsil, although those with vertigo may find it tough, even with the very good safety barriers on the route. Eorimok doesn?t have those problems but the first 2km is under forest cover, with little scenery to admire for most of the climb.If you want to hike to the summit start very early, which probably means you'll need a car in case you miss the last bus back.There are clean, normal toilets at both entrances and at the Witseoreum stop. You will have to carry all trash back down as there are no bins anywhere on the mountain. You can buy hot instant noodles at the Witseoreum but you?ll have to carry it back down. I bought several buns and pastries at Paris Baguette for my hike.

Hiked to the top of Hallasan yesterday morning through the Gwanmeusan Trail - started at about 7:10am and were back in our car at 2:30pm - so this start and finish time includes breaks, and you'll need them even if you are in okay or good shape. It was a bit disappointing to see the majority of water bodies in the mountain are dry at the moment - just a few ponds on the early parts of the trail, and the crater lake at the summit, which we expected would be much deeper. The trail has a combination of dirt, rocks, and steps/bridges. I wish the steps and parts of the trail didn't include so many sharp rocks - your feet WILL feel them! We did the hike in running shoes because we don't have hiking boots here. I can see the climb being a lot easier with hiking shoes. Some parts of the trail are very steep so if you have serious knee problems, I don't think this is the trail for you. Do bring lots of water and snacks - we had two liters of water for each of us and I still think my husband got dehydrated rather badly. There is really nothing to eat on the trails so bring snacks. Visibility yesterday wasn't great - pollution has been pretty high in Jeju the past couple of days - but it's still a GREAT, BEAUTIFUL view from the top. I loved all the flowers you see growing in the rocky sides of the mountain in the last third of the trail. Very happy I did it and it's a great hike, but there is not a lot to see before you get to the top. We went down the same trail, so a total of 17.4kms. It'd be interesting to see what the other trails are like, but I don't think I need to summit again.

Hallasan was a good challenging climb, with the hike splits into 3 parts. The first 2 hour or so, we were hiking through mostly level ground, some rocks and little steps. As we reach the middle ground, the trail gets steeper, more rocky and almost half are made up of steps, mostly made of rocks. Using a hiking stick at this time really helps in making the climb easier. When it rains, which happened the entire day when we went, the ground gets covered with puddles and pools of water, so it was extra effort trying to choose the rocks to step on to avoid getting our feet wet. Towards the top, there are flights and flights of steps, followed by a trail made of rocks where u have to use a rope to climb up the steep rocky surface. It was challenging but overall, felt good.As it was raining, we didn't manage to get any view of the crater or lake at the summit. But the sense of accomplishment making it up was great!The way down was more challenging as after a day of rain, the trail became wetter and what used to be steps, some were submerged in water. Hence, even with a good waterproof shoes, ur feet could still get wet. Also, note that the sky turns dark at around 5pm in winter and there's no lighting in the reserve. Hence, make sure u buffer enough time to reach the foot of the mountain before that time. Otherwise, u would be hiking in the dark. Nevertheless, there would be a ranger moving down the rail lines in a cabin moving on a rail line, looking for stranded hikers. So no need to panic. However, I would still recommend planning well, checking the weather and choosing a clear day to climb. Start early so as to buffer enough time to reach the 3rd rest station by 12pm, as anytime after that, they do not allow hikers to go up to the top. Think it is for safety reason to buffer enough time for the ascend and descend. Also, to wear waterproof shoes and if available, bring a hiking stick along. Do standby a raincoat in case of light drizzle. Also bring some food along. Though they sell instant ramen and some bento at the resting stations, it closes by 2pm or so and you don't want to end up hungry.  Lastly, enjoy the climb!

Hallasan is the main attraction of Jeju Island so even though we are not hiker, we need to have our feet on the mountain. We took the easiest trail: Eoseungsaengak Trail, only 1.3km. This trail does not lead to the summit. We spent about 1 hour to reach Eoseungsangak Peak, it was very windy when we got there. But we glad we did it.

Halla mountain can be hiked in 3-5 hours easily. I have hiked the Seongpanak Trail (on the east side)  and the Gwaneumsa Trail (on the north side). These are the two trails that go all the way up to the summit. If you are fit, these runnable, but Geaneumsa trail especially gets very steep at the end. Get to your trail of choice early to miss the crowds, and also note that the half way points of each trail close around 12 (depending on the time of year it is sometimes 12:30). Een when it is foggy it is beautiful, but, of course, it is best when you can see clearly down to the crater lake and across off of Jeju to the ocean. Pack a lunch and enjoy it on top of the mountain! (Or instant ramen is the traditional food to pack).My favorite time to go is in winter when the top of the mountain is covered in a few feet of snow! Make sure to bring crampons for your shoes (simple ones are OK, you aren't hiking K2!)

From the Jejusi bus terminal we took bus 201 to Udo. It took about 1 1/2 hours. Definitely download the app Naver to navigate your way around the island, as Google Maps does not have any results for public transportation. We spent 4 hours on the island. Ferry ride from the port is only about 15 minutes each way. Buying a ticket can be a little chaotic as there are no signs in English but we just held up 2 fingers for two passengers and were given 2 round-trip tickets. Upon arrival in Udo expect to be bombarded with shop owners yelling at you to rent bicycles, ebikes, motorcycles, or 3-wheeled cars (for 2 people). 2 people renting 2 ebikes for 4 hours cost us 40,000 won. Need int?l drivers license for the latter 2. I definitely recommend the ebike over the bicycle unless you really want to get strenuous exercise. Lots of hills and 11.4 km of trail to follow. Lots of little mini-towns where you can buy food, have coffee or peanut ice cream (recommend). Tons of photo opps so take your time. We finished in 3 hours, 40 mins (and my hubby wanted to stop A. LOT. Last ferry back to Jeju is at at 5 pm this time of year. Plan accordingly.

For someone with bad stamina like me, it would take about 2.5 hours to reach the end of the trail.The tip is, to go there early in the morning, then you can take some leisure time to rest from time to time. When we're going down to trail at about 10p.m., there are lots of people coming up the trail and it is quite packed with people.For person with knees or legs or ankle problems, must be really careful as I fell down several times due to rocky trails at certain places. However, the view along the trail were awesome and it feels really worth it! The warm ramyeon at the shelter was the climax!I went in April 2016. The wind is super strong on top. So make sure you're ready for that. Hotpack, jackets, windbreaker or whichever deems to keep you warm. You may not need them in the beginning of the trail but you might need it in the end of the trail.

For hiking enthusiasts, this is a must do!  The Seongpanak (9.6km) trail has an average hiking time of 4.5 hours and Guaneumsa (8.7km) trail has an average hiking time of 5 hours.  One must reach the Jindallaebat Shelter by 1pm to be permitted an attempt at the Baekrokdam summit.  My husband and I completed the hike in 7hrs 35mins but were perplexed to understand how it took us 5 minutes longer to descend, given that we did not take breaks while descending. Guaneumsa has the reputation of being the roughest trail on the crater, but does live up to its reputation for breathtaking views.  - There was one potable water area on each trail where nature provided delicious water refills.  - Emergency posts appear through the trails, each with its own number, so keep track of the number in case you need assistance, rescue workers can narrow down your location.  - There are incredibly handy signs along the way to pinpoint your progress and identify the level of difficulty along the trail.  Paths are well maintained and varied; wooden, rocky, skree, etc. - If you take the bus to there is no fee for hiking.- Although we did not have cell phones with us, many folks seemed to be talking an walking throughout the trails.- We chose to end at the Guaneumsa trail head because it was the closest in proximity to our hotel.  Cabs are available at the trailhead.

fascinating  view from bottom until top. but we went on saturday, pack with local hikers. the path is quite easy. about 18km back and forth using seongpanak trail. on the way back we tag along with the person incharge/worker of mt. hallasan, and being offered to use the little train to the way down. best of all, there is no entrence fee charge to hike the  national park.

Back in the days of yore --  how far back, no one can be certain --  three demigods came forth from three holes in the ground located near the northern coast of an island to the south of Korea.  These three demigods lived as hunter-gatherers until a ship arrived bearing three princesses, domesticated farm animals and seeds for growing grain. The princesses married with the demigods, and the Tamna Kingdom was born. Today, we know Tamna, which ended in 1404 with the coming of the Joseon Kings -- Korea's last imperial dynasty -- as Jejudo or Jeju Island.  We know that beloved and mystical site as Samseonghyeol (  sam   means three in Korean). It is a special place and, particularly for history buffs, a   must-see   in Jeju.  The holes, which likely were once active thermal vents on this volcanic isle, are surrounded by a protective Stonehenge-like ring and a mini-forest/park of lush and majestic, mature trees and flowers.  It is quite pleasant, and on a warm summer's day, a cool respite from the city that has grown around it.  There's a small museum showing a film about the founding of Tamna.  The film is in Korean, but if you look at the exhibits there before watching the film, you will understand it much better.  It is not readily possible to actually photograph the holes unless you have a ladder, a drone, a long selfie stick or happen to be about 8 feet tall...this would be my one disappointment about the site.  But there is an official photo mounted nearby.  If you have the time, plan to spend 1-1.5 hours there, to take in the walking trails, museum, movie and various historic buildings.  You will also be greeted by some of the original 18th century dolhareubangs (protective   stone grandfathers  ) remaining on the island.  It's a good outing for singles, couples, friends and families.  Even young children can enjoy the birds, flowers, stones and many benches located throughout the park.  Admission is quite nominal...2,500 KRW adults, 1,700 teens; 1,000 children 7-12.

An UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and a World Heritage Site, the Hallasan National Park is loaded with walking trails and is home to South Korea?s highest mountain named the Shield Volcano Hallasan. You?ll find about 1800 different kinds of plants and a number of alpine animals along the way up. The park is a unique place for nature lovers. Settled right in the heart of Jeju island, this park with high density woods and blooming hillsides is concidered as a treat to be at. Transportation: start with chosing a right trail for you. There many different ways up to the mountain, but only one of them will bring you to the summit. To get to the entrance you?d probably need to take one of the public busses or rent a car. Both options are convenient. Equipment: You?d definitely need to be prepared for a long and tiring walk. All the trails are devided into segments, based on their difficulty. Some of the parts of the trail would be paved, some wouldn?t be equipped at all. You?d be grateful for those parts where you?d be able to walk and step on the wooden bridges and paths. But except those short and the easiest parts of the way, you?d need to climb on the steep and narrow rocks, hop along cobblestones and boulders. Timing: don?t rush, remember when you?re on the top, that was only a half of your journey. There is the same long way down the mountain when you?re on the summit. Tips: be prepared for considerable change of the temperature and other weather conditions. We started in a pleasant sunny day and finished when it was drizzling and the fog was literally embracing us. Add up some wind and decreased temperature and you?re almost in our shoes out there. You?d definetely need to wear tracking boots or something alike, protecting and supporting your feet well. Otherwise you  risk hurting your ankles and knees. (as us, cause we were not prepared)You?d also want to change your clothes after 6-7 hours tracking up and down this mountain. Believe me you?ll be sweating af.

After nearly two years spent in Korea, I can quite easily say that Hallasan is the most beautiful place I've visited while here. Dramatic scenery, including sprawling vistas and interactive cloud-cover made this an exhilarating climb. Don't expect an easy journey! I took the   easiest   trail and it took us a good 5 hours to complete, and the hike up the mountain itself was via a crowded and steep staircase.The sheer variety of landscapes you experience as you climb up is really impressive. When you reach the mid-point, there's a rest stop where you can buy water, coffee and ramen noodles (oh, Korea!), but bring your own snacks because you'll probably be up there for a while.

A relatively easy hike going up Yeongsil trail (lots of climbing). Note that if you're taking the bus, you still need to do a pre-hike of 2.5km going up the mountain after you get off the bus stop. In my opinion, this was harder than the actual hike going up, but it was good preparation. There's also a cafe near the actual entrance. You can buy food here right before going up the trail.The cutoff time for Yeongsil trail is 2pm during the summer, but I would advise you to come early. The hike itself can be done in 1.5 hours, but with picture-taking, it can take as long as 3 hours (and the view at the top is gorgeous in many places!).Wear good hiking shoes. I've seen people wear regular sneakers (and even a guy with leather shoes -- what was he thinking?!), but I swear your feet will hurt if your shoe even manages to survive. Both Yeongsil and Eorimok trails have unpaved trails with unforgiving rocks. Hiking sticks would also help with the descent if you have weak knees.It's safe to hike solo (even for females) during popular days, so you're sure to hike with other people. It's also best to go down where most people are going if you started late (most people drive, so they go down the same trail they went up).In case of emergencies though, you can call their emergency number. (There's mobile coverage for most, if not all, of the trail). Take note of the location posts every few hundred meters. In case you get injured, there's this small train which can take you down, but you have to wait quite a while.

A difficult one if you choose to do the longest one which takes 4.5 hrs up and 4 hrs down.We went up  the  Eorimok trail which took us 2 n half hours up..its not an easy trak with steps and rocky path but the track has been laid with a lot of effort.In autumn the trees start to turn their colours .We came down the yeongsil trail which took us one hour to come down with spectac views..its an easier way to climb down than to climb up the yongsil trail.Bus 240 goes and come back at both stops with the entrance name as the stop names.But while from Eiromok entrance it's just a 10 mins walk up to the start of the trail.....its 45 mins walk to walk to the yeongsil entrance bus stop to the start of the trail.There are no tkts entrance for the hikes,but if you have rented a car then there is a parking fees.Carry some food to eat and energy bars and water n juice.
you have to walk 2km into the cave and it is cold! Nice feeling and nice view too~ bring your own umbrella as I went when raining.

With Snoopy Garden’s steep entrance fee it initially didn’t make my itinerary. But the good reviews were consistent and friends also highly recommended the Charles Schulz’s Peanuts themed museum and garden. The indoor museum part was the highlight for me which had explanations about every main Peanuts character and several comic clips that span over Schulz’s 50 years of drawing them. The old newspaper clippings old toys and old books were also cool to look at. There are dozens of great photo spots which can create some major bottlenecks on crowded days. The garden had about half a dozen themed areas (including my favorite Charlie Brown’s baseball field) that are pretty vast and would have been a lot more pleasant to walk around in cooler weather. We skipped the cafe that charged a criminal 8500 won for a lemonade. I’m not sure that the high price of admission is justified but this is a well maintained attraction(which is refreshing considering the high number of run down museums and small theme parks in Jeju) and the quality of the displays are of superb quality. Adults and children both also fans and non-fans of Peanuts both would enjoy the visit here.

when we saw the peak we know that it can be death tiring for us because we not that fit and also we not love hiking but when see all the ajusshi and ajuhmma look very spirit to hike we being very competitive and take the challenge and it's not regretful decision because the views from top really amaze us and make us feeling refresh.

Went to visit this attraction even though I saw some negative reviews as I have planned some attractions based on region and this is some thing that I think the kids would love to visit.Entrance fee is pricey at $5k won as there is practicably nothing much to see and do inside. After buying the tickets  the staff would give the adults coffee and kids chocolates. The display were very old  like it has been there for 3 or 4 decades and we felt uneasy as it looks dirty. There is a kitchen whereby apprentice showcase their skils on chocolate making. Wanted to buy some chocolates since we are there. But they dont seemed to be interested as the minimum sale item cost about $39k for a box of chocolates. Not worth my moneh and thus left empty handed. Adults ans children were disappointed.

review: Well maintained. Excellent view. Get a coffee and take a stroll. On a windy day it can be very cold there.
We went there in the morning. 2000krw for the entrance fee. Nice scenery view. Watch out for slippery rocks if you wanna take photos.

We visited at the beginning of May and it was cold. It also rained when we were on the beach. So could not enjoy the water.However beach is very nice and clean. We had coffee in the coffee shop on beach which gives you nice view of the beach.Its just opposite Hallim park so can be combined.Would nice to spend a warm and sunny day on this beach.

We stopped by Wolijeongri Beach for about 30 min. on the way to UDO; the water was very clear.  There were kids playing sand on the beach. The view was peaceful. We enjoyed our short walk along the beach. You can get some snacks and a good coffee from a caf챕 or a convenient store nearby. There is a restroom facility too.

We need to pay for the entrance fees but it is not that pricey and worth it. You need to take a few stairs to finally reached the waterfall area. The view is very sceneric and worth to take a picture on every angle of it. A must visit place when you are at Jeju Island.

We made a stop there for lunch as recommended by our B&B owner. There are now 2 coffee shops. We had lunch in the new one. The steamed bun with sausage was nice. The brunch set menu was a bit bland. The best thing in the brunch set is the homemade yoghurt with marmalade. We enjoyed the view while having lunch. Quite relaxing. More Korean day-trippers and foreigners. We had green tea ice cream from the old coffee shop afterwards. Really good green tea ice cream. Better than some that we had in Japan. If you want a quick lunch and want something non-local this is the place to go.

We finished the route #10 (17.5KM) in about 5 hours (we walked pretty slowly and took a lot of pictures). The whole experience was unforgettable. The magnificent view of the ocean on the left and mountain on the right was amazing. I thought it would be hard since I'm not that much used to walking for long hours but it didn't feel exhausting at all. Every sight was so gorgeous that I just didn't want to leave. I felt very fresh and relaxed after the walk. Even the tiredness after it was finished was worth all of those pretty shots I took and the healing. STRONGLY RECOMMEND!

We came here on a sunny morning primarily since we had never seen any tea plantations and it seemed like a sufficiently different thing to do on holiday.There is no entrance fee to the actual plantation and parking is plentiful. We started off at the viewing terrace (with a sign halfway up the stairs informing us: 'What a great view') where there were tea plants in view as far as the eye could see. I was a bit disappointed since they really don't look dissimilar from any other bush (not being a gardener myself).The main attraction for us came a bit afterwards when we went into the Innisfree shop. In there you can buy sets for making cosmetic items. We chose to buy two sets of soap making equipment which cost us 10000 won each. You then take the equipment to the craft benches in the shop each of which was equipped with an I-pad showing us in English what we had to do. Our kids (10 and 15 - both girls) just loved it and spent a good 45 minutes happily occupied. We thought it was great - I even borrowed some of their stuff and joined in (very soothing). We thus ended up with some happily entertained girls and two presents to take home to grandparents to accompany the video my husband made of the whole event.After this we ordered some green tea food and drink from the caf챕. Again the atmosphere was lovely - bright and airy. Prices as mentioned elsewhere are quite high but taken in conjunction with the atmosphere felt ok. The food was lovely.Overall we spent a lovely morning here and all came away very pleasantly surprised.

Was curious about this rock formation as read the other trip advisor comment and was not disappointed at all. Its really a very interesting rock formation and its nice to just feast your eyes on this amazing view.Only 2000kW for entry fee but try to avoid peak times as I went on a Sunday the viewing bridge was packed with visitors doing their selfie shots so you are not able to see the view as clearly due to the crowds. Must visit when you Jeju island.
Vigorous climb is SO worth the views and forest around you :) Feel as the Buddhists as you turn the drums and go within.
Views are amazing from the top and the Buddha temple in the mountain is beautiful.Amazing rustic feel in the dome shaped temple.
Very beautiful beach with azure sea. Lots of coffee shops and restaurants on the shoreline to grab a snack and enjoy the view.
Turkoise waters and great views of the beaches from multiple restaurants and coffee places all along the shoreline.May be a bit difficult to find parking though.

This was one of the most interesting things I visited in the cheesy Jeju Island. It's a piece of architecture. Everything is about meditation. The buildings are angled to frame Seongsan Ilchulbong volcano and they give you different perspectives of it. I found it very cool.The entrance fee was $5 but it is worth it. You have to walk from the parking lot to this area  it's about 10 to 15 minutes. The views are nice.

This place is rather far from where stayed (it would take about an hour from Jeju city/Seogwipo) and if you have a car you can enjoy the scenic route passing by horse farms and ATV parks and occasionally some towns. Make sure your car has enough petrol/gas as we didn't note much stations during our drive.It is located at a bay by the sea which has a good view (after you are done with the aquarium). There is a parking lot available but we were there on a super busy day despite being a Monday (we just thought that maybe it was the school holidays?) and we were lucky to get a lot.Place is stroller friendly but be mindful if the place is quite full. Everyone can get mesmerised by the display and you may just knocked by a stroller or two.The displays are quite entertaining. There are some attractions such as otter/pelicans feeding. You can check the time of these attractions at their website and you can time your visit there. There is a underwater tunnel and the manta rays will just swim pass.There was a huge aquarium display and unfortunately for us we were not able to the see the whale shark they were housing as it had been released back into the sea for research purpose. At certain times there will be a feeding session by scuba divers. The penguin display had some fake penguins in between and for some reason they look pretty realistic beside a real one when the real ones don't move. Have fun figuring out which is which!There was a show featuring synchronized swimming diving from high places. The show was about pirates and fairies. Everyone enjoyed the show (all in Korean with English displayed on the screen) and we were just clapping without really understanding what's going on but you will sort of understand the story. After about 20 minutes or so there was a seal show followed by a dolphin show. Again in Korean and you just shout and clap whenever the locals do. (For the language: it is the same in all other countries. Just be don't care and enjoy the show!) The show was about 45 minutes long and there is a stand outside selling popcorn and peanut butter roasted squid (a must try!) so get some and enjoy the show.On another wing there is a small science museum and a 3D theater. You can skip the museum and head outdoors (as most are in Korean) but there is a holographic display of the whale shark inside that is really cool. Attraction is free. For the 3D theater not sure if we had to pay an additional sum but it was featuring a shark show and we reckoned the kids would be terrified.There is a cafeteria downstairs and the food is pretty good. You will need to pay at a counter which they will give you a device which beeps when the food is ready for collection. If can get quite crowded as there's limited space. During your walk there will be pop up stands selling food so you don't have worry about getting hungry while walking around.After it all head outside for the scenic view and some outdoor picture taking. We were there on a gloomy day and wind was pretty strong.

review: This is a circular beach that turns into a lake on the rising tide  then dries again on the ebbing tide. m The water is not too deep (about a meter) and the half moon shaped beach is one of the largest in Jeju. The sand is particularly delicate and soft on the feet. The stone sculptures are worth a viewing too. Lots of things to do nearby  Folklore Village  Namwon Keunang and Seopjikoji. Loads of free parking close by.

This could be a quick stop or you could spend time enjoying the view.  There weren't too many people when we were there but of course it could be busy.  The falls are unique in that the fresh water falls directly into the sea below.  You have to take stairs to get down to the sea level.  You can't get right up to the falls but you can get close enough to feel the spray and hear the roar of the water.

There's not really much museum. I thought I turned a wrong corner but had actually walked through the whole thing. Just one wall of tea cups and pots and basically no English signage. But it's free and you really go for the tea shop and cafe.Nice teas for sale (spendy but tasty!) and there are often free samples in the tea shop. Then move to the cafe for some green tea flavored sweets. I recommend the softserve ice cream twisted with yogurt. If you're here take time to climb to the 3rd floor observatory for some nice views. If you have a little extra time it's worth two other stops:1) just through the garden path walk up hill to the natural skin care center where you can smell local essences and make your own natural soap (for a fee). They have nice sandwiches and snacks for sale.2) Climb the oreum (small mountain) just north of O'Sulloc. Walk along the road past the tea fields until you see a concrete paved walk in toward the hill. Follow paths or bushwack until you see the path entrance. You can walk to the top in less than an hour from O'Sulloc. There's a nice viewing platform with views toward Seogwipo from the top.

The tea caf챕 and museum were extremely crowded so we headed for the Innisfree Jeju House.  It was a delightful oasis of calm comprising an organic food caf챕 a large space for making your own soap and a smallish retail space dedicated to bath and arotherapy products as well as a small selection of exclusive souvenirs.  We had the house special bingsoo (the Korean ice kachang) and it was so refreshing.  Not only was the shaven ice powdery soft the red beans were tasty the selection of healthy nuts crunchy and various Korean rice cakes both soft and crispy were delicious - all in a great dessert.  Being starved of clean fresh air for a while during the haze season back in Singapore it was very refreshing to sit outside enjoying the cool clean air and view the miles of tea bushes.We were so entranced by the place that we returned for lunch the next day.  I had the rice balls with soba & oden soup while my sis had a mini hot dog with the same soup.  We then proceeded to relax with a cup of coffee.  What utter bliss!Besides enjoying the F&B we picked up body scrub facial wash and some soft drinking bottles.  The staff was friendly and fluent enough in English which made our buying experience very smooth indeed.  We will definitely return when we are next in Jeju.

The scenery is definitely beautiful and you feel achievement and reward once you make it to the top but the journey up is steep. If you are not in shape like me it can take a while but stopping along the way to look down and enjoy the view is nice.

The Sanbanggulsa Temple is located SSW of Mt. Hallasan directly at the coast. It is a very unique and colourful temple which reminds us more on the temple in Taiwan as in Korea mainland. The temple is located just below Mt. Sanbang. We had our junior with us but with older kids it is probably a nice tour on top including the temple. The view from the temple is very nice and gorgeous. Probably from top of Mt. Sanbang even better. The area is quiet and peaceful.? Except the opposite place where noisy? Korean caterwaul being played at a swing boat. The place is not reachable for stroller and wheel chair. Parking place available. Entrance fee is negligible for parking and temple access. It is definitely worth to stop and to spend some time. Religious people are probably also allowed to pray i guess. Doors are open.
The rock does look like dragon but hard to capture the same through camera. There is walking path for people to enjoy the sea view with windy feel

The most memorable thing was rather on the ferry to Udo Island.The seagulls were hovering over those who had Calbee prawn crackers ready to feed them. They followed the ferry from Jeju all the way to Udo. That was a sight!Udo generally has good scenic views and interesting coral beach with clear blue waters.

The drive from jeju airport area to aqua planet is around 1 hour 10 minutes passing by many small towns. The entry tickets were quite costly and I used klook to get some discounts with the tickets. Upon parking the rented car outside the vicinity of aqua planet then picked up a number from the machine next to the ticket counter. Waited for the number and redeemed my wristbands without much hassle. Kids under 3 can enter for free.There are plenty to see and we were in time to watch fish feeding a seal and dolphin show. Outside the facilities has really good view and many people were taking photos.Food in the food court was not too bad and similar like incheon airport have to be ordered and paid at the cashier counter and picked up from the individual sections when the device buzzes.Overall experience was great and worth every cent spent.
