The roads, save for the highways, are slightly narrower than the roads we are used to in Singapore.Generally, the speed limits are:30 Km / hr within 100 m of school zones50 Km / hr in town areas60 Km / hr in the outskirts of town70 Km / hr along highwaysThe speed limits change quite frequently, so it is advisable to keep a look-out for the change in speed limits. There are speed-cameras practically everywhere, usually positioned up on traffic lights, lamp-posts and in some places, hidden behind 'boxes' manned by a policeman. So, if you wish to spend your money supporting the policemen, speed on at your own risk.The local drivers can, at times, be quite reckless. Just like we have hell-drivers here, there are hell-drivers in Jeju too, but not too many. Just stay alert and always be on the look-out using your wing and rearview mirrors all the time. Except for the main areas of Jeju-si and Seogwipo-si, most of the roads around the island are quite free of traffic.  To estimate the time needed to travel any distances, take an average speed of 45 km/hr.Parking:Generally free parking along kerb-sides and paid parking in some buildings and are generally available easily. Most hotels have free parking for their guests ? do check with the hotel management that you have booked with. Petrol cost: As at Nov 2014: Krw 1750 / ltrPlanning Your Routes:Planning your routes is totally at your own whim and fancy, depending on the places of interest as well as the available time you have on the island. If you have a few days ( I would recommend a minimum of five days), perhaps you may wish to consider the following suggestion:1. Day 1 ? Arrival and check into hotel. This sample itinerary is on the assumption that your hotel is in Seogwipo. 2. Day 2 ? Explore the west scenic coastal drive (Route 1132) of Sagye, Gosan-Ilwa, Hagwi-Aewol and visit the places of interest along this route ( Mt Sangkaksan / Songkaksan / Yongmeori). There are many cafes (especially along the Coastal Cafe Road) and bbq restaurants for stops of aromatic coffee and grilled black pig meat. Explore Jeju-si city (underground shopping mall) and return via highway 1131 where the famous ?Forest Tunnel? is located. After dinner, take a drive to the Lotte World Resort for some very beautiful night scenery of the giant windmills.3. Day 3 ? Go East this time along the Pyeoson, Sehwa-Jongdal and Gimyeong ? Haengwon coastal routes. Stopover at Seongsan Ilchubong (Sunrise Peak). Have dinner in Jeju-si before doing a night drive back to Seogwipo. 4. Day 4 ? Alternative 1Drive to Seongsan Port in the north-east via the eastern coastal route and park your car there. Purchase your ferry tickets to Udo Island and spend a very interesting day there. You can tour the island by buying the hop-off-on bus tickets or for the adventurers, you can hire the quad-bikes or scooters. Alternative 2 ? visit the popular tourist spots such as the Trick-art museum, teddy bear museum, waterfalls, submarine tours, Green Tea museum, Geomun Oreum, Citrus fruit farms, mysterious road, etc etc....5. Day 5 ? Pretty interesting coastal erosion processes and fantastic landforms. This is a relatively easy short walk along the coast. Be careful, however, if you're bringing kids or elderly person - the rock trail can get rather slippery and some parts will see you getting very close to the sea and waves.

OUR TRAILS: Yeongsil trail (up) - Eorimok trail (down) Based on advice from friends, we (four of us) opted for the 'easiest' Yeongsil trail to embark on our climbing adventure.. (personally, my friends and I do not think the hike up was that easy). To save ourselves from walking woes (about 2km from bus drop-off point to start point), we got a cab (from Seogwipo; about KRW25,000) to drive us right to the start point, where a cafe is located. Upon arrival, the temperature was about 6 degrees with strong wind (downtown Jeju was about 13 degrees). We immediately purchased head scarves and gloves for the climb.The beginning of the trail started out easy but not much of colorful scenery (thou it was still autumn). The steps got steeper and steeper at about altitude 1,300~1,550m. These was the part where I guessed we stopped several times to gasp for air. And that was only halfway of the climb! After the steep climb, we reached the easiest portion of the entire climb. The boardwalk to Witsae-oreum Shelter. A place where we could no longer differentiate the sky and the sea, it was a great place for us to take a group photo (with Mt Halla peak as the background). When we reached the shelter, all of us dashed for quick toilet break and joined the queue to purchase some instant noodles and energy drinks. The very optimistic us then rest our feet till 4pm and made our way down the Eorimok trail. Going down the trail within 1.5hrs (before the sky turned dark) was crazy. There were just too many steps or uneven routes to descend. However, the consolation was the different colorful scenery from Yeongsil (many oreums could be seen). Our fastest speed at our physical condition then, we took 2 hours to descend (I guessed we were the last batch of humans) and the sky has already turned dark when we finally reached the exit at Eorimok trail. There was no more bus nor taxi but thank god for the kindness and efforts of the nearby workers; they drove us to the foot of the mountain and got us a cab. Without them, we would never return back to our guesthouse safely. God bless them!LEARNING POINTS & OBSERVATIONS 1) Yeongsil (grand) and Eorimok (colourful) trails offer different sceneries. 2) Always double the time/ distance, advised by a Korean. (LOL). They are fast walkers and climbers. Few occasions, we managed to reach our destination after 2x their estimation.3) Saw many Korean seniors and children ascending/ descending Mt Halla. They lead a healthy lifestyle!4) Do not stop for photo taking. Take few shots and proceed with the climb.5) Lessen individual's weight for the climb. Forget about DSLR and tripod! LOL.6) Apart from a solid windbreaker/ jacket, small haversack with water, museli bars, gloves, scarf and hp are a must. Hiking sticks are recommended.7) Experienced strong telecom signals up in the mountains.8) The only toilet (after the starting point) available can be found at Witsae-oreum Shelter only (No tap for hand wash).9) Rubbish (@ Witsae-oreum Shelter) can only be thrown at the exit only. 10) Not to proceed further and U-turn if very tired. Because descending can be more demanding and tired too.11) @ Witsae-oreum Shelter, all climbers have to proceed down the mountain by 4pm (October). Please refer to Mt Hallasan's website as the information are very accurate and informative.SUMMARYWe took more than 6 hours exploring these two trails. Of course, time would be lesser if we did not make many stops along the way.  We were gasping for air while climbing up Mt Halla but the overall scenery was really breathtaking. Despite suffering muscle pains for the next 5 days, all our efforts were worth it.RECOMMENDATIONHighly recommended if individual is fit, adventurous, loves beautiful scenery and has time on his/ her plate. Personally, I recommend to teenagers and above. : )

Our stamina is not so good so it took us 5 hours round trip for Yeongsil Trail up to Witsae Oreum Shelter and back. There was no Ramen available at the shelter so if you plan to go, better bring lunch box, you will be tired and eat a lot anyway. There are plenty of hikers from old people to children so you wont get lost, even if you want. Yeongsil trail has 4 parts of itFirst part is wooden steps, you will pass some creeks and a lot of shade / trees.Second part is the most strenous part. Lots of rocks and steep climbs , so watch your step. There are some observation deck for you to take photos and rest. And more wooden steps with crazy inclination. After you pass the big rocks crossing,(third part) it will be open area with no shade and this has the best view. And the most leisure part because its flat with almost no inclination. There is water fountain where you can fill up your drink for free. Walk 10-15 minutes from the water fountain and you will reach Witsae Oreum Shelter. Tips : Use sunscreen all over your body, even if its windy and cold at the beginning of the trail, when it reach the open area with no shade, the sun ray will hit you so hard. Wear hat. My scalp got sunburnt. Even better go with long sleeve and long pants. Go very very early like 7 am because the parking lot will be full later.

Our guide dropped us at Seonimgyo Bridge at around 8am, and said he would pick us up around 11.30am.  3.5hrs for waterfalls?  I thought he must have made a mistake...Surprise surprise... We enjoyed the morning stroll across the park near Seonimgyo Bridge (with autumn leaves still visible in end Nov).  After a million selfies, we made our way to the 1st waterfall and was awestruck!  So beautiful!  Well strictly speaking, this is not a waterfall but a lake of some sort.  But who cares about the misnomer?To reach the 2nd falls, there is a well-marked trail.  A medium-distance walk with its fair share of up and down slopes.  Not arduous and I would definitely recommend it.  The waterfall is not Niagara, but I found it pretty in its subtlety.The 3rd falls has a warning - the trail may be difficult for children and elderly.  Since I am neither, I had assumed incorrectly that I would find it manageable.  Wrong!  It was a very very long way down (which was fine), and an equally long long way up (nearly killed me).  Was it worth it?  I am afraid not... for the 3rd falls. So my recommendation would be to visit the first 2 falls, but give the 3rd a miss (unless you want a workout).

Our guide brought us to this place, let us alight and asked us to observe the strange phenomenon. He switched off the car engine and we saw the car still moving uphill without the engine switched on. He then demonstrated by pouring a bottle of water at one spot along the road and we could see the trail of water wriggled its way uphill without the application of any external interferences. The phenomenon was strange and unexplainable. Was it that a magnetic force beneath the earth on this road had triggered off that momentum? My guide did not explain and I could not find any explanation on any of the signboards around the vicinity. I remembered few years back when I was in Shanghai, I visited the mausoleum of the great Chinese revolutionary martyr, Song Qingling which was located at the western part of the city. Prior to her demise, she had requested that her body be buried at this cemetery site beside her late parents, the influential and rich Song family. I was astonished to learn from our tour guide and saw with my own eyes the strange phenomenon of the cypress and pine trees planted around the mausoleum was bending inwards and downwards from all angles towards the direction of the cemetery site where her body was buried. It was not just the left rows of trees, not just the right rows of trees but the trees planted at all the other corners surrounding the rectangular burial plot that were seen pointing inwards and downwards with the focus at the burial ground. The lush green trees appeared like bodyguards saluting, bending their heads and standing humbly for her directions. My guide informed us that the cemetery was a specially chosen grand and auspicious geomancy burial ground and that account for the strange phenomenon. The Chinese believed that if your body is buried on an auspiciously good Fengshui geomancy chosen ground, your future generations will benefit and prosper. I am not an expert in Fengshui and was hoping to get a scientific explanation for the weird phenomenon. Right here, at this strange mysterious road in Jeju, I was also trying to observe if the trees growing around the vicinity of the mysterious road bend towards and focused at the core center where the strange phenomenon occurred but I could not see what I saw at Song Qingling's mausoleum. Both strange phenomenon seemed to be unrelated in their nature and in terms of scientific theory of explanation that a strong magnetic force beneath the earth is in operation. The `Bermuda Triangle' is also another unexplainable phenomenon whereby it was unexplainable as to where so many ships vanished in strange occurring environment. I had watched a Chinese TV series on science whereby the film director sought to provide scientific explanations to the many strange `unexplainable' and `supernatural' phenomenon around China. I really hope that some days, the same film director could incorporate the strange phenomenon that occurred at this mysterious road, the ship vanishing Bermuda Triangle and that of the Song Qingling's burial site in his series and provide a scientific theoretical explanation for the weird occurrence. The visit to this mysterious road had triggered off my curiosity and I left the place, confused and thinking of the limits in science.

Our destinations on Jeju were varied and sparse hence the need to engage private transport. We spent 4 days in Jeju and visited locations including Seongsan Ilchulbong, Samganburi Oreum, Jeongbang waterfall, Seogwipo submarine and Jeju Folk Village. We also hiked up to Sara Oreum, two thirds of the way up to Hallasan along the Seongpanak trail (we will try to scale Hallasan next time with some better planning).

One of the most popular trails in Hallasan National Park.To get here, take bus 781 from Jeju City. The fare was 1 800 KRW (the driver can give change). The journey is about 40 minutes. The stops are announced in English. The stop is Seongpanak.Set out early as you have reach Jindallaebat shelter by 1 pm in summer (12 pm in winter). Otherwise you wouldn't be allowed to reach the summit.The trail is 9,6 km long (one way), about 4,5 hours without breaks. The trail is in some parts very ROCKY so good hiking shoes and walking holes are strongly recommended. Don't worry you wouldn't climb alone. A lot of Korean will be faster than you.The view on the summit is well worth and rewarding.Bring water and sun block.You can buy a certificate for 1 000 KRW.

One of 3 famous waterfalls in Jeju, along with Cheonjiyeon Waterfall and Cheonjeyeon Waterfallis but apparently the only waterfall in Asia to fall directly into the ocean.  Definitely worth the short climb down to get as near the fall for nice shots and a sea splash. If lucky, you might even catch a rainbow over the fall.  Walking shoes recommended to navigate the rocky boulders.  Do come early before the tourist horde arrive.  Adventurous hiking enthusiasts can continue to the Olle trail from the carpark entrance.

On Jeju Island's Halla Mountain--at 1,950 meters, South Korea's tallest-- can be found Korea’s highest paved roadway, known as 1100 Meter Road or the 1100 Highland Rest Area.? There, you can take a self-paced nature hike on an elevated wooden walkway through a “volcanic” wetland; with its many lava rocks, trees and wildflowers, this place has an otherworldly beauty that you and your camera will love.? You’ll likely see lots of ravens, magpies and maybe some roe deer (be sure to stay alert for them along the highway if you are driving). Across the road, there’s a colorful cafe and shop, offering local beverage favorites and snacks, as well as souvenirs.? (They carry a good selection of galot clothing, made locally using persimmon-dyed fabrics.)? From the cafe’s observation deck, enjoy a perfect view of some of Halla’s most famous landmarks, including Yeongsil Folding Screen Rocks and the 500 Generals Rocks.This area takes on a very different character with each season, and locals often drive up to see the magnificent ice formations that form on the trees and rocks in the winter and spring, when Halla’s higher-elevation trails may be closed to hikers.? But it’s also a good choice for visitors who have limited time to climb, even when the higher trails are open, because it is possible to experience these incredible scenes at the 1100 Meter Road area.Not only is this a beautiful area, these days the 1100 Meter Highland is part of the Jeju Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO and World Natural Heritage Site.A couple of points:? this attraction is actually located on Highway 1139, which will also take you past Eorimok, Yeongshil and Mysterious Road. You can drive or take an intercity-bus from either the Jeju City (north) or Jungman Resort area (south) side.? If you take a taxi, you should make a roundtrip reservation, allowing 1-2 hours there.? It’s a good idea to take at least a light jacket, even on a summer day, and for late fall to late spring, have a heavier coat, gloves and even a hat.? And don’t forget your shades and skin protection; even in winter, the sunlight can be strong on Hallasan.

Not your typical stroll on a beach. This is more to walking on stones by the cliff. Please do wear comfortable shoes for walking at this location; not easy to walk on the uneven stones. Wind will be a little strong too, prepare a light windbreaker will help. There's certain times that you can't enter this attraction due to high tide (you can walk along the cliff) or strong wind. Please do check the opening time before heading there. The journey took us around 1hr to complete the cliff tour. There's a trail leading to a temple, but we did not go for it. There will be fresh seafood sold long the cliff, it cost us around 20,000 won for a plate of it. My guide told us that the price still can be negotiated.

Not so much of a theme park, there isn't any rides apart from a train. But we had fun there, many gardens, landscapes and things to see. We walked the long Eco trail. The place is well maintained and clean. Wouldn't advise to go in winter tho, as many of the flowers won't be in bloom.

Not only was the view after climbing to the top of Trail no. 2 breathtaking, the track up the steps and steep trail will also leave most breathless! There are markers that state you are at 2-1, 2-2 etc., the 2 in front meaning trail no. 2, but none tells you how much higher you must climb! Incidentally the top is 2-5. Its quite a struggle to reach the top but if you take it easy and take regular breaks along the way to admire the fauna & flora, take some photos and generally get your breath back, you should reach the top in about half an hour. The journey down is much easier and faster. The view on top is magnificent and definitely worth the climb! The fresh cool mountain air was great too. Highly recommend you try. PS : There were two ladies in their seventies from San Francisco who completed the climb and decent at the same time as my group. Two thumbs up to them!!There is also a museum and sculptured garden at the base of the mountain where you can sit on park benches and enjoy the air and general view of the Hallasan mountain and its surroundings.

Not many things beat the sound of a waterfall, and this one is no exception. Situated right where the river meets the ocean, it is a beautiful sight to see.There is a parking area right by the entrance to the trail. The entrance fee is ??2000 per person, and you should be careful when walking along the rocks - they tend to get quite slippery.Note: definitely not wheelchair accessible!

My wife and I hiked the Seongpanak Trail up Hallasan in late May 2015. The trail starts relatively easy but gets more difficult after the first shelter. Make sure you have the rights shoes as the rocks can be pretty hard on your feet. This is a long climb, and for most of the trip you will be in a forest. Keep your eyes open and you may spot some of the elusive small native deer, we saw three on our trip. I am not in great shape, so it was a tough climb for me and took us 9 hrs. round trip. The rocks are really hard on your feet on the way down. Leave early since if you don't make it to the last shelter before 1 PM they will not allow you to ascend to the summit. The last shelter sells ramen and water and a few other items, but be aware you are expected to pack all of your own trash off of the mountain. There are some stores and shops in the parking lot at the entrance to the park, we bought some kimbop for lunch and packed it up with us. This is the tallest mountain in South Korea and the summit provides wonderful views at over 1900 meters high. Climbing Hallasan was a   bucket list   item for my wife, who was born in South Korea, and a memorable experience.

My wife and I hiked Hallasan last weekend, which was our first trip to Jeju Do. We've lived in Seoul for 5 years and finally made that trip south. We decided to take the Seongpanak Trail since it allows you to get to the top. Overall, the hike was great - beautiful scenery (although it was a hazy day for us so visibility was limited), challenging hike and it's something that will take up a whole day. We took a different trail down once we reached the top and the views were nicer on that one. I think there are only two trails that go all the way up. We're not hikers by any means so our legs were pretty tired on the way down the mountain. They estimate 8-9 hours total but we did it in 7! Be sure to pack some snacks and water as there's not much available on the hike. There's a small place at a checkpoint a couple hours into the Seongpanak trail where you can get some water, ramen and chocolate bars (along with some basic hiking gear) but don't expect much. We had only taken water with us (rookie mistake) and I was wishing for some extra snacks on the way down. There's also a store/small restaurant at the first entrance to the hike so you can stock up there. Overall, it's definitely worth doing as its one of the main attractions on Jeju.

My number one favourite place in Jeju. The views are amazing and it's free! As you walk along the trail, you can get different views and there is a pool right down there where one can go for a dip or a swim. Although I didn't go for a swim there, just watching others dive and swim there is already a joy

My husband and I consider ourselves pretty fit people, we regularly run and ski seasonally but we were impressed at the older Korean folks who visited the same track we did!We visited the Eorimok Trail which was advertised as a 3 hour walk one way. This time estimate is definitely accurate especially if it's consistent walking (which we did with very little breaks) if you take a 10 min breaks every so often, it would take you longer. Definitely allocate a full day for this walk and start early in winter as day time is shorter and sun sets early. We started around 10am and made it down by 4.30pm with about an 30-45 min break at the top of the trail. Remember to bring your rubbish down with you, there are no bins at the top!This trail is definitely not pram or wheelchair friendly. If you have had any leg or hip surgery recently I would also not recommend. Even though this is an 'easier' trail the walkway access is not well paved, there are large rocks and very uneven surfaces much of the way up the trail. Near the end of the day, my husband and I witnessed at least half a dozen people needing assistance down the mountain on their 'conveyor belt pulley' which was supposed to only be used for stock to be transported up and down the mountain, but in these cases of emergency some elderly and struggling walkers were transported two at a time, down the mountain. I also witnessed an old man cramping up on his way down, but lucky he was with a walking group, so they managed to organise for him to go down safely.Like many reviews say, there are consistent reminders around noon for walkers to start making their way down the mountain for your safety.This walk was beautiful and we definitely will be back to attempt another trail of this mountain! We were lucky with the weather and there was no cloud cover when we went up, but got really windy when we descended the mountain.If you are driving to Eorimok trail by rental car and are using their rental gps, the telephone number for Eorimok trail for input into the gps is: 7139950 or 7139953, definitely go early if you can, otherwise like us we arrived around 10am and had to park at the trail driveway entrance and hiked up to the full car park :)

My friends and I drove up to the visitor centre (attitude of 950 meters on the mountain) and started the hike at 5.30am on the Seongpanak Trail. It was really cold so early in the morning. The trail was clearly marked out and easy to follow. It got tiring and cold really easily so it is best if you travel as a group to motivate each other. The trail is made up of sections of large stones, forest ground and wooden blocks. Some parts are steep so hikers must practise caution especially during the descent.There are two toilet points along the trail but I heard from my friends that they were really gross. There is a checkpoint near the middle of the trail which hikers must pass by a certain time (was 1.30 pm for the month of May). At that checkpoint, there is a small shop selling essentials such as drinks and food.The ending part of the trail was the most scenic as there are few trees to block the views. However, it was very cold here and I was not dressed according. I am not sure if it was due to the season (end of spring) or the attitude.We reached the top of the mountain after hiking and resting for almost 6 hours. At the top (attitude of 1950 meters), many koreans had there mini picnics while I had to take a long break to recover from the monstrous hike. There is a crater lake at the top of the mountain but it seemed like it was drying up. Remember to take photos at the summit as it is really an achievement to complete the seemingly impossible hikers for urban dwellers like us.We took the same way down as we needed to get to the car. However, if you are not driving, you can try to take the Gwaneumsa Trail down as recommended by some people online. One must be careful on the way down, especially in sections which are steeper. Do not be shy to take breaks if you are really tired. We took nearly 4 hours to get down the mountain to the car from the top.

My family and I visited this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument cave on a late afternoon for 2 hours. There were not many visitors and we didn?t find any tour buses when we reached here.   Getting there & fees: Manjanggul Cave is located in the north western part of Jeju-do. To get (drive) to Manjanggul Cave, key in GPS coordinate 7834818. There is no parking fee at the huge car park. Entrance fee is 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.Manjanggul Cave Museum: Upon climbing up the stairs from the car park, you will reach the Museum and a cafeteria/restaurant on its right. You could go in and have a look at the interesting exhibits, including how the Manjanggul Cave was formed from the volcanic activities.Manjanggul Cave: To get to the underground Cave, we followed the sign-posts ? it?s within 5 minutes? walk from the Manjanggul Cave Museum. Trek the entire 1 km stretch that?s opened to public and you will end with a colourful lit lava column - created from the dripping of lava from a hole in the ceiling ? which at about 8 meters high, is the tallest lava column on Earth. Nevertheless, there are a few things you have to take note while you are in the Cave:(1) The entrance to the Manjanggul Cave is also the exit ? there?s no exit at the end of the 1 km trail, which means you are walking 2 km return (2) Make sure you bring and wear a jacket or sweater with you because it?s freezing cold and chilly inside the cave. (3) Wear a cap or the jacket or sweater can be waterproof because you get water ocassioanlly dripping from the cave top onto you (4) The surface (floor) of the Cave is full of solidified lava flow terrain (i.e. extremely uneven surface) and water puddles, so you have to wear a pair of good walking shoes and walk carefully. Hold on to the railings of the stairs.(5) You probably don?t need a torchlight because the Cave is illuminated just enough by ground lightings. Some parts of the cave even have colourful lights shining at the dome shaped ceiling (cupola) (6) If you would like to take photographs inside the cave, you would need a tripod and switch to manual mode for long exposure (I used 4 seconds to 10 seconds exposure on my digital SLR).   There are displays at certain parts of the cave in English explaining the geology of the cave and the formation of the interesting structures (e.g. stalactites). In particular, there?s one structure ? ?Stone Turtle? ? in which the shape looks like Jeju-do Island, and which you could reach in about 30 minutes of one-way walking as it?s about 400m from the entrance. Along the Manjanggul Cave wall, we saw varied patterns of lava flow lines, some are straight while some are wavy. Really interesting! I have been to over 10 limestone caves around the world, but this is my first visit in a lava tunnel cave or lava tube cave (and Asia?s longest lava tube cave for that matter). You have to experience being transported to another world in this ?out of this world? cave for yourself ? don?t miss it!

My family and I drove to this awesome natural attraction and walked along the layered rocks and cliffs produced as a result of a volcanic eruption on a beautiful non-windy and sunny morning. Safety concerns: Yeongmeori (Dragon's Head) Coast is opened from 8 am to 6:30 pm from May to September. It will be closed when the weather changes in a way that impacts people?s safety (e.g. high tidal waves, strong winds), so it is better to call to check before going. Also a rainy day means that the rocks and coast will become slippery and you may have problems taking photographs. in any case, you definitely need a good pair of walking shoes.2 walking trails: You have to take note that there are 2 trails and entrances to Yeongmeori Coast. Both trails meet each other but are not connected due to safety issue, which means you have to pay separate entrance fees. However, I saw a white bridge is presently being constructed that links the 2 trails, but it remains unclear as to when it will be opened. Between the 2 trails ? Trail 1 and Trail 2 (described below) ? I found Trail 2 to be  safer for walking and has more spectacular sandstone rock formations and cliffs, and because of that my family and I spent about 3 hours admiring the attraction and taking photographs.  Trail 1: This trail is where the tourists go, and starts after the Hamel Castaway Memorial and the Hamel vessel. You park your car (along with the tour coaches) at a car park that?s next to a mini theme park (with the Viking amongst others). You then walk along the seaside promenade next to sandstone layered rocks along the sea, which takes about 1.5 to 3 hours return after the ticket booth (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children). Since certain stretches of the promenade are narrow, you have to walk carefully so as not to fall into the sea and onto the rocks.Trail 2:  This is a shorter trail that in theory should only take about 30-60 minutes return after the ticket booth. You park your car just beneath the temple. Parking is free. Cross the road and look for 3 bronze circular structures with inscriptions of ?Jeju Island Geopark?, ?Global Geopark Networks? and ?New 7 Wonders of Nature? and a green signage ?Yongmeori Coast Entrance -> 300m? From there, you just walk down the steps and follow the path which will take you past several shops. After about 10 minutes? walk, you will reach a ticket booth. After buying the tickets (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children), turn left and you would come to the top of a narrow and steep passageway to the coast. Take your time to carefully choose the big rocks as your steps for your descent (and then I realised what the term ?stepping stone? means). There are no handrails. Once you reached the bottom after about 6 minutes (longer when there are many people), turn around and look up at the challenging and difficult passageway and appreciate your achievement! Looking across the sea, we saw Mount Hallasan. Instead of going left, I recommend you go to the right and once through a archway or hole in a rock wall, and you will soon encounter the spectacular irregular layered and wavy sandstone cliffs that often contain ?pot-holes?. The rock formation at certain places was carved out by  a blade that cut itself into the layered rocks, creating v-shaped clefts. And when the waves crashed into the rocks, it sounds like roaring thunder ? awesome!  There?s a short cement bridge where standing on it allows you to take a superb photograph of the rock formation and the narrow stretch of turquoise-coloured sea. It is also around this same spot that you can take another superb photograph of the cliffs with Mount Sanbangsan in the background. There were 2 ladies (I didn?t think they were the famed ?Haenyeo? sea-divers) at the shoreline with 3 basins of sea animals - sea snail (sora), sea squirt (myeonggye) and sea cucumber (haesam) ? who would be happy to enable you  to experience Korean culture of eating raw seafood by the shoreline. I didn?t like to eat raw seafood so I didn?t try.Overall, my family and I think that Yeongmeori Coast is one attraction in Jeju that ranks it as among the top 3 attractions in Jeju. Don?t miss it! It will blow your mind away!

Mt Halla is known as Korea's jewel. It is its highest peak. And well worth the trip to Jeju. We left Seagwipo very early (around 7 am) and took bus 182 (181 also goes there) to Seongpanak because we wanted to climb up to the peak. We got to the mountain around 7:45 and started the hike. The weather was super nice when we left, and we planned it that way, because we wanted to at least get some nice views of the city, and while at the summit. This is a long day of hiking, so be prepared. Bring snacks (and a trash bag, because you have to carry everything back down), and water. There are 2 checkpoints along the way that have bathrooms. The last checkpoint sells ramen for about 1500w with hot water. This is the checkpoint you have to get to before 12:30. We made it there around 11, and up to the summit before noon On the Seongpanak trail, there is also a lake with an observatory that's worth the detour.The last part of the hike up to the summit is pretty steep and rocky, so watch your footing, especially because you might be tired from walking up. Wear adequate footwear, make sure they are sturdy and comfy!Unfortunately, we didn't get that lucky with the weather as it because overcast as we were getting up there. I guess it really depends on your luck (the next day, it was super clear! Damn you Mt Halla!!) hahaha.We took the same trail down (from the summit, there is another trail, but no buses stop there. And this is where your comfy shoes are a must. The hike up was not bad, but the hike down, was torture! Our feet kept hitting the front of our hiking shoes, so we were bruised and hurt by the time the hike was done. We were also sore for the next 2 days (and we're pretty sporty, but we rarely walk for 8 hours) Overall, it's a great hike. The trail up is covered by trees, so it is cooler than it seems, but there are still some great views, especially with the fall foliage. We'd be surprised at the range of people walking the trail, old and young love to hike up this trail, and we understand why!

Like other hikes in Korea there are a lot of stairs. But that also means that there are plenty of places to rest which is great when you're hiking with small children. My 8 year old and 4 year old made it up and back without difficulty. They were hot but we were lucky to have had a breeze the entire time. The views were great from the top and along the way. There are two covered rest areas on the way up and plenty of benches if you get tired. The cost is the same as many other nature sites on Jeju, ??2000 per adult and ??1000 per child. There are horse rides for ??5000 at the trailhead. There is an adjacent beach and divers show but we decided not to go to and opted for food instead. Just outside the entrance there are a number of shops for ice cream, food, and fresh squeezed mandarin juice. The hike took about 60 minutes total going at a slow pace. Without kids one could do it quite a bit faster. Overall it was a great way to spend about half a day.

Just did the hike on 30 March.Trail: seongpanak up and gwaneumsa down. Goes to summit. (highly recommend to do this trail Cos going up by gweumusa is really steep though the view is nicer for gweumusa) Time taken: 4.5hrs up and 4hrs down (please go early and check the time that you need the reach the shelter and summit by.  Think should be by 1230 reach shelter and by 2 to leave summit) Weather: good.  Cold in the morning but as you hike,  you will perspire and definitely need minimum sweaters. I was only wearing teeshirt and windbreaker. In the end only tee-shirt cos it's getting warmer and you climb and when the sun is out. Need crampons?  Yes!!! It helped alot especially at the icy areas both going up and down. Not too sure where you can buy it but I managed to rent it from my hostel. Though I did see people without it,  and they did just fine.  I was wearing track shoes kind. So crampons helped alot!  How to get there: I went there from Jeju city and took bus 281 from bus terminal to seongpanak bus stop. Coming back from gwaneumsa trail: took bus 475 back to jeju  national university and change bus 360 to Jeju city.  Please check with bus driver or use kakao map/bus to help as Google Map doesn't seem to help much with he routes. Bus 475 have some timings going back. You can always find out from the visitors center at the gweumusa base. It is situated at the left side as you make your way down passing through the car park.  Shelters and food: not sure if I did miss it..  But I didn't see any food vendors, drinks stall as I hiked up and down. So I was really thirsty as the end of the trail. There's a small restaurant and a convenience store at gwaneumsa trail end. So please bring ALOT of water like at least 1.5L. Bring along food to eat up there and also plastic bag to put your trash and there are no rubbish bins around.

Just an ordinary road but countless of tourist buses and vans parked along it. Explore the mystery personally to appreciate the magical side of it. We'd done all tricks - stopped the car engine and let it roll uphill, poured water on road and see the trail running upward, closed our eyes and walked both ways where we found the gravity is totally against us !! Great fun ~!

Jeju Olle Trail is completely round the island broken up into 21 different routes.In total we walked about 13km, about 3.5 to 4 hours time taken. Photography time included.We started our walk from Hyatt Jeju along the Jungmun Beach (we did Route 8 going eastwards) heading towards the Daepo Pego (port) and ended our walk at the Yakcheon Temple.Ensure that you look out for arrows (blue&orange) along the ground and olle trail ribbons (blue & orange as well) tying on trees along the way. Terrain is very varied, from easy tarmac lanes to quite difficult lava rocks along the bays. Suggest you wear proper walking shoes. Bring along your own water & snacks. There are a few restrooms along the way. If you are staying around Jungmun resort area (many hotels there), take airport bus limousine no 600 to go back to your hotel. Its about 1000 Korean Won per person.Overall is an interesting walk because you will see village, seaside, port & temple along the way. This is one of the very popular walk in Jeju, so its like a   must walk   walk.. We just did a short segment of the Olle Trail & apparently other segments are even more interesting.. Check out some photos for illustration.

Jeju Island is indeed a unique island with so many gorgeous scenery, i had a great time travelling there in Winter, a low season with lesser tourist gives a different experience from visiting it in busy Summer. I have seen pictures about Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff (?ъ＜ⓒ\由) and was amazed by the neat shapes of hexagon stone pillars formed by volcanic lava, i totally recommend tourist to spend time walking around the nicely design olle trail in the beautiful, as well as to visit Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff during your trip in Seogwipo or Chungmun area. you don't have to plan for a long stay, a good two hours should be more than enough, as it was just a viewing spot rather than you can actually walk-in and visit. Don't worry about the transport, bus services are available (in fact it is very convenient to reach most of the travel spot around Jeju island), just drop by Jeju International Convention Center (ICC) and walk about 15 minutes to the park entrance, bus drivers in Jeju are very friendly and can basic communication woudn't be a concern. there is a entrance fees of 2000won in the park.there are steps to walk down to have a clearer view, description board with picture will explain how the hexagons shapes are formed, you can take amazing pictures and enjoy the sea view too.speaking of the weather, i have quite an experience, it was sunshine at first while i was taking the bus, and soon it become heavy downpour and even snow flakes begin to attack me during my walking! i think an umbrella or raincoat is necessary for either bright sunshine or unexpected rain. i gotta say, Jeju Island's weather is unpredictable! although this is not a spot to actually feel and touch the pillars, it can be quite boring to certain people who expected more attraction, but seeing the amazing cliff, the neat pillars, it was totally worth it to witness it by your own eyes, even the finest artist surrender to this piece of art, isn't it?

Jeju Island features a trail system that circumnavigates the island allowing the most highly motivated to hike the island, on foot.  If you want to see some great coast line and get the most out of a modest walk, look for trail #7.  It takes you along some great coastline with fantastic views of the cliffs, rocks and water.  In several areas, there are steps that take you from up high down to the surf.  If you stick to the trail, the elevation changes are modest and should be doable for anyone of moderate fitness.

I've climbed Hallasan twice now, once in December and once in early March, and both times I took this route. This route is slightly longer than Gwaneumsa, but it's also a gradual incline with several easy portions. I took this route primarily because there is not a lot of public transportation available to/from the Gwaneumsa trail, plus I'm not sure I can do a steep incline the entire way up to the summit. For Seongpanak, you have about 5 km that are easy, 2.5 km that get harder, and then a pretty brutal last 2 km. Regardless, know that there are other hiking trails around the island and even around the volcano, but only the two mentioned above will lead you all the way up to the summit.Given some of the reviews I saw that are either inaccurate or not very helpful, I hope to compile a quick list to help you decide if this is something you want to do and if so, what you will need:1) It's definitely going to be an all-day kind of thing. You will be tired afterward, so you likely won't want to schedule too many other activities for the evening. Also, it's likely that you will be sore and tired the next day or two. 2) You need to start climbing no later than 8:30 AM. As several people have mentioned, you will not be allowed to access the last chunk of the way if you're not at the second shelter by 12:30 PM (this is winter time, so the schedule varies slightly from season to season... always check the Korean tourism sites).3) Even if it's sunny, there's a chance you might need crampons. In the winter months you will need them for sure, but even last weekend people were sliding down and falling repeatedly without them. I hear that it's even worse on the Gwaneumsa trail since it's a lot more shielded from the sunshine. 4) Bring food and water! The only place you can buy something is at the very beginning of the trail, and even then the options aren't fantastic. A little protein or fruit will go a long way whenever you're starting to feel tired, and it'll help you push through. Please make sure you do not leave any of your trash along the way; there are zero trashcans, so if you carry something particularly messy, you might want to pack a bag for the waste.5) Do not use the toilet in the first shelter! It's the worst smelling bathroom ever, which is rare for Korea since things are usually so clean... I suppose it's the septic system. I suggest using the toilets at the parking lot and at the last shelter (there are two). The first one is seriously a nightmare. 6) It's not an easy hike, but it's doable even for people who don't exercise strenuously. I've seen people carrying babies all the way to the top, and I've seen small children and old people make it, too. Definitely wear the right clothing, though, and especially the right shoes. If you're hiking at a time without snow, you will spend hours circumventing rocks of all sizes and ankle support will be extremely helpful for this. Anyway, thanks for reading, I hope you have a fantastic hike!

Its very important to choose the suitable route, as there are different route to go to the top.  I didn't notice and chose a long route, and so not enough time to pass the check point at designated time and not allowed to go to the top.  Better get there earlier.  The trail is easy to walk.  Better bring suitable gear such as stick to prevent slippery ice surface  on top of the mountain.

its my first mountain hike, its a straightforward trail but tricky with rocky stone paths at some incline parts. not recommend for those with weak knees and ankles or just go slow n wear ur ankle guards. go up seongpanak (easier as more gradual)and down gwaneumsa (alot of steps, steeper) but gwaneumsa has valley view, creek view and there?s a tiny cave opening near the base with blast out icy wind even in summer.. pretty cool. there?s a bus to and from seongpanak and take taxi from gwaneunsa or prearranged pickup as there?s hardly a bus there.its a total of 9 hrs including rest stops though i rested longer at the peak and pressed on at rest stops. do pace yourself.. calves been killing me midway down the descent. needless to say its a painful walk for the next couple of days.. i slathered all the muscle aches cream..

It's a very long beach with very gentle slope; you can walk pretty far towards the sea. The water is clear and has very beautiful blue color. The nearby hill offers a (short) trail and a fantastic view, both towards the sea and Mt. Halla.
It's a long trail... the track is quite easy at the beginning but become more challenging to the top. But the view its worth it... But if you can, avoid go on the weekend. Too many people on weekend.

It was my first hiking trip and I decided to take the Seongpanak trail (9.6km one way) so that I can reach the summit. The hike is long and steep at certain stages. Very rocky road and proper hiking shoe is strongly recommended. The hike starts from visitor center is at 750m. At 1500m, there's a Jindalrae shelter where you can take a break for hot instant noodle and refill your drinks. The hike is tough for me (someone who jog/cycle once or twice a week). Walking stick is my best friend to support me all the way. Reaching the submit at 1950m is breathtaking. You will see the beautiful Baengnokdam lake. On the way down, at 1324m we hike to see Saraoreum Lake too. The whole trail with break took me almost 10 hrs (9.15am till 7pm). It's seems to be an easy hike for the Koreans, including the elderly but to me is a lot of determination and perseverance. Will definately hike at the other trails if I have the chance to go back to Jeju. ** I saw deer **

It is an archetypal tuff cone formed by hydrovolcanic eruptions upon a shallow seabed about five thousand years ago.  Situated on the eastern seaboard of Jeju Island and resembles a gigantic ancient castle, this tuff cone is 182 meters high, has a preserved bowl-like crater. There are two hiking trails to reach the peak , take the white path uphill and the orange path downhill. You just follow the crowd and the signages along the trail. During May and the coming summer, you do not need a jacket or pullover as it will be  hot and you will sweat a lot on the climb up. Wear covered sports shoes and  a cap / hat. The first part of the hike is the easiest and the least steep.  The rest of the path comprises steps of varying steepness. The final stretch gets very steep. Along the hiking trail, there are benches and pavilions to rest. Take a sip of water, rest your aching legs before proceeding . Toilets are available along the way. From the peak, you can see beautiful landscapes of Jeju island and do take a photo with the signage saying you are at Sunrise Peak. It took us 30 minutes to reach the top. The downhill walk was much easier, just follow the wooden stairs meandering its way down.  At the bottom, you can go for drinks at the cafetarias.

It has always been something i try to do everytime i go for a holiday, is to go trekking in the mountains or forest. I went in late December and took a cab up to the start of yeongsil trail, and went down Eorimok trail. It was near a six hours journey, with a 20 mins lunch break. As i went during late december, the drive up the mountain area was really foggy and the visibility is only like 5 metres in front of us which is kinda scary because there were many windy roads. but as soon as we are nearing the trail, the fog seems to have been lifted due to the heights. Good info to know: Yeongsil trail have many flights of steps. Depending on what you prefer, manmade steps means relatively safe walkway but it is up most of the time.Eorimok trail has more stones steps and is more natural. But it could mean that it is more tedious, really depends on your preference.Lunch is ramen noodle at the shelter, they sell small snacks and drinks too. PS: As i went during the winter, the timing to enter certain trail is really strict because the sun sets really early like 5ish in the afternoon. So it is definitely a thing to take note of especially if you are not fast paced. Also during winter, along the trail, there will be snow left from the night before, and it IS really Slippery!! I nearly slipped many times because i was wearing a normal sneaker and not trekking shoe. And a really helpful thing to have is a walking stick! Other than that, enjoy your time with nature there!

Is a relatively user-friendly trail from Seongpanak trail head, with plenty of well-laid staircase.  In areas with no staircase, the path is pretty rocky.   Is just a very long trail, about 10km each way and you need to adhere to the cut off time.

interesting shapes of rocks and lovely blue water.not too difficult, short walk along the trail. there are 2 different trails starting from different car park. both trails are not connected at the moment due to safety issue so make sure you visit the right one.by the look of it no.2 may not available or can be very wet @ low tide.i like the both but personally like no.1 trail little more.

If you want to see some nature trails but can?t do long distances over natural rocky ground, then this will suit. The train ride to each destination makes it easy to travel. The walks are well groomed. Plentiful toilets. There are some theme park like features, such as boats & a pirate ship, to keep the young ones entertained along the way (at extra cost for some).

If you visit Jeju, this volcanic mountain should be on your shortlist! It has excellent hiking trails which are well maintained. Trails are all well documented and give explanation about the distance, altitude and rest areas along the trail. At the top you have an amazing 360 degrees panorama view on the complete island. Plan your hike carefully. Check the weather before you leave. Bring along some warm clothing and rain protective clothing. Climbing 100 meters means a temperature drop of 1 degrees Celsius. It can get cold and humid up there!

If you like trails and hikes, this is it. Do it korean style and eat ramen at the top and even cucumber (take them along with you and even other snacks cause you'll get hungry). Plus, go in the morning, I want at 12:00 and thank goodness made friends in the way to get me back to my hostel. Around 17:00 there are no more buses and I would have been stuck there if it weren't for my new friends!

If you enjoy nature, hiking one of the olle trails is a must-do while you're in jeju. It will not be an easy hike and not all parts of the trail are scenic but there are sufficient sights to blow you away and be left in awe of nature. This is also the best way to experience jeju's natural beauty (after all this is what its most famous for and not for teddy bears). It is also arguably the least touristy thing to do during your trip here. You can do as long or as short of the trails as you like; there are trails passing through hot tourist destinations where you'll see many tourist buses, local villages, rice fields, even resorts. You'll walk on sand, on rocks by the ocean, and if you time it correctly you'll be able to catch a gorgeous sunset along jeju's coastline. Be sure not to get stuck in a remote area after sunset as it can be difficult to get out. If you're doing a multi-day hike, there are many pensions located along the olle routes and you can just pop in for a night.Suggest to go with at least one other person in case you get lost (there are some places where the markings are not so visible/well maintained). If you rented a car, dont drive. Wear comfortable shoes and bring lots of water and snacks!

If doing Hallasan is not in your plans, then go take some nice walks on Jeju's Olle Trail Routes. They are shorter mostly and they appear all over the place in Jeju. Sometimes just 20 minutes walks and some much longer. We were impressed with the conservancy of nature and the trails on Jeju.

I visited Hallasan in early March, some parts of the trail were still covered in snow. At the lower area I had some difficulties because of the melting snow. It's doable without crampons or walking sticks, but be careful. Past Witseoreum shelter, it's recommended to have walking gear. I have an average condition and I did the Yeongsil trail up in 2h15 and the Eorimok trail down in less then 2h. I think it's better to do the opposite. Yes, Yeongsil trail is longer, but easier. The Eorimok trail is covered with rocks, and if you don't watch out, it is easy to twist your ankle when coming down.

I took the eorimok trail which took about 2.5 hours to get to the top with the rest rooms, the first part of the trek is hard work and quite strenuous. After reaching the top I took the yeongsil trail back down which had some of the most stunning views along the way. As I came by bus the walk down from the yeongsil trail to the yeongsil ticket office where the bus stop is located takes another 40minuts or so depending on the pace. I Would highly recommend visiting this area and trying the trails.

I took Gwanuemsa trail up and down with Seongpanak. I find that there is nothing much to see from this trail as most of the pathways are rocky pathways with trees all around. There are 2 stations which provide toilet facilities, and one at the higher level sells called jindaraebal shelter also sells food and crampon. If you are coming in winter, do check the weather. If the pathways are filled with snow, it is better to bring along the crampon as the path will be really slippery.

I started from Eorimok Trail and came down by Yeongsil Trail. Eorimok trail starts off with steps then followed by wooden walk way before you reach Witseoreum Shelter. Shelter is a basic one with just toilets and resting rooms. We took around 2hrs to reach the shelter. Yeongsil trails starts off (from shelter) with wooden walk way then followed by countless stairs. You are like literally hiking on the edge of the mountain up/down. We took 1.5hrs to descend.Definitely recommend going down by Yeongsil trail rather than heading up due to the countless number of stairs. Both trails offer truly beautiful scenery and great for photos. I cant forget the view which the horizon mixed with the sea level that you can differentiate. Stunning!Advice:Bring food like energy bar, fruits etcBring water enough to reach water points. There are a couple of water points for you to refill along Eorimok trail. Else 1.5 litres for 2 pax is enough.Bring jacket and wear hiking shoes. Sports shoe is possible like what most korean did but be v careful as you will be walking on uneven rocks at times. Probably suggest ankle guard to go with sports shoe.For those who want to scale the mountain but doesn't wish to try the 9-10hrs climb to summit, i would really recommend this 2 trails.

I made the climb on 22.11.2013 but few days before my climb, I have been keeping my eye on the weather on the mountain. The first snowstorm hit the mountain top a few days earlier and I know that my hike will be much difficult with the snow along the path to the top of the mountain. I chose to ascend from Gwanuemsa trail and descend from Seogpanak trail and I know that I have made the right choice. Starting from Gwanuemsa trail was much tougher, with the rocky pathways in the beginning to the steep climb in the middle of the trail and snowy trail all the way up to the mountain top. Along the way, there is no food on sale but there is a shelter for people to fill up their water, at the Samgakbong Shelter. The total length of Gwanuemsa Trail is about 8.7km and Samgakbong shelter is about 6km from the starting point. To make it here will take about 2 hrs of normal walk. There is also a toilet available here but the you wouldn't want to spend more time at this toilet. The trail after Samgaokbong SHetlter has obviously been much tougher, with a lot of steep steps, or even no steps at all (all covered by thick snow) and at some point, the is a need to pull the rope along the trail to move upwards. The efforts are all worthwhile upon reaching the top of the mountain. It is good to come on a clear day because the view along Gwanuemsa trail especially upon approcahing the mountain top is spectacular.At the top of the mountain, the wind can be really strong. Be prepared with the chill and wear enough layer to prevent from getting cold. As mentioned, I descend from Seogpanak trail and this is somehow a boring trail. The total length is about 9.5km but all I can see is trees along the way. There is nothing much to see but it was quite a flat trail that make it the choice among many hikers. There are food on sale at the Samgakbong Shelter, and also a big toilet there. A good stop for hikers to build up their energy before continuing their hike. Crampon also on sale for 5000 won. Overall, it was a fresh and good place for first time traveller. If there is a chance to come back to Hallasan, I will sure try the other 2 trails on the western side of the mountain.

I like that you can kind of 'customize' a trail to suit your time, difficulty and type of view you want. Views of the peak are spectacular with it's craggy face and the raised wooden trails make walking a breeze. There are fresh natural-water springs along the way, so drinking water is in good supply.

I hiked up Hallasan via Seongpanak trail and went down the Gwaneumsa trail. The hiking was almost torturous, for a person who does only some jogging as preparation to hike Halla, but it indeed worth every step towards the peak because of the heavenly view of Jeju from there. Expect rocky trails, crazy steep staircases and trails. Bring at least 2 litres of water (you can refill your bottles at fresh water springs along Seongpanak and after the bridge in Gwaneumsa trail). There's a small shop selling hot noodles, drinking water and hot coffee at Jindallae Bat shelter. Toilets are available at Sokbat and Jindallabaet and a few more somewhere along Gwaneumsa. Start early to complete the hike early. Be sure to bring your camera. Get walking sticks too if you can, I didn't but I could still do the hike :D I went to Jeju on a solo trip and did the hike alone, but a lot of other hikers were very kind giving me words of encouragement and even waited for me along Gwaneumsa trail. A must do if you get to Jeju! No entrance fee! :D

I hiked to the top today.  I had decided not to do this but at breakfast this morning a gal from Korea highly suggested I go, so I did. I took the Seongpanak trail up and back. I got there a little after 10 and was told that it was a bit late to make it to the top so I went out very quickly so I would make it to the Check station by 1 PM. If you get there after that time they won?t let you up to the top. I made it and got to the top. At 2:30 they make everyone come down. I came down slowly and at the end I was all by myself walking those trails as it got darker. I didn?t get down until about 7 PM. Because I was in such a hurry to get up it took me much more time to come down than it did to go up. As I was walking down a deer jumped right in front of me And then jumped away. I brought two bottles of water and lunch. That was perfect for me. There are restrooms on the way up but not at the top. They are outhouses. I do not have hiking shoes with me, just my slip on sketchers, so my feet are still sore from walking on those lava rocks with these shoes. This is also the reason it took me so long to get down, my feet were really sore At that point and I had to rest them during the descent. There is a Monorail track next to the trail. Today I saw them taking down some people who couldn?t make it down on that.

I hiked the Seongpanak Trail which goes all the way to the top of Halla Mountain. In order to reach the top though, you must get to the last shelter before 12:30pm. The path is covered with uneven rocks and stairs so wear good shoes. I really enjoyed the hike but was underwhelmed by the view. Most of the path is shaded and when you do finally clear the trees it was cloudy and grey. The crater lake looked more like a big puddle of mud.If you like long, challenging hikes then the Seongpanak Trail is for you. If you're only in it for the view, perhaps try going in the early spring.

I found much of Jeju island to be very commercialized and crowded with loud tour groups. This is a great place to enjoy the natural beaty of Jeju with smaller groups of people. There is a small entrance fee.  The first half mile is along a wide crushed rock road. It is lined with young   nutmeg   trees. The trees are in the yew family. They are Torreya nucifera and are native to Japan. I  visited in October when the small edible nuts ripen. The nuts are encased in a thin husk that has a wonderful aroma. You will see people collecting them under the large trees.  Eventually the road ends and then you follow a loop trail that is about 2 feet wide it is covered with a hemp rope mat that felt lovely to walk on with bare feet.  The crowds end at the beginning of the narrow trail so you can walk through this section in peace and really marvel at the enchanting colors and smells of the forest and hear the songs of the many birds.  There were signs to watch for snakes but I saw none. The yews are huge.  Make sure to investigate the tree bark it is fabric like and soft. Also many of the other plants have English name labels which is nice. The trail is flat and should take a leisurely couple of hours or less if you rush.  I noticed a lot of people sitting on benches in the first section enjoying picnic lunches.

I do a fair amount of hiking in the Green Mountains of Vermont, and I found Seongpanak trail to the summit of Mount Hallasan to be enchanting and beautiful! Though the hike may be challenging for folks with knee problems, it is a very well maintained trail (though long) that is worth the effort.Start your day out early and bring plenty of water!

I decided to go with Seongnapak trail, and was planning to go up to the summit!Rocky and stony path made me really exhausted, I managed my breath okay and left the last 1.5km as my keens!You will be accompanied by many people along the trail! It?s highly recommended to start early, I arrived by 8am, reached the shelter around 11:00am!Weather was mild as you?ll be covered by trees most of the time!

I completed every single course over a period of a year so the following comments are just my opinions. If you are staying for a short period of time in Jeju courses 6 and 7 are the most popular and will probably get the most from. Both are very scenic and you will get to see some of the major sights. If you start at one of the information sites, you can pick up a Jeju Olle guide which has maps and information of the trails, guides for the Buses, to get to and from the starting points. Also I'd recommend downloading Kakao Maps app on your phone and you can zoom in and see the actual trail that you are following when you are on it. It comes in handy especially for me when I made a wrong turn on my trips. If your doing the entire course I'd recommend buying a jeju Olle Passport. Carry it with you and get it stamped at the starting points and halfway way points of the trails. I was living near jeju city and caught most of Buses from the Jeju inter city bus centre. The 101/201 express buses will take you to/ or near a lot of the starting points but I'd recommend picking up the Olle Guide first and the info in that is invaluable.Most of the Starting points are close to the roads unless you are going to one of the 3 islands. I used booking.com most of the time to book places to stay overnight as I don't speak Korean. Jeju has a lot of places to stay and there would be abundant places to stay except for maybe a couple of the more remote locations on the trail. There are offical Olle trail Hostels throughout the trails to which are very nice. If planning for no Korean speakers just check before hand that you are not traveling on a Jeju holiday as a lot of paces close down and might be harder to find a place to stay. Of course take plenty of water and there's usually 7/11 of CV's around the place where you can get snacks to eat.The trails themselves are very beautiful , Different scenes ranging from Black volcanic rock on the coastlines, Forest trails, Beautiful beaches, Hill sides, a lot of Oreums (Jeju extinct volcanoes) small towns with a chance to see wildlife and a lot of friendly people. For myself my favourite trails were routes 11, 18-1 Chuja-Do island), 1-1 (Udo island), 7. For me the stronger trails were on the southern eastern point of the island starting from route 6 through to 15.Getting to the supporting islands it you might take note you will need your Passport to catch the ferry to Udo. You must show it when buying a ticket. There are a lot of ferries going most of the day to Udo. They have a very nice Peanut ice cream there. The smaller island Gapado at the time I went there were only 2 ferries in the day and its not the most reliable service and the ferries can be cancelled due to bad weather can be cancelled due to bad weather so check beforehand if you can. Chuja-Do island was one of my favourites. When I done it they had 2 ferries a day and you can not do the whole trail in time to catch the next ferry back so be prepared to stay over night. I have heard of instances when the weather turned bad and people had to stay a couple of nights on the island because the ferries were cancelled so just plan for that just in case. it is a beautiful Island though and one of my favourites.I would also recommend going and joining the Olle Walkers Facebook group. They take guided walks along certain courses and have great information about weather and so forth. all you need to do is contribute to the group from time to time.

I choose the most difficult route (Gwaneumsa Trail) as the website said it offers the best view of the mountain and I stupidly assumed their difficult is not too difficult if compared to Malaysia's route (because Malaysia's one is not a proper/well maintain path).And so I was wrong :p It is all the way up up up and up, stone path (which I hate most) and wooden staircase (so descending is definitely more blessing but very challenging to your knee). I hike @ 26 April, didn't get to see much fantastic scenery as I guess I'm not at the right season as I saw some other people's review they saw great scenery. So this was more like a physical training to myself. To train the mind especially. But, the sound of the wind is like ocean waves, this was indeed very beautiful, I even record it down during descending. It took me 4hrs 10mins to reach the top, in between there are... 2 toilets I think, and if you manage to reach samgakbong shelter (1500m) not later than 12.30pm (spring/fall) you are allow to continue to hike to the top, else you'll need to return. Cross this check point there is a spring water ahead before the bridge for you to refill your water! Then what's lying ahead is the super strong wind and the sturdy steep stone/wooden staircase path ==|Long story short:1) Hike at the right season I'm sure you can see more than what I see2) choose the trail wisely. I would say as long as you have a strong will, even you are not very fit also you can do this trail, just start little bit earlier than others to give yourself more time (say 5hrs to the top). 3) Make sure you are well equip to keep yourself warm. Windbreaker and glove is a must. I had 4 layers (t shirt, thermal, windbreaker & sweater & I was still shivering at top, the wind is just too strong that we couldn't even stand still) 4) Bring water, food, chocolate and candies! 5) Good shoes is a must for less struggling during descending & less stress to your knee. Personally I don't use hiking stick so suit yourself for this. 6) count the time and familiar with your own pace if you want to reach the top. Just make sure you reach the check point then you can take your own sweet time to get to the top.Last but not least, just don't under estimate this well develop stone & wooden staircase path. Although it's only 8.7km, 1950m height, it took me 4hrs plus up and 3hrs 15mins down (with very little time rest at top coz its just too cold!)Good luck!

I absolutely recommend you to take a day trip and hike up Hallasan if you are in Jeju. Even though if it takes the whole day, since it is about 20km walking, it is worth it. If you are in okay shape I'd recommend you to go up on the Seongpanak trail. It is longer but easier than Gwaneumsa trail. The hike has a lot of stairs, so don't expect climbing. Once getting up, the most thing that shocked us what the loads and loads of bugs, since we never heard about that. They don't bite but they do get on you which is annoying. That said, the view is beautiful, to the island but also to the crater. Going down I'd recommend Gwaneumsa trail since it is a lot more beautiful and more to see. It is only the first third part that is the hardest, after that it gets okay. Remember to start climbing early since you have to reach the checkpoint before a certain time depending on the year. It takes about 3 hours to get to the checkpoint so try to check what time you have to be there before. The time is there because it takes a longer time to get down than you expect. Also bring water with you. There is only one point where you can buy going up, and only one point where you can fill your water bottle on both trails!

Hyeopjae is a beautiful beach with everything you would want in a beach it's very long with thick soft sand. But, the best thing about Hyeopjae beach is the Ollhe trail that starts at the Northeast end of the beach and goes for ever. The trail runs along the shore so close to the sea that at high tide on a windy day it becomes inpassable because of the waves submerging the trail in some places. The volcanic rock along the trail forms different things. If you look at the rock closely you might see a dragon or a horse or maybe a bird. If you stay on the trail long enough you walk by G-Dragon's cafe. If you go even further you will come across a Smoke Tower that is hundreds of years old used to send a signal of a enemies ship approaching.So, while Hyeopjae Beach is 1st rate when you are done swimming take a walk through history down the Olleh trail.I'm an American that has been living in Jeju for the last 12 years and I walk this trail 3 to 4 times a week and it never gets old.

Hiking up Mt Hallasan was such an incredible adventure - you really can't experience the island for what it is without giving it a go. The vegetation on the volcano changes as you get higher, ranging from lush dark-green forests and pines, to beautifully unusual flowers and scrub as you get closer to the summit. There are several trails up the mountain, but only two reach the summit - Seongpanak and Gwaneumsa. Seongpanak is the easiest, but is a long trail (19.2km return), whereas Gwaneumsa is one of the most scenic. The views from the summit really are breathtaking, and quite unusual if you have never hiked up a volcano before. Hiking up Hallasan was a great way to experience South Korea's natural beauty.

Hiked from the Yeongsil Hiking Trail Entrance (1280m) to Witseoreum Shelter (1700m). It was a total of 3.7km (one way) hike and took me 3.5 hours up.  Note that I do not exercise regularly and this was my first hiking experience.  I guess it is manageable for anyone as long you are determined to hike up regardless of your physical condition.  The trail was tricky involving a variety of tall rocks, wooden steps, pebbles and wooden planks, a tad steep at times.  My DSLR became cumbersome by midpoint that I've decided to use it at specific points for me to better soak in the sights and watch my steps at the same time.  The sights at various points are nothing but rewarding.A hiking stick and a good pair of shoes are definitely helpful.  Note that you have to bring your trash down after your hike!Bring more water and join the locals at various rest points with some snacks (eat what the Koreans do! Gimbap / tangerines / hard boiled eggs) and just immerse yourself in listening to their chatters while looking out far at the horizon!I would love to hike on the other trails of Hallasan again.

Highly recommend everyone to do at least one of the Jeju Olle trail routes. We chose route 6 as it?s being classified as the easiest route. The route is filled with beautiful sceneries. Some part of the route takes you onto the roads, into the bush, along the coastal and up some hilly roads. We meet a lot of locals along all way and they are helpful & friendly. Lot of cafes for one to take a rest too.

Hallasan was a good challenging climb, with the hike splits into 3 parts. The first 2 hour or so, we were hiking through mostly level ground, some rocks and little steps. As we reach the middle ground, the trail gets steeper, more rocky and almost half are made up of steps, mostly made of rocks. Using a hiking stick at this time really helps in making the climb easier. When it rains, which happened the entire day when we went, the ground gets covered with puddles and pools of water, so it was extra effort trying to choose the rocks to step on to avoid getting our feet wet. Towards the top, there are flights and flights of steps, followed by a trail made of rocks where u have to use a rope to climb up the steep rocky surface. It was challenging but overall, felt good.As it was raining, we didn't manage to get any view of the crater or lake at the summit. But the sense of accomplishment making it up was great!The way down was more challenging as after a day of rain, the trail became wetter and what used to be steps, some were submerged in water. Hence, even with a good waterproof shoes, ur feet could still get wet. Also, note that the sky turns dark at around 5pm in winter and there's no lighting in the reserve. Hence, make sure u buffer enough time to reach the foot of the mountain before that time. Otherwise, u would be hiking in the dark. Nevertheless, there would be a ranger moving down the rail lines in a cabin moving on a rail line, looking for stranded hikers. So no need to panic. However, I would still recommend planning well, checking the weather and choosing a clear day to climb. Start early so as to buffer enough time to reach the 3rd rest station by 12pm, as anytime after that, they do not allow hikers to go up to the top. Think it is for safety reason to buffer enough time for the ascend and descend. Also, to wear waterproof shoes and if available, bring a hiking stick along. Do standby a raincoat in case of light drizzle. Also bring some food along. Though they sell instant ramen and some bento at the resting stations, it closes by 2pm or so and you don't want to end up hungry.  Lastly, enjoy the climb!

Great walking trail with beautiful view of the sea and cliffs. There are plenty of places for nice photo spots and the cafes hidden here and there are added bonus. If you enjoy good long walks with nice ocean breeze, this is a must for you.

Great hike! We were late for the long hike to the lake at the top of the mountain so we went on a 4 hour hike instead. Yeoingsil trail and then down Eoimok Trail. Lovely. We took a cab for 25,000 won to Yeoinsil from Ramada Plaza. Taxi home was 25,000 won from Eoimok. Crazy driver!!! but we made it back to the hotel safe.
Good place to have a relaxing walk in a natural forest. It's not a long hike, about an hour, and there are flat trails. Check out the cafe that has nice tea beside the car park.

For someone with bad stamina like me, it would take about 2.5 hours to reach the end of the trail.The tip is, to go there early in the morning, then you can take some leisure time to rest from time to time. When we're going down to trail at about 10p.m., there are lots of people coming up the trail and it is quite packed with people.For person with knees or legs or ankle problems, must be really careful as I fell down several times due to rocky trails at certain places. However, the view along the trail were awesome and it feels really worth it! The warm ramyeon at the shelter was the climax!I went in April 2016. The wind is super strong on top. So make sure you're ready for that. Hotpack, jackets, windbreaker or whichever deems to keep you warm. You may not need them in the beginning of the trail but you might need it in the end of the trail.

For hiking enthusiasts, this is a must do!  The Seongpanak (9.6km) trail has an average hiking time of 4.5 hours and Guaneumsa (8.7km) trail has an average hiking time of 5 hours.  One must reach the Jindallaebat Shelter by 1pm to be permitted an attempt at the Baekrokdam summit.  My husband and I completed the hike in 7hrs 35mins but were perplexed to understand how it took us 5 minutes longer to descend, given that we did not take breaks while descending. Guaneumsa has the reputation of being the roughest trail on the crater, but does live up to its reputation for breathtaking views.  - There was one potable water area on each trail where nature provided delicious water refills.  - Emergency posts appear through the trails, each with its own number, so keep track of the number in case you need assistance, rescue workers can narrow down your location.  - There are incredibly handy signs along the way to pinpoint your progress and identify the level of difficulty along the trail.  Paths are well maintained and varied; wooden, rocky, skree, etc. - If you take the bus to there is no fee for hiking.- Although we did not have cell phones with us, many folks seemed to be talking an walking throughout the trails.- We chose to end at the Guaneumsa trail head because it was the closest in proximity to our hotel.  Cabs are available at the trailhead.
